questions.question:
A $100$ kg object is projected from a point located $6371$ km from the centre of the Earth.

What is the launch velocity of the projectile so that the velocity would never fall below $2000\ \text{m s}^{-1}$?
questions.answer:
The speed is least as $r \to \infty$, where $U \to 0$. By conservation of energy, require $\tfrac12 mv^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{r} = \tfrac12 m(2000)^2$, so
$$v = \sqrt{v_{esc}^2 + 2000^2},\qquad v_{esc} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}} = \sqrt{\frac{2(6.67\times10^{-11})(6.0\times10^{24})}{6.371\times10^{6}}} \approx 11\,208\ \text{m s}^{-1}$$
$$v = \sqrt{11\,208^2 + 2000^2} \approx 11\,386\ \text{m s}^{-1}. \quad\textbf{(C)}$$
(B) is just the escape velocity; (D) wrongly adds the speeds ($11\,208 + 2000$) instead of the kinetic energies.

questions.question: Rachel is driving her car at a constant speed around a curve of fixed radius. Which of the following correctly describes the acceleration of Rachel's car?
questions.answer: At constant speed on a circle of fixed radius the centripetal acceleration $a=\frac{v^2}{r}$ has a constant magnitude, but it always points towards the centre of the circle, so its direction changes continuously (B).

questions.question: While calibrating a spectrometer attached to a telescope, Yatha records a hydrogen line in the Balmer series with a wavelength of 656.28 nm. Later, a star is observed, and the same hydrogen line in its spectrum is recorded as 680 nm. Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.answer: 680 nm is longer than 656.28 nm, so the line is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum (red shift). A red shift means the source is moving away from the observer (C).
options: The star is blue shifted and moving towards us.
The star is red shifted and moving towards us.
The star is red shifted and moving away from us.
The star is blue shifted and is moving away from us.

questions.question: According to Max Planck, which characteristic of an object determined the peak wavelength of radiation emitted by a hot object?
questions.answer: In Planck's black-body model the spectrum and its peak wavelength depend only on the temperature (Wien's law, $\lambda_{\max}T=b$), not on the material or shape (B).
options: The type of material the object is made of.
The type of material and its temperature.
The temperature of the object and its shape.

questions.question: Ravindu is driving his father's SUV around a banked circular track at constant height. Which of the following correctly shows the forces acting on the SUV?
questions.answer: For an ideal banked track the only real forces are the weight $mg$ (down) and the normal reaction force from the track (perpendicular to the surface). The horizontal component of the normal force supplies the centripetal force and the vertical component balances $mg$ (constant height). $F_c$ is the net force, not an additional force, so it must not be drawn separately, and friction is not needed. Diagram A shows only these two forces (A).

questions.question: The individual stars in a single star cluster are plotted on a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, as shown (spectral classes O, B, A, F, G, K, M from left to right). The relative under-representation of O and B type stars is most likely due to:
questions.answer: The diagram shows a main-sequence turn-off with a red-giant branch, which is characteristic of an old cluster. Massive O and B stars burn their hydrogen very rapidly and have short main-sequence lifetimes, so they have already used up their core hydrogen and left the main sequence to become red giants (and later supernovae), leaving the upper main sequence under-populated (C).
options: the cluster being too young for these stars to have formed yet.
too much gas and dust existing between the stars preventing such stars from forming.
these stars having depleted their hydrogen fuel and becoming red giants.
the main sequence stars that formed in the cluster were not sufficiently large.

questions.question: What was Schrödinger's main contribution to the current model of the atom?
questions.answer: Schrödinger developed the wave equation for the electron, which gives the probability distribution of the electron around the nucleus (orbitals) and is a foundation of modern quantum mechanics (C). Diffraction experiments were by Davisson and Germer, and Bohr was the first to apply quantum ideas to the atom.
options: Diffraction experiments verifying the wave properties of electrons.
His work was the basis of the Bohr model of the atom.
His wave equations were very important in the development of modern quantum mechanics.
He was the first to apply quantum ideas to the understanding of the atom.

questions.question: A satellite is in a stable geostationary orbit around the Earth. Which of the options below best shows the satellite's path if the gravitational force on it was somehow removed when it was at point X?
questions.answer: Gravity provides the centripetal force. With no net force, by Newton's first law the satellite continues in a straight line at constant velocity, along the tangent to the orbit at X (A).

questions.question: A reason that the observations from the Geiger–Marsden experiment were unexpected at the time was that:
questions.answer: Before the experiment the accepted model was Thomson's 'plum pudding' model, in which negative electrons are embedded throughout a diffuse positive sphere. This model predicted only small deflections of alpha particles, so the observed large-angle scattering and back-scattering was unexpected (D).
options: atoms were believed to have a positive nucleus.
atoms were thought to be capable of reflecting alpha particles.
electrons were believed to be orbiting the nucleus.
atoms were thought to have the negative charges embedded throughout a continuous positive fluid.

questions.question: Two masses have a gravitational force of 12 N between them. If the distance between them is doubled, what would be the new gravitational force between them?
questions.answer: $F\propto\frac1{r^2}$, so doubling $r$ reduces $F$ by a factor of 4: $\frac{12}{4}=3$ N (A).

questions.question: How much work is done on an electron being accelerated between two charged plates with a voltage drop of 20 V?
The diagram shows a DC electric motor, but when a current flows through the coil, it does not turn. Which of the following is required so that the coil turns?
questions.answer: In the position shown the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the magnetic field, so the forces on the two sides of the coil act along the same line (the coil's axis) and give zero torque ($\tau=nIAB\sin\theta$ with $\theta=0$). The coil is stuck at this 'dead spot'. It must be started from a different position so the torque is non-zero; changing the size or direction of the current or the field strength will not produce a torque in this position (A).
options: The starting point of the coil must be changed.
The magnetic field must be reduced.
The magnitude of the current must be increased.
The direction of the current must be reversed.

questions.question: Stirling observed that a space probe at rest is 40 m long. However, when he sees the space probe travelling in space it is only 32 m long. What was the speed of the space probe relative to Stirling?
questions.answer: Length contraction: $L=L_0\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}$, so $\frac{32}{40}=0.80=\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}$, giving $\frac{v^2}{c^2}=1-0.64=0.36$ and $v=0.60c$ (A).

questions.question: A Physics student got a flat tyre and had to undo the wheel nuts using a wheel wrench. Which of the following shows that they have the poorest understanding possible of how to undo the wheel nuts with a minimum applied force?
questions.answer: Torque is $\tau=r_\perp F=rF\sin\theta$. To minimise the force needed, the force should be applied perpendicular to the wrench ($\sin\theta=1$) and as far from the nut as possible (large $r$), as in D. The poorest understanding combines both mistakes: a small lever arm and an angle that is not $90^\circ$, giving the smallest torque for a given force. This is B.
options: The force should be applied at right angles to the wheel wrench at the smallest distance possible from the wheel nut.
The force should be applied at $45^\circ$ to the wheel wrench at the smallest distance possible from the wheel nut.
The force should be applied at right angles to the wheel wrench at the middle distance along the tyre lever.
The force should be applied at right angles to the wheel wrench at the largest distance from the wheel nut possible.

questions.question: Photons of wavelength $\lambda$ are incident on a metallic surface in a vacuum. The number of photons incident on the surface per second is $n$. No electrons are emitted from the surface. Which of the following actions is more likely to cause electrons to be emitted from the surface?
questions.answer: Emission requires each photon to have energy $hf\ge\phi$. No emission means $hf<\phi$. Increasing the number of photons (intensity) does not help, since each electron absorbs a single photon. Decreasing the wavelength increases the frequency and photon energy, which could exceed the work function (B). Changing to a different metal could help only if the new metal had a lower work function, which is not guaranteed.
options: Decrease the frequency of the incident light.
Decrease the wavelength, $\lambda$, of the incident light.
Increase the number of photons per second, $n$, incident on the surface.
Change to a different metallic surface.

questions.question: Maxwell's equations apply to the:
questions.answer: Maxwell's equations describe light as an electromagnetic wave, predicting its wave behaviour and speed. They do not explain the photoelectric effect, which requires a particle (photon) model (D).
options: particle and wave models of light.

questions.question: A charged particle $q$ enters a uniform magnetic field $B$ at velocity $v$ and follows a circular path of radius $r$. If the magnitude of the magnetic field was doubled and the other variables were kept constant, what would the new radius be?
questions.answer: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: $qvB=\frac{mv^2}{r}$, so $r=\frac{mv}{qB}\propto\frac1B$. Doubling $B$ halves the radius: $r/2$ (B).

questions.question: A conductor connected to an ammeter is moved by a force $F$ through a magnetic field (directed into the page) in the direction shown (to the right). The direction of the conventional current in the conductor and the reason why it must be in this direction is:
questions.answer: Using the right-hand palm rule for a positive charge moving right through a field into the page, the force (and so the conventional current) is up the page. This direction is required by Lenz's law (conservation of energy): the induced current's own magnetic force on the conductor must oppose the motion, so work done by the applied force $F$ is transferred to electrical energy (B).
options: Up the page; the motor effect
Up the page; the law of conservation of energy
Down the page; the law of conservation of energy
No current; there is not a complete circuit

questions.question: Michelson and Morley expected to see a change in the interference pattern in their experiment, yet they obtained a null result. Why did they obtain a null result?
questions.answer: The school's key gives A: the result was consistent with the principle of relativity (no experiment can detect absolute motion through a stationary aether, and the speed of light is the same in all inertial frames), whereas a positive result would have identified a preferred frame. The apparatus was sensitive enough (B is false), the null result was repeatable (C), and the experiment (1887) pre-dated Einstein's postulates (1905) (D).
options: A positive result would violate the principle of relativity.
The Earth's speed through space is too small compared to the speed of light for the experiment to give a significant result.
Any variation in the speed of light could be explained by experimental errors.
Einstein had proven that the speed of light was a constant in a particular medium.

questions.question: Danindu moves a square copper plate at a constant speed through a magnetic field (dots show a field out of the page), as shown. The plate is shown at positions P, Q, R and S. Which of the following best shows the emf induced in the plate?
questions.answer: An emf is induced only while the flux through the plate is changing ($\varepsilon=-\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$). While the plate is entering the field the flux increases at a constant rate (constant emf of one sign); when it is fully inside a uniform field the flux is constant, so the emf is zero; as it leaves the flux decreases at a constant rate, giving a constant emf of the opposite sign; outside the field the emf is zero. Constant-valued sections (not ramps) because the speed is constant. This is graph B (the school's answer).

questions.question: Mars has a mass of $6.39\times10^{23}$ kg and a diameter of $6.679\times10^{6}$ m, and a negligible atmosphere. Calculate the acceleration due to gravity that astronauts would experience on the surface of Mars.

On Mars (surface gravity $3.82\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, radius $3.3395\times10^6$ m, negligible atmosphere) a 1.25 kg food canister is thrown upward at an angle of $25^\circ$ to the horizontal with an initial velocity of $2.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the maximum distance the canister rises above the launch point (and state its maximum distance from the centre of Mars).
questions.answer: Vertically, $u_y=2.5\sin25^\circ=1.0565\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and $v_y=0$ at the top. Taking up as positive with $a=-3.8218\ \text{m s}^{-2}$: $v_y^2=u_y^2+2as$ gives $s=\frac{-u_y^2}{2a}=\frac{-(1.0565)^2}{2(-3.8218)}=0.146$ m. So the canister rises 0.146 m above the launch point, i.e. its maximum distance from the centre of Mars is the radius of Mars (plus the launch height) plus 0.146 m, about $3.34\times10^6$ m. (The school's key gives 0.146 m.)

questions.question: On Mars (surface gravity $3.82\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, negligible atmosphere) a food canister is thrown at an angle of $25^\circ$ to the horizontal with an initial velocity of $2.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from a height of 2 m above level ground. How far does the canister land from where it was thrown (horizontal distance)?

prev.question: On Mars (surface gravity $3.82\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, radius $3.3395\times10^6$ m, negligible atmosphere) a 1.25 kg food canister is thrown upward at an angle of $25^\circ$ to the horizontal with an initial velocity of $2.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the maximum distance the canister rises above the launch point (and state its maximum distance from the centre of Mars).
prev.answer: Vertically, $u_y=2.5\sin25^\circ=1.0565\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and $v_y=0$ at the top. Taking up as positive with $a=-3.8218\ \text{m s}^{-2}$: $v_y^2=u_y^2+2as$ gives $s=\frac{-u_y^2}{2a}=\frac{-(1.0565)^2}{2(-3.8218)}=0.146$ m. So the canister rises 0.146 m above the launch point, i.e. its maximum distance from the centre of Mars is the radius of Mars (plus the launch height) plus 0.146 m, about $3.34\times10^6$ m. (The school's key gives 0.146 m.)

questions.question: Calculate the minimum velocity that astronauts would need to throw a food canister vertically from the surface of Mars (mass $6.39\times10^{23}$ kg, radius $3.3395\times10^6$ m) if it was to just escape Mars' gravitational field.
questions.answer: For escape, the initial kinetic energy equals the energy needed to reach infinity: $\frac12mv^2=\frac{GMm}{r}$, so $v=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\times6.67\times10^{-11}\times6.39\times10^{23}}{3.3395\times10^6}}=5.05\times10^3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (about 5052 m s$^{-1}$).

questions.question: In 1990, the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) was placed in orbit around the Earth. In the diagram (not to scale), Earth and HST are drawn on orbits around the Sun with identical orbital periods. This appears to contradict Kepler's law of periods. Fully explain why it is possible for the HST to orbit the Sun with the same orbital period as the Earth.
questions.answer: Kepler's law of periods, $\frac{r^3}{T^2}=\frac{GM}{4\pi^2}$, relates the period of a body to its orbital radius for bodies orbiting the **same central mass** $M$. The Earth orbits the Sun, so $M$ is the mass of the Sun, whereas the HST orbits the Earth, so $M$ is the mass of the Earth. The diagram is misleading because the HST is not in a separate orbit around the Sun: it orbits the Earth, and the Earth carries it around the Sun, so the HST's period around the Sun is the Earth's period (one year). The Sun's gravitational force on the HST is much weaker than the Earth's at the HST's altitude, so the HST stays bound to Earth and follows it. There is therefore no contradiction with Kepler's law, which applies separately to the HST–Earth and Earth–Sun systems.

questions.question: Protons are accelerated in the Large Hadron Collider to travel at $2.2\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The LHC has a diameter of $8\times10^{3}$ m. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of these protons.

Protons in the Large Hadron Collider (diameter $8\times10^{3}$ m) travel at $2.2\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ around a circular path. Calculate the momentum of a proton at that speed and the force required to keep it on the circular path.
questions.answer: At $2.2\times10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ($v/c=0.0073$) the Lorentz factor is $\gamma\approx1.00003$, so relativistic effects are negligible and $p=mv=1.673\times10^{-27}\times2.2\times10^{6}=3.7\times10^{-21}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$. The path has radius $r=4\times10^3$ m, so the centripetal force is $F=\frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{1.673\times10^{-27}\times(2.2\times10^{6})^2}{4\times10^{3}}=2.0\times10^{-18}$ N. (The school's key gives $2.2\times10^{-18}$ N; recalculating gives $2.0\times10^{-18}$ N.)

questions.question: Assess the validity of the following statement: 'Particle accelerators cannot accelerate particles to any speed beyond the speed of light.'
questions.answer: The statement is valid. According to special relativity the relativistic momentum $p=\gamma m_0v$ and total energy $E=\gamma m_0c^2$ both increase without limit as $v\to c$ because $\gamma=\frac1{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}\to\infty$. Accelerating a particle with mass to $v=c$ would require an infinite amount of energy (and force), which cannot be supplied, so particles can be accelerated ever closer to $c$ but can never reach it, let alone exceed it. This is confirmed in accelerators such as the LHC, where particles gain energy and momentum but their speed only approaches $c$.

questions.question: Two parallel plates are 2.50 mm apart and connected to a power supply which produces a potential difference of 320 V. An electron is at rest at point P between the plates. Calculate the force acting on the electron.
questions.answer: $E=\frac Vd=\frac{320}{2.50\times10^{-3}}=1.28\times10^{5}\ \text{V m}^{-1}$ and $F=qE=1.602\times10^{-19}\times1.28\times10^{5}=2.05\times10^{-14}$ N, directed towards the positive plate.

questions.question: Two parallel plates are 2.50 mm apart and connected to a 320 V supply. An electron is at rest at point P between the plates and experiences a force of $2.05\times10^{-14}$ N. Describe quantitatively the effect of the field on the electron's motion.
questions.answer: The force on the electron is directed towards the positive plate (opposite to the field direction, since the electron is negative). From $F=ma$, $a=\frac{F}{m}=\frac{2.05\times10^{-14}}{9.109\times10^{-31}}=2.25\times10^{16}\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. So the electron accelerates uniformly from rest towards the positive plate at $2.25\times10^{16}\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. (The school's key prints this as $10^{-16}$, a typo.)

questions.question: Describe ONE experiment conducted by a scientist that provided a previously unknown property of the electron.
questions.answer: **Millikan's oil-drop experiment** showed that electric charge is quantised. Oil droplets were sprayed from a nozzle into the space between two charged parallel plates; they became charged by friction with the air as they were sprayed. Millikan adjusted the voltage (electric field $E$) between the plates until a droplet was suspended at rest, so that the upward electric force equalled the downward weight: $qE=mg$, giving $q=\frac{mg}{E}$. He found that the charge on every droplet was an integer multiple of a smallest value, about $1.6\times10^{-19}$ C. This showed that the charge of the electron is a fundamental unit of charge: charge exists only in whole multiples of the electron's charge.

questions.question: A phone charger is plugged into a 240 V AC supply. The transformer in the charger converts this to an output of 6 V DC. The phone draws a 1 A current from the charger when being charged. Determine the current drawn by the charger on the 240 V supply.
questions.answer: For an ideal transformer, $V_pI_p=V_sI_s$, so $I_p=\frac{V_sI_s}{V_p}=\frac{6\times1}{240}=0.025$ A $=2.5\times10^{-2}$ A.

questions.question: Use a labelled diagram to model the structure of the transformer in a phone charger (240 V AC input, 6 V output).
questions.answer: The diagram should show: a closed, laminated soft-iron core (a rectangular loop); a **primary coil** (connected to the 240 V AC supply) wound on one side of the core and a **secondary coil** (connected to the output/load) wound on the other side, each insulated from the core and from one another. Since the output is much lower than the input, the primary coil has many more turns than the secondary coil ($n_p>n_s$): a step-down transformer, with $\frac{V_p}{V_s}=\frac{n_p}{n_s}=\frac{240}{6}=40$. Label the AC supply, primary coil, secondary coil, load and laminated iron core.

questions.question: Explain TWO methods that could maximise the efficiency of a phone charger's transformer.
questions.answer: **1. Laminated core:** build the core from thin sheets of iron separated by insulating material, with the layers parallel to the direction of the magnetic flux. This reduces the size of the eddy currents induced in the core, so less energy is lost as heat, which increases efficiency. **2. Better linkage of flux (soft-iron core and coil winding):** use a soft iron core and wind the primary and secondary coils close together (or over each other with insulation between), so that nearly all the flux produced by the primary passes through the secondary. Reducing flux leakage means more of the input energy is transferred to the secondary coil. (Alternative: use thicker, low-resistance copper wire to reduce resistive $I^2R$ heating in the coils.)

questions.question: A handle of length $L$ is used to rotate a cylinder containing multiple copper windings between two permanent magnets (a simple generator). When the cylinder is rotated, an emf is generated across the copper windings. Describe and explain quantitatively how doubling the handle length ($L$) will change the emf generated in the copper windings in the cylinder if the handle continues to be turned at the same angular velocity.
questions.answer: The emf is given by Faraday's law, $\varepsilon=-N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, where the flux through the coil is $\Phi=BA\cos\theta$ and $\theta=\omega t$. So $\varepsilon_{\max}=NBA\omega$, which depends on the number of turns, the field strength, the coil area and the angular velocity, but not on the length of the handle. The handle and cylinder rotate together, so at the same angular velocity the coil cuts the field lines at the same rate and the emf is **unchanged** (it does not double). A longer handle increases the torque produced by a given applied force (the lever arm, $\tau=r_\perp F$, doubles), so the same turning torque is obtained for half the applied force, but the emf stays the same.

questions.question: Clearly explain the production of absorption spectra by the atmosphere of stars.
questions.answer: The hot, dense photosphere of a star emits a continuous (black-body) spectrum. This light passes through the cooler, less dense gases of the star's outer atmosphere. Atoms in the atmosphere absorb photons whose energy exactly matches the difference between two of their energy levels ($E=hf=E_2-E_1$), raising electrons to higher levels. The atoms then de-excite by re-emitting photons of the same frequency, but in random directions, so far fewer photons of those frequencies continue in the original direction towards the observer. The observed spectrum therefore shows a continuous background crossed by dark absorption lines at the wavelengths characteristic of the elements in the star's atmosphere.

questions.question: Describe clearly how the study of a star's spectrum can give us information about TWO specific features of that star.
questions.answer: **Chemical composition:** the pattern of dark absorption lines in the star's spectrum is unique to each element, so comparing the wavelengths of the lines with known laboratory spectra of elements (e.g. hydrogen's Balmer series) identifies the elements present in the star's atmosphere. **Radial (translational) velocity:** the absorption lines are shifted relative to their laboratory wavelengths by the Doppler effect. A shift to longer wavelengths (red shift) shows the star is moving away from us and a shift to shorter wavelengths (blue shift) shows it is moving towards us; the speed is found from $\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda}=\frac vc$. (Other acceptable features: surface temperature from the peak of the black-body curve using Wien's law $\lambda_{\max}T=b$; rotational velocity from line broadening; gas pressure from line widths.)

questions.question: Outline Hubble's observations and their significance in terms of our understanding of the nature of the universe.
questions.answer: Hubble measured the red shift of the absorption lines in the spectra of other galaxies and found that nearly all galaxies are red-shifted, i.e. moving away from us. He also found that the recession velocity is proportional to the galaxy's distance ($v=H_0d$), so more distant galaxies recede faster. This showed that the universe is expanding, which led to the hypothesis of the Big Bang (everything was once concentrated in a much smaller volume). He also showed that some 'nebulae' were actually separate galaxies far outside the Milky Way, which showed that the universe is far larger than the Milky Way alone.

questions.question: For electricity to be transmitted over large distances between generators and households, transformers are used. Two transmissions take place over the same transmission lines at different times: Transmission A: 28 kV AC; Transmission B: 280 kV AC (the same power is supplied at the start of each). Compare the power losses that occur in transmissions A and B. Include relevant equations and calculations in your response.
questions.answer: The power supplied is $P=VI$, so for the same power the line current is $I=\frac PV$. The power lost in the line (resistance $R$) is $P_{\text{loss}}=I^2R=\left(\frac PV\right)^2R\propto\frac1{V^2}$. Transmission B has a voltage 10 times larger, so its current is 10 times smaller and its loss is $10^2=100$ times smaller: $\frac{P_{\text{loss,A}}}{P_{\text{loss,B}}}=\left(\frac{280}{28}\right)^2=100$. Transmission A loses 100 times as much power in the lines as transmission B.

questions.question: With the aid of a labelled diagram, outline Bohr's model of the atom and state the limitations of the model.
questions.answer: **Bohr's model (diagram: a small central positive nucleus with electrons in circular orbits labelled $E_1$, $E_2$, $E_3$, and an arrow showing a transition with a photon emitted):** electrons orbit the nucleus only in certain allowed orbits (stationary states) with fixed, discrete energies. Electrons in these orbits do not radiate energy. Electrons can jump between orbits by absorbing or emitting a photon with energy equal to the difference between the levels, $\Delta E=E_2-E_1=hf$. **Limitations:** it works well only for hydrogen and hydrogen-like (single electron) atoms and cannot explain the spectra of atoms with more electrons; it cannot explain the relative intensities of spectral lines, the splitting of lines in magnetic fields (Zeeman effect) or fine structure; it gives no reason why orbits are stable (an accelerating charge should radiate according to Maxwell); and it treats the electron as a particle in a definite orbit, which conflicts with the wave nature of the electron and the uncertainty principle (later replaced by Schrödinger's quantum mechanical model).

questions.question: Outline experimental evidence that supported ONE of Bohr's postulates and explain how the experimental evidence provided this support.
questions.answer: **Postulate:** electrons can only exist in orbits with discrete energy levels, and they emit or absorb a photon of energy $\Delta E=hf$ when moving between them. **Evidence:** the line emission spectrum of hydrogen. A discharge tube of hydrogen gas viewed through a spectroscope shows only a few discrete bright lines (the Balmer series: 656.3, 486.1, 434.0, 410.2 nm, ...), not a continuous spectrum. This supports the postulate because if electrons could have any energy a continuous spectrum would be seen; discrete lines show only specific energy differences are allowed. Bohr's model predicts these wavelengths using $\frac1\lambda=R\left(\frac1{n_f^2}-\frac1{n_i^2}\right)$, in agreement with the measured wavelengths.

questions.question: Fully explain the production of torque in the device shown (a simple DC motor: a rectangular coil between the poles of a magnet, with a split-ring commutator and graphite brushes). In your answer, refer to the diagram and include two relevant graphs.
questions.answer: The device is a simple DC motor. When current flows through the coil, each of the two sides of the coil that are perpendicular to the field experiences a force $F=nIlB\sin\theta$ (the motor effect), given by the right-hand palm rule. Because the current flows in opposite directions in the two sides, the forces are equal and opposite, so one side is pushed up and the other down, producing a torque about the axis, $\tau=nIAB\sin\theta$ ($\theta$ is the angle between the coil's plane normal and the field). The graphite brushes press against the split-ring commutator, which reverses the current in the coil every half turn, just as the coil passes the vertical (zero torque) position. This ensures that the torque always acts in the same rotational sense, so the coil continues to rotate in one direction. **Graphs (see image):** (1) without a commutator the torque varies as $\sin\theta$ and reverses direction every half turn, so the coil would just oscillate; (2) with a split-ring commutator the torque is always in the same direction, varying between zero (coil plane perpendicular to the field) and a maximum (coil plane parallel to the field), $\tau\propto|\sin\theta|$.

questions.question: In 1911 Ejnar Hertzsprung and in 1913 Henry Norris Russell independently plotted the luminosity of stars versus their surface temperatures, as shown in the diagram. Identify the predominant nuclear reactions involved in the three groups A, B and C.
questions.answer: **Group A (upper right: giants):** helium fusion by the triple-alpha process (and CNO-cycle hydrogen fusion in a shell around the core). **Group B (lower left: white dwarfs):** no fusion occurs; they are cooling remnants. **Group C (lower main sequence, cool red dwarfs):** the proton–proton chain (hydrogen fusion), not the CNO cycle, since the core temperatures are lower.

questions.question: On a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram of luminosity against surface temperature, with reference to the diagram, outline the stellar evolution of the Sun.
questions.answer: The Sun is currently a main-sequence star (like those in the band running from top-left to bottom-right, near group C but hotter), fusing hydrogen into helium in its core by the proton–proton chain. When the core hydrogen is exhausted the core contracts and heats up, hydrogen fuses in a shell around it, and the outer layers expand and cool: the Sun moves off the main sequence to become a red giant (up and to the right, group A on the diagram), later fusing helium in its core. Finally, since the Sun is not massive enough to fuse heavier elements, the outer layers are shed as a planetary nebula and the remaining core becomes a white dwarf (down and to the left, group B), which slowly cools.

questions.question: What evidence supports the classical wave model of light and what predictions can be made using this model? In your answer, include a relevant diagram and state TWO observations concerning light that are unable to be explained by the classical model.
questions.answer: **Evidence for the classical wave model.** In the 17th century Newton's particle (corpuscular) model competed with Huygens' wave model. The wave model was accepted because of experiments which only waves can explain: Young's double-slit experiment (1801) produced an interference pattern of bright and dark fringes, as the waves from the two slits interfered constructively and destructively; light also shows diffraction around obstacles and through single slits; polarisation (e.g. Malus's law) shows light is a transverse wave; and Foucault's measurement of the speed of light in water showed it to be slower than in air, as the wave model predicts (the particle model predicted faster). Maxwell's theory of electromagnetic waves gave the wave model a full theoretical basis. **Diagram:** a double-slit set-up (see image): monochromatic light incident on two slits, producing bright and dark fringes on a screen. **Predictions:** double-slit fringe spacing $\Delta y=\frac{\lambda L}{d}$ and $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ for gratings and slits; the intensity transmitted through polarisers, $I=I_{\max}\cos^2\theta$; refraction ($n=\frac{c}{v}$) and the speed of light in a medium; and the speed of EM waves, $c=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}$. **Two observations the classical model cannot explain:** (1) *Black-body radiation* – the classical wave model predicts that intensity rises without limit at short wavelengths (the ultraviolet catastrophe), but experiment shows a peak that depends on temperature; Planck explained it by quantised energy $E=hf$. (2) *The photoelectric effect* – electron emission depends on the frequency (not the intensity) of the light, has a threshold frequency, and is instantaneous, which the wave model cannot explain; Einstein explained it with photons, $K_{\max}=hf-\phi$.

questions.question: Which statement about an object undergoing projectile motion is correct? (Point $Y$ is the highest point of the path.)
questions.answer: Launch and impact are at the same height (ground), so the potential energy is the same and, with no air resistance, the kinetic energy is the same (C). At $Y$ the vertical velocity is zero but the horizontal velocity is not, so $E_K\ne0$, and the potential energy at $Y$ is a maximum. Also $E_K$ at launch equals $E_K$ at $Y$ plus $E_P$ at $Y$, not $E_P$ alone.
options: Its kinetic energy at point $Y$ will be zero.
Its potential energy at point $Y$ is a minimum.
Its kinetic energy will be the same at launch as it is at impact.
Its kinetic energy on launch will be the same as the potential energy at point $Y$.

questions.question: Which is a correct expression for the total energy of an orbiting satellite? ($U$ is the gravitational potential energy and $E_K$ the kinetic energy.)
questions.answer: $U=-\frac{GMm}{r}$ and $E_K=\frac12mv^2=\frac{GMm}{2r}$, so $E_K=-\frac U2$ and $E_{total}=E_K+U=-E_K=\frac U2$ (C).

questions.question: Two satellites are in the same Low Earth Orbit. Satellite $X$ has four times the mass of satellite $Y$. What is the ratio of their orbital speeds?
questions.answer: $\frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{GMm}{r^2}$ gives $v=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$, which is independent of the satellite's mass. Same orbit means the same speed, a ratio of $1:1$ (A).

questions.question: Students discuss the best way to increase speed when on a swing in a children's playground. Which statement is correct and supported by physics principles?
questions.answer: Raising the centre of mass at the top of the swing does work, adding gravitational potential energy to the system, which becomes extra kinetic energy as the swing descends. (B is the school's answer. The rope force acts through the pivot, so it provides no torque about it, ruling out C.)
options: Straighten your legs at top of swing to increase speed, as the leg movement adds to available kinetic energy.
At top of swing, straighten your legs and pull on the support ropes, because both actions raise your centre of mass, adding potential energy.
Pull on the support ropes at top of swing to provide a torque around the pivot point where the rope is attached.
At top of swing, straighten your legs and pull on the support ropes, because both use force and therefore increase the centripetal acceleration.

questions.question: The diagram shows an electron which moves with a constant velocity, entering an electric field at a right angle. Which alternative describes the path of the electron in the electric field?
questions.answer: The field points down the page, and the electron is negative, so the force on it is up the page and constant. A constant force perpendicular to the initial velocity gives a parabolic path, up the page (C).
options: A parabolic path down the page
A circular path down the page
A parabolic path up the page
A circular path up the page

questions.question: Which graph could show the relationship between the force between parallel current-carrying conductors and the distance between them?
questions.answer: $\frac Fl=\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$, so $F\propto\frac1d$: a decreasing hyperbola (D).

questions.question: A proton with a velocity of $1.2\times10^{3}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ is fired into a uniform magnetic field of $3.0\times10^{-2}$ T, directed out of the page, as shown. It moves in a vacuum in a semi-circle of radius $r$. Which choice best gives the speed of the proton as it exits the magnetic field?
questions.answer: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and the speed is unchanged: $1.2\times10^3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (B).

questions.question: The arrows in the diagrams represent the motion direction of the magnet or the coil. The speeds are identical in each diagram. Which alternative shows the correct direction of the induced current $I$ in the coil?
questions.answer: By Lenz's law the induced current produces a magnetic field that opposes the change in flux through the coil caused by the relative motion of the magnet and coil. The direction of $I$ is found by working out whether the flux is increasing or decreasing and applying the right-hand grip rule to the coil. Diagram B matches the school's answer (B).

questions.question: Which wave behaviour provided evidence for the transverse nature of light waves?
questions.answer: Only transverse waves can be polarised, so polarisation showed that light waves are transverse (A).

questions.question: Which is the best description of an electromagnetic wave?
questions.answer: An electromagnetic wave consists of electric and magnetic fields oscillating perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation (A).
options: Perpendicular oscillating electric and magnetic fields
Perpendicular constant electric and magnetic fields
Radiating parallel electric and magnetic fields

questions.question: A student set up a model generator and attached a galvanometer across the points $X$ and $Y$ (split-ring commutator). Which graph best shows how the current through the meter changes as the coil is rotated $360^\circ$ from the position shown?
questions.answer: A split-ring commutator reverses the connections every half-turn, so the output current always has the same direction, giving a rectified pattern of positive humps that fall to zero twice per rotation. The school's answer is C.

questions.question: A laser beam goes through two close slits $0.10$ mm apart onto a screen $1.6$ m away from the slits. The distance between maximum at $R$ and minimum at $T$ on the interference pattern is $18$ mm. According to the information in the diagram, what is the wavelength of the incident light used in this experiment?
questions.answer: From the diagram, $R$ (a maximum) and $T$ (a minimum) are $2.5$ fringe spacings apart, so $\Delta x=\frac{18}{2.5}=7.2$ mm. $\lambda=\frac{d\,\Delta x}{L}=\frac{0.10\times10^{-3}\times7.2\times10^{-3}}{1.6}=4.5\times10^{-7}$ m (C).

questions.question: Which statement about the spectra of incandescent and laser lights is correct?
questions.answer: An incandescent (black-body) source emits a continuous spectrum over a wide range, while a laser is essentially monochromatic, with a very narrow range of frequencies (A).
options: Incandescent light has a continuous spectrum, laser light has a spectrum specific to its narrow frequency range.
Laser light has a continuous spectrum, incandescent light has a spectrum concentrated in the yellow region.
Laser light has a very wide spectrum concentrated in the infra-red, incandescent has a very narrow spectrum.
Both laser light and incandescent light have a very narrow spectrum.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most accurate statement regarding limitations of special relativity?
questions.answer: Special relativity applies only to inertial (non-accelerating) frames; accelerating frames and gravity require general relativity (D). It has been tested extensively, applies everywhere, and its effects are measurable (if tiny) at low speeds.
options: It has never been tested due to shortcomings in technology
Its equations only apply to space travel
Its effects can only be measured when objects are travelling close to the speed of light
It only applies to inertial frames of reference

questions.question: A rocket is heading directly towards the surface of the Earth at a constant speed of $0.75c$. Physicists on Earth calculate the time that the rocket will take to reach the surface of Earth as $850$ microseconds. How long does the pilot in the rocket calculate it will take him to reach the surface of Earth?
questions.answer: The Earth observers' time is the dilated time $t$; the pilot measures the proper time $t_0=t\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}=850\sqrt{1-0.75^2}=850\times0.6614=562\ \mu$s (A).

questions.question: A road has a curve of radius $63$ m and is banked at an angle of $12^\circ$. The diagram shows a car approaching the curve in wet, slippery conditions. Assuming that there is no friction, calculate the maximum speed at which the car can safely make the turn.
questions.answer: With no friction, $\tan\theta=\frac{v^2}{rg}$, so $v=\sqrt{rg\tan\theta}=\sqrt{63\times9.8\times\tan12^\circ}=11.45\ \text{m s}^{-1}=41.2\ \text{km h}^{-1}$ (D).

questions.question: A Physics teacher drew two magnetic fields and asked students to explain the difference between the magnetic flux of each field. The two magnetic fields are shown in the diagram. Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.answer: Both regions show the same number of field lines (9), so the same flux $\Phi$. The smaller region has the same flux through a smaller area, so a greater flux density $B=\frac\Phi A$ (D).
options: The two magnetic fields show the same amount of flux, and the smaller magnetic field shows less flux density.
The two magnetic fields show different amounts of flux, and the smaller magnetic field shows less flux density.
The two magnetic fields show different amounts of flux, and the smaller magnetic field shows greater flux density.
The two magnetic fields show the same amount of flux, and the smaller magnetic field shows greater flux density.

questions.question: A light meter measures $150\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ of unpolarised light at a fixed position from a light source. A polarising sheet, $P_1$, is placed at this position with an axis of polarisation $30^\circ$ to the vertical. A second polarising sheet, $P_2$, is placed so that any light that passes through $P_1$ also passes through $P_2$. $P_2$ has an axis of polarisation oriented horizontally. What intensity of light is transmitted through $P_2$?
questions.answer: $P_1$ halves unpolarised light: $I_1=75\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. The angle between $P_1$ ($30^\circ$ to vertical) and $P_2$ (horizontal) is $60^\circ$. Malus's law: $I_2=75\cos^260^\circ=18.75\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ (B).

questions.question: The diagram shows a set-up that uses three rods ($A$–$C$), each carrying a current in the direction indicated by the arrows. What is the magnitude and direction of the force per unit length on rod $C$?
questions.answer: Rod $B$ (4 A, 20 cm away) has current in the same direction as $C$, so attracts it (up): $\frac Fl=\frac{\mu_0 I_BI_C}{2\pi d}=2\times10^{-7}\frac{4\times5}{0.20}=2\times10^{-5}$ N m$^{-1}$ up. Rod $A$ (3 A, 30 cm away) has current opposite to $C$, so repels it (down): $2\times10^{-7}\frac{3\times5}{0.30}=1\times10^{-5}$ N m$^{-1}$ down. Net $=1\times10^{-5}\ \text{N m}^{-1}$ up (B).

questions.question: A conducting rod is rolling horizontally along a metal conducting loop in a magnetic field (into the page), as shown in the diagram. Which row of the table is correct?
questions.answer: The loop's area (flux into the page) is increasing as the rod moves right, so the induced current creates a field out of the page: anticlockwise. By Lenz's law the magnetic force on the rod opposes its motion (to the left), so the rod slows, the emf $\varepsilon=Blv$ falls and the globe dims (A).
options: Force on the rod: to the left; current around the loop: anticlockwise; brightness of the light globe: decreasing
Force on the rod: to the left; current around the loop: clockwise; brightness of the light globe: constant
Force on the rod: to the right; current around the loop: anticlockwise; brightness of the light globe: decreasing
Force on the rod: to the right; current around the loop: clockwise; brightness of the light globe: constant

questions.question: The diagram shows a totem tennis set-up, as viewed from above. A tennis ball is tied to a pole with a cord so that it moves in a clockwise, circular motion around the centre pole. Label the velocity of the ball and the forces acting on it at the point shown in the diagram. Explain your answer.
questions.answer: Sample answer: The ball's velocity is tangent to the circle, in the direction of motion (down the page at the point shown, since the motion is clockwise). The tension in the cord acts towards the centre of the circle, and the weight force acts vertically downwards (into the page when viewed from above). The ball is accelerating towards the centre of the circle, so the net force is the centripetal force, which here is provided by the horizontal component of the tension. Gravity acts downwards, and the vertical component of the tension balances it. The velocity is a tangent to the circle in the direction of the motion of the ball.

questions.question: The ball has a mass of 60.0 g and the cord is 1.80 m long. The ball rotates around the centre pole at an angle of $45^\circ$ to the pole. Calculate the radius of the ball's circular path.
questions.answer: $\sin45^\circ=\frac r{1.80}$, so $r=1.80\sin45^\circ=1.27$ m.

questions.question: The ball has a mass of 60.0 g and rotates around the centre pole at an angle of $45^\circ$ to the pole. Determine the magnitude of the net force acting on the ball at the point shown.
questions.answer: The vertical component of the tension balances the weight: $F_T\cos45^\circ=mg=0.0600\times9.8=0.588$ N. The net (centripetal) force is the horizontal component, $F_{net}=F_T\sin45^\circ=mg\tan45^\circ=0.588$ N $\approx0.59$ N, directed towards the centre. (The school's diagram labels the weight as 1.96 N, which does not match $0.0600$ kg, but its working and answer of $0.59$ N are correct.)

questions.question: In an experiment involving an evacuated gas tube, electrons were accelerated from rest through a voltage of 2400 V, then entered a uniform magnetic field strength of $1.8\times10^{-3}$ T at right angles to the electron beam. Calculate the speed of these electrons upon entering the magnetic field.
questions.answer: The work done by the electric field becomes kinetic energy: $qV=\frac12mv^2$, so $v=\sqrt{\frac{2qV}{m}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\times1.6\times10^{-19}\times2400}{9.1\times10^{-31}}}=2.9\times10^{7}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. (The magnetic field does not change the speed.)

questions.question: In science, observations lead to hypotheses and further experimentation. Robert Millikan conducted experiments to determine the charge on an electron. One of these experiments is shown in the diagram (plates $2.5$ cm apart connected to a $4500$ V supply, with a charged oil drop between them). Explain the observations Millikan made that led to his determination of the charge of an electron.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Millikan observed oil drops falling through the small gap between the plates. When the electric force was equal to the opposing gravitational force, the drop remained in static equilibrium, so $mg=qE$ where $E=\frac Vd$ (here $E=\frac{4500}{0.025}=1.8\times10^5\ \text{V m}^{-1}$). From this he calculated the charge on each drop. He observed that the charge on the oil droplets was always a whole-number multiple of $1.6\times10^{-19}$ C, which is the charge on an electron.

questions.question: The diagram shows a strobe photo of a ball projected into the air. The camera took 7 images per second of the ball. What was the maximum height of the ball above the ground?
questions.answer: From the highest point there are 6 image intervals to the ground, so the fall time is $t=\frac67$ s, with vertical velocity zero at the top. $s=ut+\frac12at^2=0+4.9\left(\frac67\right)^2=3.6$ m. The maximum height is $3.6$ m.

questions.question: The table shows data for three of the moons of Jupiter. On the axes provided, graph relevant data to verify Kepler's Law of Periods. Include a line of best fit.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Plot $r^3$ (vertical axis, $\times10^{26}\ \text{m}^3$) against $T^2$ (horizontal axis, $\times10^{10}\ \text{s}^2$): points $(2.34,1.2)$, $(9.61,4.1)$, $(38.4,14.9)$ with a ruled straight line of best fit through them, passing through the origin, with labelled axes and units.

questions.question: The graph of $r^3$ against $T^2$ for the three moons of Jupiter is a straight line through the origin. Explain how the graph provides evidence for Kepler's law of periods.
questions.answer: Sample answer: From Kepler's law, $\frac{r^3}{T^2}=\frac{GM}{4\pi^2}=$ constant, which is the gradient of the graph. Since the graph has a constant gradient (a straight line through the origin), it shows that Kepler's law of periods holds for these three moons of Jupiter.

questions.question: Using the graph of $r^3$ against $T^2$ (gradient about $\dfrac{8\times10^{26}}{20\times10^{10}}=4\times10^{15}\ \text{m}^3\text{s}^{-2}$), determine the mass of Jupiter.
questions.answer: The gradient is $\frac{GM}{4\pi^2}$, so $M=\frac{4\pi^2}{G}\times\text{gradient}=\frac{4\pi^2\times4\times10^{15}}{6.67\times10^{-11}}=2.4\times10^{27}$ kg.

questions.question: The diagram below shows a simple electric motor. The square coil $WXYZ$ has sides of 4.0 cm and lies completely in the horizontal uniform magnetic field $B$ of strength 2.0 T. The magnetic field is perpendicular to the sides $WZ$ and $XY$. The coil has 20 turns and rotates about the axis shown. The current drawn from the battery is 2.5 A. For the position of the coil in the diagram, determine the torque on the side $WZ$.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Force on $WZ$: $F=nBIl=20\times2.0\times2.5\times0.040=4.0$ N. By the right-hand push rule the force on $WZ$ is upwards. The distance from the axis is half the coil width, $2.0\times10^{-2}$ m, so $\tau=Fd=4.0\times2.0\times10^{-2}=8.0\times10^{-2}$ N m, directed to rotate the coil upwards on the $WZ$ side.

questions.question: Explain the continuous movement of the coil in a simple DC motor in relation to the changing torque acting on the coil.
questions.answer: Sample answer: As the coil rotates, the torque on sides $WZ$ and $XY$ reduces to zero, as the perpendicular distance from the force to the axis of rotation reduces to zero. The momentum of the coil moves it past the vertical position. In the vertical position, the commutator setup changes the direction of the current in the coil and hence the direction of the torque acting on $WZ$ and $XY$ is changed every $180^\circ$, resulting in continuous rotation.

questions.question: Using a mass spectrometer, some students did an experiment to determine the relationship between the charge on a particle and its radius of curvature in a magnetic field. The diagram shows the path of only two of the six charged particles observed. Their results: charge (electronic charges) 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 gave radii of curvature ($\times10^{-11}$ m) of 6.1, 2.9, 2.1, 1.5, 1.2, 0.9. The students plotted their results (radius against number of charges, a smooth falling curve) and concluded that the radius of curvature of a charge in a magnetic field is inversely proportional to the magnitude of the charge. Evaluate their conclusion and identify any problems with their method.
questions.answer: Sample answer: The conclusion is invalid. A conclusion cannot be made because the graph is not a straight line, so their conclusion cannot be based on a graph plotting radius against charge (they would need to plot $r$ against $\frac1q$ to test for inverse proportionality). Also, the experiment description does not have the necessary controlled variables stated: the mass and velocity of the charged particles will affect the radius of curvature, as well as the charge. Centripetal force: $\frac{mv^2}{r}=Bqv$, so $r=\frac{mv}{B}\times\frac1q$. This shows that radius is inversely proportional to charge only if mass and velocity are constant, as well as the magnetic field.

questions.question: The rest life, or proper lifetime, of a meson is $2.5\times10^{-8}$ s. An observer measures the distance travelled by a meson moving at $2.95\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in the laboratory. Compare the expected distance travelled by the meson in the absence of time dilation with the distance that would be measured by the observer.
questions.answer: Time in the observer's frame: $t=\frac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}}=\frac{2.5\times10^{-8}}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{2.95\times10^8}{3.0\times10^8}\right)^2}}=1.37\times10^{-7}$ s. The observer measures $s=vt=2.95\times10^8\times1.37\times10^{-7}=40.4$ m (with time dilation). Without time dilation, $s=vt=2.95\times10^8\times2.5\times10^{-8}=7.38$ m. So the observer measures about $5.5$ times the distance expected without time dilation.

questions.question: A spacecraft of mass 79 000 kg is moving at $0.3c$. Compare the momentum of the spacecraft measured by the spacecraft's pilot with the momentum measured by an external observer, and explain why objects cannot accelerate to the speed of light.
questions.answer: The pilot is inside the spacecraft, so would assume their momentum to be 0 kg m s$^{-1}$. For the external observer, $p_v=\frac{m_0v}{\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}}=\frac{79000\times0.3\times3.0\times10^8}{\sqrt{1-0.3^2}}=7.45\times10^{12}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$ (about $7\times10^{12}$). As the speed approaches $c$, the momentum (or relativistic mass) approaches infinity, so an infinite amount of energy would be needed to reach the speed of light, so an object with mass cannot accelerate to the speed of light.

questions.question: The diagram represents an important experiment done by a group of scientists in 1907 (alpha particles from a radium source striking gold foil, with a fluorescent screen around it). Outline the background to the experiment, its results and the proposed model of the atom based on the experimental results.
questions.answer: Sample answer: This experiment, eventually known as the Rutherford alpha particle scattering experiment, was done by two of Rutherford's postgraduate students, Geiger and Marsden. It had been shown that alpha particles were deflected when passing through very thin gold foil, and it was not understood how this occurred based on Thomson's plum pudding model of the atom, a random arrangement of positive and negative charge. Rutherford expected that the alpha particles would pass through the gold foil with very small deflections. Most of the alpha particles were observed to pass straight through the foil or to be scattered only one or two degrees. The surprising result was that a few alpha particles were observed to be scattered at larger angles and a very few were reflected almost straight back. Rutherford proposed that the force causing the large deflections and repulsion of the positively charged alpha particles could only be caused by a positively charged small object with concentrated mass in the centre of the gold atoms. He also proposed that this centre, called the nucleus, was surrounded by a much larger region of mainly empty space and circling electrons, too small to cause the occasional deflections of the alpha particles. Rutherford's new model of the atom was able to explain the experimental results of the alpha particle scattering experiments.

questions.question: A student sets up an aluminium disc which is able to rotate in the vertical plane. The axle of the disc has a pulley wheel turned by a motor in series with an ammeter, battery and switch. A clamp with a horseshoe magnet can be attached so that a horizontal magnetic field passes through one part of the disc. The student observes the current and the speed of disc rotation, before and after the magnet is attached with its magnetic field passing through the disc. When the magnet is in place, the current through the ammeter is more and the speed of rotation of the disc is less. By applying Lenz's Law, explain each observation.
questions.answer: Sample answer: When a motor is switched on, the motion of the motor's rotating coil in its magnetic field will induce a back emf in the coil according to Faraday's law of induction. The direction of this emf must be such that it opposes the motion of the coil (Lenz's law) and therefore does not contravene the law of conservation of energy. The net voltage decreases, and therefore the current through the motor is less. The back emf is proportional to the rotational speed of the motor coil.\n\nWhen the horseshoe magnet surrounds part of the aluminium disc, eddy currents are set up in the disc because the disc is a conductor moving in a magnetic field (changing flux). By Lenz's law, the direction of the currents will be such as to oppose the magnetic field and oppose the motion of the disc, which is known as the braking effect, reducing the rotational speed of the disc and the motor coil. Consequently the back emf is also less, so the net emf (supply emf minus back emf) is greater, resulting in the greater current seen on the ammeter.

questions.question: For electricity to be transmitted over the large distances between generators and households, transformers are used. Two transmissions take place over the same transmission lines. In transmission A, energy is transmitted at 28 kV AC. In transmission B, the same amount of energy is transmitted at 280 kV AC. Compare the power losses that occur in transmissions A and B. Include relevant equations and calculations in your response.
questions.answer: Sample answer: $P=VI$ so for the same power the current is inversely proportional to the voltage. The voltage in B is 10 times greater than in A, so the current in A must be ten times that in B. $P_{loss}=I^2R$: with the same line resistance $R$, $P_{loss,B}=\left(\frac1{10}\right)^2P_{loss,A}$, so transmission B loses $\frac1{100}$ of the power lost in A (A loses 100 times more). Less energy is wasted as heat in the lines at the higher voltage, in line with conservation of energy.

questions.question: In the 1840s, French physicist Hippolyte Fizeau performed an experiment to measure the speed of light. He shone an intense light source at a mirror 8 km away and broke up the light beam with a rotating cogwheel. He adjusted the speed of rotation of the wheel until the reflected light beam could no longer be seen returning through the gaps in the cogwheel. The diagram shows a similar experiment. The cogwheel has 50 teeth and 50 gaps of the same width. Explain why specific speeds of rotation of the cogwheel will completely block the returning light. Support your answer with calculations.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Light travels at $3.00\times10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, so for an 8 km journey to the mirror and 8 km back the time taken is $t=\frac{2\times8000}{3.00\times10^8}=5.33\times10^{-5}$ s. If the wheel is stationary, light travelling through a gap will return completely through the gap, but if the wheel is rotating, a tooth will begin to block the returning light. If a tooth moves exactly the width of a gap in the time it takes the light to return, it will completely block the light. To completely block the light, the tooth must move into the path of a gap in this time. Since there are 50 teeth and 50 gaps, the wheel will have rotated $\frac1{100}$th of a rotation, which is $\frac{2\pi}{100}$ radians. The rotational speed is $\omega=\frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}=\frac{2\pi/100}{5.33\times10^{-5}}=1180\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$. Spinning the cogwheel at 3, 5 and 7 times this rate (any odd multiple) would also completely block the returning light, as the light will be blocked by subsequent teeth.

questions.question: A communications company launched a satellite of mass 250 kg. The satellite is in an orbit with an altitude of 27 129 km above the Earth. Calculate the gravitational potential energy of the satellite and its escape velocity. In your response, explain what the term 'escape velocity' means.
questions.answer: The orbital radius is $r=27\,129\text{ km}+6371\text{ km}\approx3.35\times10^7$ m. $U=-\frac{GMm}{r}=-\frac{6.67\times10^{-11}\times6.0\times10^{24}\times250}{3.35\times10^7}=-2.99\times10^9$ J. The escape velocity is the minimum speed that the satellite requires to escape Earth's gravitational field; this occurs when the satellite's kinetic energy is equal to the magnitude of the gravitational potential energy: $\frac12mv^2=|U|$, so $v=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}}=4888\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (about $4.9$ km s$^{-1}$).

questions.question: In an experiment, students used a light source that emitted a wide range of frequencies. They used filters so that only specific frequencies could fall onto a photoelectric plate. Most of the filters produced frequencies which did not cause emission. Julie says that if the intensities of these frequencies were increased, emission will occur. They experimented with this variable and found that emission still did not occur. Explain the student's observations and how they provide evidence for the nature of light.
questions.answer:
Sample answer: This result can only be explained if light waves are made up of particles, packets of wave energy called photons. The term 'intensity', when applied to electromagnetic radiations, refers to the number of photons in a beam; it does not refer to an increase in the energy of each photon. That is, increasing intensity means more photons, but each has the same energy.

For the photoelectric emission of electrons, the electrons must receive an amount of energy known as the work function of the material, to enable the electron to be emitted. One photon has to have greater energy than the work function for emission to occur ($K_{max}=hf-\phi$, with $E=hf$), so below the threshold frequency no emission occurs, which would explain why increasing the intensity did not result in emission, as Julie predicted.

If the light photons were waves, then the electrons of the emitter would be subjected to a continuous supply of energy and eventually, if the intensity is increased, enough would be absorbed to cause emission at any frequency. The fact that this does not happen means that these observations provide evidence for the particle nature of light. Experiments show that light does exhibit wave behaviour and is described as having a dual nature.

questions.question: In science, there is a close link between developments in technology and developments in knowledge and understanding. Evaluate this statement with reference to the cathode ray debate and Thomson's discovery of the electron.
questions.answer: Sample answer: The statement is well supported. Developments in technology enabled new observations that changed understanding of the nature of cathode rays. High voltage supplies (e.g. induction coils) connected to cathode and anode in evacuated Crookes tubes (vacuum technology) produced cathode rays. Modified tubes, such as the Maltese cross and paddle-wheel tubes, showed that the rays travel in straight lines and carry momentum (supporting the particle view), while a thin gold foil or fluorescent screen allowed the rays to be observed. Electromagnets and oppositely charged electric plates were used to deflect the beam, and Thomson's experiment, using both fields to balance the deflections, determined the charge-to-mass ratio $\\frac{q}{m}$ of the particles, showing that they were negatively charged and much smaller than atoms, so a new subatomic particle, the electron, had been discovered. Each technological advance (better vacuum pumps, fluorescent screens, field plates and electromagnets) therefore supplied the evidence that resolved the debate between the wave (aether) and particle models of cathode rays and led to the development of knowledge about atomic structure.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about nuclear radiation is true?
questions.answer: Alpha particles are the most massive and most highly charged, so they interact most strongly with matter: they are the most ionising (and least penetrating), then beta, then gamma (D). Beta particles, having a much larger charge-to-mass ratio, are deflected more than alpha particles by electric and magnetic fields, so A and B are false, and C has the penetrating order reversed.
options: Alpha particles are deflected most by a magnetic field, then beta, then gamma.
Alpha particles are deflected most by an electric field, then beta, then gamma.
Alpha particles have the highest penetrating power, then beta, then gamma.
Alpha particles have the highest ionising ability, then beta, then gamma.

questions.question: The electromagnetic radiation emitted by a blackbody peaks at a wavelength of 345 nm. What is the temperature of the blackbody?
questions.answer: Wien's law: $T=\dfrac{b}{\lambda_{\max}}=\dfrac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{345\times10^{-9}}=8.40\times10^{3}$ K (C).

questions.question: According to Maxwell's classical theory of electromagnetism, which of the following statements is **incorrect**?
questions.answer: In an electromagnetic wave the oscillating electric and magnetic fields induce each other, are perpendicular to each other and oscillate **in phase**. So the incorrect statement is C.
options: An oscillating electric field induces an oscillating magnetic field.
An oscillating magnetic field induces an oscillating electric field.
Electric and magnetic fields oscillate out of phase with each other.
Electromagnetic waves consist of electric and magnetic fields oscillating at right angles to each other.

questions.question: When monochromatic light, above a threshold frequency, is incident on a metallic surface, electrons are emitted from the surface. Which changes will result in electrons of greater kinetic energy being emitted from the surface?
questions.answer: $K_{\max}=hf-\phi$, so the kinetic energy increases if the frequency increases or the work function decreases. Intensity only changes the number of photons (and so the number of electrons), not their energy. Only B has frequency increasing and work function decreasing.
options: Frequency: decrease; intensity: increase; work function: decrease
Frequency: increase; intensity: increase; work function: decrease
Frequency: decrease; intensity: decrease; work function: increase
Frequency: increase; intensity: decrease; work function: increase

questions.question: A satellite in a circular orbit at position X (original orbit shown as a solid line) fires its thrusters briefly, once. This has the effect of reducing its orbital speed. Which of the following shows a possible final orbit (dotted line) for the satellite?
questions.answer: Reducing the speed at X reduces the satellite's total energy, so it can no longer stay in the circular orbit and falls inwards. The new orbit must still pass through X (where the burn happened), with X now the furthest point (apogee) of a smaller elliptical orbit. Only A shows an ellipse inside the original orbit touching it at X.

questions.question: What is the wavelength of an electron travelling at $0.01c$?
questions.answer: $v=0.01\times3.00\times10^8=3.0\times10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (non-relativistic). $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv}=\dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}}{9.109\times10^{-31}\times3.0\times10^{6}}=2.4\times10^{-10}$ m (B).

questions.question: A person pulls on a rope attached to the top of a 5.0 m flagpole with a tension force of 350 N. The rope is 7.2 m long and makes an angle of $51^\circ$ with the flagpole ($39^\circ$ with the horizontal), as shown. What is the magnitude of the torque the person exerts on the flagpole, which is attached to the ground at its base?
questions.answer: Torque about the base: $\tau=rF\sin\theta$, where $r=5.0$ m is the distance from the base to where the force acts (the top of the pole) and $\theta=51^\circ$ is the angle between the pole ($r$) and the rope (the force). So $\tau=5.0\times350\sin51^\circ$ N m (D). The rope length 7.2 m is irrelevant.

questions.question:
Consider the following two statements.

**Statement A:** In the Schrödinger model of the atom, the wavefunction can be used to compute the probability of finding the electron at a particular position.

**Statement B:** Modelling electrons as standing matter waves according to de Broglie's hypothesis is consistent with the postulates of Bohr's model.

Which of the above statements is correct?
questions.answer: A is correct: the square of the wavefunction gives the probability of finding the electron at a position. B is correct: fitting a whole number of de Broglie wavelengths around an orbit, $2\pi r=n\lambda=\dfrac{nh}{mv}$, gives $mvr=\dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$, exactly Bohr's quantised angular momentum postulate, and a standing wave does not radiate, consistent with Bohr's stationary states. So both (C).
options: Both statement A and statement B.
Neither statement A nor statement B.

questions.question:
Calcite is a crystal which produces two images of an object when viewed from above. This phenomenon (double refraction) occurs because calcite has a different refractive index for different polarisations of light.

Double refraction in calcite played an important role in the debate between Newton and Huygens over the nature of light. Newton explained it by hypothesising that light particles had "sides" and the two types of light particles were separated by the crystal. Huygens, who assumed light was a wave like sound, was unable to explain this phenomenon with his model.

Newton could also explain colour in his model by proposing that different colours corresponded to different sized particles, whereas Huygens' original model had no explanation for colour.

How did the wave model of light change from Huygens' original model so that it could successfully explain the phenomena of polarisation and colour?
questions.answer: Only transverse waves can be polarised (a longitudinal wave like sound has no direction of oscillation across the direction of travel), so the new model treated light as a **transverse** wave. Colour was explained by the **wavelength** (frequency) of the wave; amplitude determines intensity, not colour. (B)
options: Type of wave: longitudinal; origin of colour: wavelength
Type of wave: transverse; origin of colour: wavelength
Type of wave: longitudinal; origin of colour: amplitude
Type of wave: transverse; origin of colour: amplitude

questions.question: A student set up Crookes tubes to investigate the nature of cathode rays. Which of the following matches the contents of the tube with the conclusion made in Crookes' time about the nature of cathode rays?
questions.answer: A small paddle wheel placed in the path of the cathode rays was made to rotate, which was interpreted as the rays carrying momentum (i.e. being particles with mass) (C). The Maltese cross tube showed a sharp shadow, i.e. that cathode rays travel in straight lines, not reflection or diffraction.
options: Paddle wheel: cathode rays have a high velocity.
Maltese cross: cathode rays reflect according to the law of reflection.
Paddle wheel: cathode rays have momentum.
Maltese cross: cathode rays can diffract.

questions.question:
A person (X) on a spacecraft is flying at a speed of $0.8c$ directly away from Earth towards a space port. An observer (Y) located on the space port is at rest with respect to an observer (Z) on Earth.

Person X switches on a light. The flash is then detected by a sensor towards the rear of the spacecraft (on the Earth side of X), as shown.

Which of the following is correct when comparing the time taken for the pulse to reach the sensor according to observers X, Y and Z?
questions.answer:
Y and Z are in the same inertial frame, so they must measure the same time, which rules out B and D.

In X's frame the sensor is a distance $L$ away and at rest, so $t_X=\dfrac{L}{c}$.

In the Earth/space-port frame the light travels backwards at $c$ (second postulate) while the sensor moves forwards towards it at $0.8c$, and the separation is length-contracted to $L\sqrt{1-0.8^2}=0.6L$. So $t_{Y}=t_Z=\dfrac{0.6L}{c+0.8c}=\dfrac{L}{3c}$, which is less than $t_X$.

So both Y and Z measure a shorter time than X (A). (Time dilation alone does not apply because the emission and detection happen at different places in X's frame.)
options: Z: less than X; Y: less than X
Z: more than X; Y: less than X
Z: more than X; Y: more than X
Z: less than X; Y: more than X

questions.question: The graph shows gravitational field strength as a function of distance from the centre of Mars. Using information on the graph, determine which of the following is closest to the mass of Mars.
questions.answer: Read a point from the graph, e.g. $g=10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ at $r=2\times10^6$ m. From $g=\dfrac{GM}{r^2}$: $M=\dfrac{gr^2}{G}=\dfrac{10\times(2\times10^6)^2}{6.67\times10^{-11}}=6\times10^{23}$ kg (C).

questions.question: An ideal transformer is used to convert 240 V AC to 12 V AC. A small electric motor draws a current of 2.0 A from the secondary coil of the transformer. Which row shows the correct number of turns and current in the primary coil if the secondary coil has 50 turns?
questions.answer: $N_p=N_s\dfrac{V_p}{V_s}=50\times\dfrac{240}{12}=1000$ turns. $I_p=\dfrac{V_sI_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{12\times2.0}{240}=0.1$ A (B).

questions.question: A very long straight wire carries a DC current $I$. A rectangular metallic wire loop moves with velocity $v$ in the same plane as the wire, in three different ways (I) directly away from the wire, (II) diagonally away from the wire and (III) parallel to the wire, as shown (top view). In which cases will the coil experience an induced current?
questions.answer: The magnetic field of the wire decreases with distance from the wire, $B\propto\dfrac{1}{r}$. In I and II the loop moves (or has a component of velocity) away from the wire, so the flux through it decreases and, by Faraday's law, an emf and current are induced. In III the loop stays the same distance from the wire, so the flux does not change and no current is induced. (A)

questions.question: A simple model of a current balance is assembled as shown. When current $I$ flows through the setup, the wire frame is balanced (the torque from the weights on one side of the pivot balances the torque from the magnetic force on the end of the frame on the other side). If the strength of the magnetic field $B$ is halved, which of the following changes to the setup could ensure that the wire frame remains balanced?
questions.answer: Halving $B$ halves the magnetic force $F=BIl$ and so halves its torque. To restore balance, either the torque of the magnetic force must increase or the torque of the weights must decrease. Shifting the pivot towards the weights reduces the lever arm of the weights and increases the lever arm of the magnetic force, so balance can be restored (C). Doubling the weights or halving the current makes it worse, and reversing the current reverses the magnetic force.
options: doubling the mass of the weights
reversing the direction of the current
shifting the pivot in the direction of the weights
reducing the magnitude of the current $I$ by half

questions.question: A 1000 kg satellite is to be moved from a circular low-Earth orbit with a radius of 6800 km to a geostationary orbit at a radius of 42 000 km. What is the minimum energy that must be supplied to insert the satellite into the new orbit?
questions.answer:
Total orbital energy $E=-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$, so
$$\Delta E=\frac{GMm}{2}\left(\frac{1}{r_1}-\frac{1}{r_2}\right)=\frac{6.67\times10^{-11}\times6.0\times10^{24}\times1000}{2}\left(\frac{1}{6.8\times10^{6}}-\frac{1}{4.2\times10^{7}}\right)=2.5\times10^{10}\ \text{J}\ \text{(A)}.$$

questions.question: Light with an intensity $I_0$, which is polarised in a direction $\theta$ to the vertical, passes through a polarising filter with a vertical polarising axis. Which of the following is a possible combination of $I_0$ and $\theta$ that could produce transmitted light with an intensity of $15\ \text{W m}^{-2}$?
questions.answer: Malus' law: $I=I_0\cos^2\theta$. Checking: $20\cos^2 30^\circ=20\times0.75=15\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ (B). (The others give 5, 7.5 and 22.5 W m$^{-2}$.)

questions.question: Three parallel current-carrying wires A, B and C are placed perpendicular to the plane of the paper at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side $a$ metres, with A at the top and B and C at the bottom. A carries current into the page and B and C carry current out of the page; all three currents are equal, $I$. Which shows the correct magnitude and direction of the net force per unit length acting on wire A?
questions.answer:
A's current is antiparallel to both B's and C's, so A is repelled by each. Each force has magnitude $\dfrac{F}{l}=\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\dfrac{I^2}{a}$, directed along BA and CA away from B and C, i.e. at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal. The horizontal components cancel and the vertical components add:
$$\frac{F_{net}}{l}=2\times\frac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi a}\sin60^\circ=\frac{\mu_0}{2\pi a}\sqrt3\,I^2,\ \text{upwards (B).}$$

questions.question: The first four lines of the Balmer series for the hydrogen emission spectrum lie in the visible spectrum (400–700 nm). These involve transitions from higher states into the $n=2$ state. The Lyman series involves transitions from higher states into the $n=1$ state, the Paschen series transitions into the $n=3$ state and the Brackett series transitions into the $n=4$ state, as shown in the diagram. What is the wavelength of the shortest infra-red line in the hydrogen spectrum?
questions.answer:
The Lyman series is ultraviolet and the Balmer series is visible/near-UV, so the infra-red lines are the Paschen series and beyond. The shortest IR wavelength is the highest-energy Paschen transition, $n=\infty\to3$:
