Potential energy increases; kinetic energy decreases

questions.question: Which diagram best shows diffraction of plane wavefronts at a single slit?
questions.answer: Diffraction does not change the wavelength, so the wavefronts remain equally spaced after the slit. In B and D the spacing of the wavefronts near the slit is inconsistent with the incident wavelength. For a slit a few wavelengths wide, the wavefronts stay nearly plane in the centre and curve (spread) at the edges, as in A. In C the wavefronts are shown as perfect semicircles, which would only be right for a slit about one wavelength wide, not the wider slit drawn.

questions.question: The diagram shows two lines of equipotential in a region of a uniform electric field. Line $X$ has a potential of $+50$ V and line $Y$ has a potential of $+100$ V. The distance between $X$ and $Y$ is $2.0$ cm. Which one of the following correctly gives the direction of the electric field and its strength?
questions.answer: The electric field points from high to low potential, i.e. from $Y$ to $X$. Its strength is $E=\frac{\Delta V}{d}=\frac{50\ \text{V}}{2.0\ \text{cm}}=25$ V cm$^{-1}$ (C).

questions.question: Two satellites of equal mass, $S_1$ and $S_2$, orbit the Earth. $S_1$ is orbiting at a distance $r$ from the Earth's centre at speed $v$. $S_2$ orbits at a distance $2r$ from the Earth's centre at speed $\dfrac v{\sqrt2}$. The ratio of the centripetal force on $S_1$ to the centripetal force on $S_2$ is
questions.answer: $F=\frac{mv^2}r$. For $S_1$: $\frac{mv^2}r$. For $S_2$: $\frac{m(v^2/2)}{2r}=\frac{mv^2}{4r}$. The ratio is $4$ (C). (Consistent with $F\propto\frac1{r^2}$.)

questions.question: Which one of the following is a correct definition of electric potential difference between two points?
questions.answer: Potential difference $V=\frac Wq$ is the work done per unit charge moving a small positive test charge between the two points (D).
options: The power to move a small positive charge between the two points.
The work done to move a small positive charge between the two points.
The power per unit charge to move a small positive charge between the two points.
The work done per unit charge to move a small positive charge between the two points.

questions.question: The acceleration of free fall of a small sphere of mass $5.0\times10^{-3}$ kg when close to the surface of Jupiter is $25$ m s$^{-2}$. The gravitational field strength at the surface of Jupiter is
questions.answer: Gravitational field strength is the force per unit mass, $g=\frac Fm$, which equals the acceleration of free fall: $25$ N kg$^{-1}$ (C). The mass of the sphere does not matter.

questions.question: The waves from two light sources meet at a point. Which condition is essential for interference to be observed?
questions.answer: A stable interference pattern requires coherent sources, i.e. a constant phase difference (which also requires the same frequency) (A). Equal amplitudes only affect the contrast.
options: Constant phase difference between the waves

questions.question: The escape speed of an object of mass $m$ from a planet of mass $M$ and radius $r$ depends on the gravitational constant and
questions.answer: $\frac12mv^2=\frac{GMm}r$ gives $v_{esc}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}r}$. The mass $m$ of the object cancels, so it depends only on $G$, $M$ and $r$ (A).

questions.question: Explain the term black-body radiation.
questions.answer: Black-body radiation is the electromagnetic radiation emitted by a perfect emitter (a perfect absorber), whose spectrum depends only on its temperature.

questions.question: The diagram is a sketch graph of the black-body radiation spectrum of a certain star, with intensity on the vertical axis. Label the $x$-axis of the graph.
questions.answer: The $x$-axis is wavelength $\lambda$ (e.g. in nm or $\mu$m).

questions.question: On the graph, sketch the black-body radiation spectrum of a star that has a lower surface temperature and lower apparent brightness than this star.
questions.answer: A curve with the same general shape, lower intensity at every wavelength, and with its peak shifted to a longer wavelength (Wien's law).

questions.question: The star Betelgeuse in the Orion constellation emits black-body radiation that has a maximum intensity at a wavelength of $0.97\ \mu$m. Deduce that the surface temperature of Betelgeuse is about $3000$ K.
questions.answer: Wien's law: $\lambda_{max}T=b=2.90\times10^{-3}$ m K. $T=\frac{2.90\times10^{-3}}{9.7\times10^{-7}}=2990\ \text{K}\approx3000$ K.

questions.question: State what is meant by polarised light.
questions.answer: Light in which the electric field vibrations are always (or predominantly) in the same plane (direction).

questions.question: Polarised light of intensity $I_0$ is incident on an analyser. The transmission axis of the analyser makes an angle $\theta$ with the direction of the electric field of the light. Calculate, in terms of $I_0$, the intensity of light transmitted through the analyser when $\theta=60^\circ$.
questions.answer: Malus' law: $I=I_0\cos^2\theta=I_0\cos^260^\circ=\frac{I_0}4$.

questions.question: On the axes provided, sketch a graph to show the variation with angle $\theta$ of the intensity of the transmitted light, for $\theta$ from $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$.
questions.answer: A $\cos^2\theta$ curve: maximum $I_0$ at $\theta=0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, touching zero at $\theta=90^\circ$.

prev.question: Polarised light of intensity $I_0$ is incident on an analyser. The transmission axis of the analyser makes an angle $\theta$ with the direction of the electric field of the light. Calculate, in terms of $I_0$, the intensity of light transmitted through the analyser when $\theta=60^\circ$.
prev.answer: Malus' law: $I=I_0\cos^2\theta=I_0\cos^260^\circ=\frac{I_0}4$.

questions.question: Outline how polarising sunglasses reduce glare from a reflecting surface.
questions.answer: Light reflected from a horizontal surface (water, road) is partially polarised, mostly in the horizontal plane. Polarising sunglasses have their transmission axis vertical (at $90^\circ$ to the plane of polarisation of the reflected light), so most of the reflected (glare) light is blocked, reducing its intensity.

questions.question: Light of wavelength $590$ nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating with $6.0\times10^5$ lines per metre. Determine the total number of orders (both sides) of diffracted light, including the zero order, that can be observed.
questions.answer: Slit spacing $d=\frac1{6.0\times10^5}=1.67\times10^{-6}$ m. From $d\sin\theta=m\lambda$, the maximum order occurs when $\sin\theta\le1$: $m\le\frac d\lambda=\frac{1.67\times10^{-6}}{590\times10^{-9}}=2.8$. So the maximum order is $m=2$. The orders observed are $0,\pm1,\pm2$: a total of $5$ orders.

questions.question: The incident light is replaced by a beam of light consisting of two wavelengths, $590$ nm and $589$ nm. State two observable differences between a first order spectrum and a second order spectrum of the diffracted light.
questions.answer: (1) The first order is brighter (more intense) than the second order. (2) The second order is more widely dispersed, so the two wavelengths (lines) are more likely to be seen as separate lines in the second order (and the second order lies at a larger angle).

questions.question: A satellite goes round a planet at constant speed. Explain why, although its speed is constant, it is accelerating.
questions.answer: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a vector. The direction of the satellite's motion is continually changing, so its velocity changes, i.e. it accelerates (centripetally, towards the centre of the planet).

questions.question: A marble rolls down a track from end $A$, which is $0.80$ m above the ground; the bottom part of the track is a loop of diameter $0.35$ m ($B$ is the lowest point and $C$ the highest). The mass of the marble is $0.050$ kg. Friction and the kinetic energy of rotation can be ignored. Consider the marble when it is at point $C$. On the diagram, draw an arrow to show the direction of the resultant force acting on the marble.
questions.answer: The resultant (net) force points vertically downwards, towards the centre of the loop, since at the top of the loop the centre is directly below $C$.

questions.question: At the top ($C$) of the loop, state the names of the two forces acting on the marble.
questions.answer: The weight (force of gravity) and the normal (reaction) force from the track.

prev.question: A marble rolls down a track from end $A$, which is $0.80$ m above the ground; the bottom part of the track is a loop of diameter $0.35$ m ($B$ is the lowest point and $C$ the highest). The mass of the marble is $0.050$ kg. Friction and the kinetic energy of rotation can be ignored. Consider the marble when it is at point $C$. prev.answer: The resultant (net) force points vertically downwards, towards the centre of the loop, since at the top of the loop the centre is directly below $C$.

questions.question: Deduce that the speed of the marble at $C$ is approximately $3.0$ m s$^{-1}$.
questions.answer: By conservation of energy, the loss in gravitational potential energy from $A$ to $C$ equals the gain in kinetic energy: $mg(0.80-0.35)=\frac12mv^2$. So $v=\sqrt{2\times9.8\times0.45}=\sqrt{8.82}=2.97\approx3.0$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.question: Determine the resultant force acting on the marble at $C$ and hence determine the reaction force of the track on the marble. (Take $v\approx3.0$ m s$^{-1}$, radius $=0.175$ m.)
questions.answer: The resultant force is the centripetal force $F_{net}=\frac{mv^2}r=\frac{0.050\times3.0^2}{0.175}=2.6$ N (downwards). At the top, the weight and the normal force both point downwards: $F_{net}=mg+N$, so $N=\frac{mv^2}r-mg=2.6-0.050\times9.8=2.6-0.49\approx2.1$ N (downwards, from the track on the marble). (Using the unrounded $v^2=8.82$ gives $F_{net}=2.5$ N and $N=2.0$ N.)

questions.question: A stone is thrown from the top of a cliff of height $28$ m above the sea at a speed of $14$ m s$^{-1}$ at an angle above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. By considering the energy of the stone, determine the speed with which the stone hits the sea.
questions.answer: Initial kinetic energy plus loss in gravitational potential energy equals the final kinetic energy: $\frac12m(14)^2+mg(28)=\frac12mv^2$. The mass cancels: $v=\sqrt{14^2+2\times9.8\times28}=\sqrt{744.8}=27$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.question: The stone leaves the cliff at time $t=0$ and reaches its maximum height at $t=T_H$ (the maximum height reached above the launch point is $8.0$ m). On the axes provided, draw a sketch graph to show the variation with time $t$ of the magnitude of the vertical component of the speed of the stone from $t=0$ to $t=T_S$, the time just before the stone strikes the sea.
questions.answer: The vertical velocity decreases uniformly (slope $-g$) from $v_{y0}=\sqrt{2g(8.0)}\approx12.5$ m s$^{-1}$ to zero at $T_H$. After $T_H$ the magnitude increases at the same rate ($g$) until $T_S$, ending at $\sqrt{12.5^2+2g(28)}\approx26.6$ m s$^{-1}$, which is larger than the initial vertical speed. The graph is a V shape with equal slope magnitudes.

questions.question: A small coil is placed with its plane parallel to a long straight current-carrying wire. State Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction.
questions.answer: The magnitude of the emf induced in a circuit is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux through (linking) the circuit: $\varepsilon=-N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$ (the negative sign expressing Lenz's law).

questions.question: Use the law to explain why, when the current in the wire changes, an emf is induced in the coil.
questions.answer: The magnetic field of the wire is proportional to the current, so when the current changes the magnetic field (and hence the flux) through the coil changes. A changing flux induces an emf in the coil.

prev.question: A small coil is placed with its plane parallel to a long straight current-carrying wire. State Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction.
prev.answer: The magnitude of the emf induced in a circuit is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux through (linking) the circuit: $\varepsilon=-N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$ (the negative sign expressing Lenz's law).

questions.question: The graph shows the variation with time $t$ of the current in the wire (sinusoidal, starting at zero and increasing). Draw, on the axes provided, a sketch graph to show the variation with time $t$ of the magnetic flux in the coil.
questions.answer: The flux is proportional to the field, which is proportional to the current, so the graph is sinusoidal and in phase with the current.

questions.question: Construct, on the axes provided, a sketch graph to show the variation with time $t$ of the emf induced in the coil.
questions.answer: $\varepsilon=-N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$: the emf is sinusoidal with the same frequency as the flux, but $90^\circ$ out of phase with it (the negative of the gradient of the flux graph, i.e. $-\cos$ if flux is $\sin$). It is zero when the flux is at a maximum or minimum, and at its extreme values when the flux is zero (changing fastest).

prev.question: The graph shows the variation with time $t$ of the current in the wire (sinusoidal, starting at zero and increasing). Draw, on the axes provided, a sketch graph to show the variation with time $t$ of the magnetic flux in the coil.
prev.answer: The flux is proportional to the field, which is proportional to the current, so the graph is sinusoidal and in phase with the current.

questions.question: State and explain the effect on the maximum emf induced in the coil when the coil is further away from the wire.
questions.answer: The maximum emf is reduced. The magnetic field of the wire is weaker further away, so the flux through the coil, and its rate of change, are smaller, which gives a smaller induced emf.

questions.question: Such a coil may be used to measure large alternating currents in a high-voltage cable. Identify one advantage and one disadvantage of this method.
questions.answer: Advantage: there is no direct electrical contact with the high-voltage cable (so it is safe and the cable need not be cut or disconnected). Disadvantage: the emf depends on the distance (and orientation) of the coil relative to the cable, so this must be fixed and known; it works only for alternating (changing) currents.

questions.question: Kepler's third law states that the period $T$ of the orbit of a planet about the Sun is related to the average orbital radius $R$ of the planet by $T^2=KR^3$, where $K$ is a constant. Suggest why the law specifies the average orbital radius.
questions.answer: Planetary orbits are elliptical rather than circular, so the distance from the Sun varies during the orbit; the average radius (semi-major axis) is used.

questions.question: State the name of the force that causes the acceleration of the planets orbiting the Sun.
questions.answer: Gravity (the gravitational force).

prev.question: Kepler's third law states that the period $T$ of the orbit of a planet about the Sun is related to the average orbital radius $R$ of the planet by $T^2=KR^3$, where $K$ is a constant. Suggest why the law specifies the average orbital radius.

questions.question: State an expression for the magnitude $F$ of the force in (ii) in terms of the mass $M_S$ of the Sun, the mass $m$ of the planet, the radius $R$ of the orbit and the universal gravitational constant $G$.
questions.answer: $F=\dfrac{GM_Sm}{R^2}$.

questions.question: Hence deduce, explaining your working, that the constant $K$ is given by $K=\dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM_S}$.
questions.answer: Treat the orbit as circular with speed $v$; the centripetal acceleration is $\frac{v^2}R$. By Newton's second law, $\frac{GM_Sm}{R^2}=\frac{mv^2}R$. The speed is $v=\frac{2\pi R}T$, so $\frac{GM_Sm}{R^2}=\frac{4\pi^2mR}{T^2}$. Rearranging, $T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{GM_S}R^3$, so $K=\frac{4\pi^2}{GM_S}$.

questions.question: Ganymede is one of the moons of Jupiter. Its average orbital radius is $1.1\times10^9$ m and its orbital period is $6.2\times10^5$ s ($G=6.67\times10^{-11}$ N m$^2$ kg$^{-2}$). Deduce that the gravitational field strength of Jupiter at the surface of Ganymede is approximately $0.1$ N kg$^{-1}$.
questions.answer: The field strength equals the centripetal acceleration of Ganymede: $g=\frac{v^2}R=\frac{4\pi^2R}{T^2}=\frac{4\pi^2\times1.1\times10^9}{\left(6.2\times10^5\right)^2}=0.11\approx0.1$ N kg$^{-1}$.

questions.question: Using the data for Ganymede (orbital radius $1.1\times10^9$ m, period $6.2\times10^5$ s, $G=6.67\times10^{-11}$ N m$^2$ kg$^{-2}$), estimate the mass of Jupiter.
questions.answer: From $T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{GM_J}R^3$: $M_J=\frac{4\pi^2R^3}{GT^2}=\frac{4\pi^2\left(1.1\times10^9\right)^3}{6.67\times10^{-11}\left(6.2\times10^5\right)^2}\approx2.0\times10^{27}$ kg. (Alternatively $g=\frac{GM}{R^2}$ gives $M=\frac{gR^2}G=\frac{0.1\times\left(1.1\times10^9\right)^2}{6.67\times10^{-11}}\approx1.8$–$2.0\times10^{27}$ kg.)

Deduce that the gravitational field strength of Jupiter at the surface of Ganymede is approximately $0.1$ N kg$^{-1}$.
prev.answer: The field strength equals the centripetal acceleration of Ganymede: $g=\frac{v^2}R=\frac{4\pi^2R}{T^2}=\frac{4\pi^2\times1.1\times10^9}{\left(6.2\times10^5\right)^2}=0.11\approx0.1$ N kg$^{-1}$.

questions.question: Describe one historical method used to determine the speed of light experimentally, including its limitations.
questions.answer: Sample answer (Fizeau's toothed wheel, 1849): Light from a source is reflected by a half-silvered mirror through a gap in a rapidly rotating toothed wheel, travels a long distance $d$ (about $8.6$ km) to a distant plane mirror and is reflected back along the same path to the wheel. If the wheel turns by half a tooth-spacing during the light's round-trip time $t=\frac{2d}c$, the returning light hits a tooth and is blocked (observer sees eclipse). The wheel's rotation rate $f$ and the number of teeth $N$ give $t=\frac1{2Nf}$, so $c=\frac{2d}t=4dNf$ (Fizeau obtained about $3.1\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$ with $N=720$, $f\approx12.6$ rev s$^{-1}$). Principles: light travels in straight lines at a finite speed, reflection at a mirror (return of the beam along its path), and speed = distance/time determined from the angular speed of the wheel. Limitations: (1) the distance travelled by light was short, so the time was very small and hard to measure; (2) the judgement of the point of 'eclipse' (minimum brightness) by eye was subjective, and the wheel speed could not be controlled and measured with great precision; (3) the light beam spreads and is attenuated over the long path, so the image is faint.

questions.question: In 1983, the speed of light was declared to be exactly $299\,792\,458$ m s$^{-1}$. Explain the currently accepted relationship of the speed of light to the measurement of distance and time.
questions.answer: The second is defined by the caesium-133 atom (the time for $9\,192\,631\,770$ periods of the radiation from a specific energy transition), and the speed of light in a vacuum is fixed exactly. So the metre is defined as the distance travelled by light in a vacuum in $\frac1{299\,792\,458}$ of a second. The speed of light is therefore a defined constant that links the units of distance and time, rather than something that is measured.

questions.question: The magnetic flux passing through a loop of wire varies as shown by the straight line below. Which of the following gives the magnitude of the emf induced in the coil?
questions.answer: Faraday's law gives $\varepsilon=-N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$. The magnitude of the emf is proportional to the rate of change of flux, which is the gradient of the flux–time graph (A).
options: the reciprocal of the gradient of the graph
the area between the straight line and the time axis
the area between the straight line and the magnetic flux axis

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a property of an inertial frame of reference?
questions.answer: An inertial frame is one that is not accelerating: it moves with constant velocity (constant speed in a straight line). Its speed can be anything below $c$, so only A is a defining property.
options: It is travelling at a constant speed.
It is travelling at speed close to $c$.
It is travelling at speed much slower than $c$.
It is travelling with increasing speed.

questions.question: An object travels in circular motion due to a centripetal force $F$. What is the centripetal force acting on the object when the radius of the circle halves and the kinetic energy of the object doubles?
questions.answer: $F=\frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{2K}{r}$. Doubling $K$ and halving $r$ gives $F'=\frac{2(2K)}{r/2}=4F$ (D).

questions.question: A water pipe is placed on the edge of an elevated platform that is $9.5$ m above the ground. Water runs off the hose with a (horizontal) velocity of $4.5$ m s$^{-1}$. The water hits the ground after $t$ seconds. What is the value of $t$?
questions.answer: The vertical motion is independent of the horizontal motion. Vertically $u_y=0$, so $9.5=\frac12(9.8)t^2$ and $t=\sqrt{\frac{2(9.5)}{9.8}}=1.39$ s (C).

questions.question: A current-carrying straight wire is placed next to a loop of wire as shown in the diagram. What is the direction of the induced current in the loop if the current in the straight wire decreases with time?
questions.answer: The current in the wire flows to the right, so below the wire the magnetic field points into the page (right-hand grip rule). The current decreases, so the flux into the page through the loop decreases. By Lenz's law the induced current opposes this change by producing a field into the page inside the loop, which requires a clockwise current (B).

questions.question: An ideal step-down transformer is used in a smart watch charger to transform the voltage from $240$ V to $6.0$ V. The smart watch draws a current of $2.4$ A while charging. What is the current drawn from the primary coil of the charger?
questions.answer: For an ideal transformer $V_pI_p=V_sI_s$, so $I_p=\frac{6.0\times2.4}{240}=0.06$ A (B).

questions.question: Two satellites, $P$ and $Q$, are both in circular orbit about the same planet. The mass of $P$ is greater than the mass of $Q$. The radius of $P$'s orbit is less than that of $Q$. Which of the following is the correct comparison of the orbital and escape velocities of $P$ and $Q$? (Escape velocity is taken from the satellite's orbit.)
questions.answer: $v_{orbit}=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$ and $v_{esc}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}}$, where $M$ is the planet's mass. Neither depends on the satellite's mass, and both increase as $r$ decreases. $P$ has the smaller radius, so both its orbital and escape velocities are greater (B).
options: Orbital velocity of $P$ compared to $Q$: greater; escape velocity of $P$ compared to $Q$: less
Orbital velocity of $P$ compared to $Q$: greater; escape velocity of $P$ compared to $Q$: greater
Orbital velocity of $P$ compared to $Q$: less; escape velocity of $P$ compared to $Q$: less
Orbital velocity of $P$ compared to $Q$: less; escape velocity of $P$ compared to $Q$: greater

questions.question: A simple generator is connected to an external circuit with a light globe as shown in the diagram. Which of the following best describes the function of the split-ring commutator?
questions.answer: A split-ring commutator reverses the connections to the external circuit every half rotation, just as the induced emf in the coil reverses. The current in the external circuit therefore always flows in the same direction, i.e. direct current (D).
options: It ensures the force on the section $AB$ is always up.
It ensures the force on the section $AB$ is always down.
It ensures that alternating current is delivered to the light globe.
It ensures that direct current is delivered to the light globe.

questions.question: A proton has kinetic energy equal to that of a photon with a wavelength of $715$ nm. What is the speed of the proton?
questions.answer: Photon energy: $E=\frac{hc}{\lambda}=\frac{(6.626\times10^{-34})(3.00\times10^8)}{715\times10^{-9}}=2.78\times10^{-19}$ J. For the proton $\frac12mv^2=E$, so $v=\sqrt{\frac{2(2.78\times10^{-19})}{1.673\times10^{-27}}}=1.8\times10^4$ m s$^{-1}$ (C).

questions.question: Which of the following is the mass defect for a nuclear reaction which releases $5.42$ MeV of energy?

A magnet moves towards a coil with five turns as shown in the diagram. During the time interval $\Delta t$, the magnetic flux changes by $0.07$ Wb and the average induced emf is $1.5$ V. Which of the following is closest to the time interval $\Delta t$?
questions.answer: $\varepsilon=N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, so $\Delta t=\frac{N\Delta\Phi}{\varepsilon}=\frac{5(0.07)}{1.5}=0.23$ s (B).

questions.question: Monochromatic light is incident on a double slit to produce a pattern of bright and dark fringes on a viewing screen as shown in the diagram. Which of the following is correct when the spacing between the slits increases?
questions.answer: The fringe spacing is $\Delta y=\frac{\lambda L}{d}$. Increasing the slit separation $d$ decreases $\Delta y$, so the fringes are closer together (A).
options: Fringes are spaced the same but the fringes are sharper.
Fringes are spaced the same but the fringes are more diffuse.

questions.question: A helium nucleus has four times the mass of a proton and two times the charge of a proton. A helium nucleus and a proton are both accelerated from rest through the same potential difference. Which of the following gives the ratio of the final kinetic energy of the helium nucleus to that of the proton?
questions.answer: The kinetic energy gained is $K=qV$, which does not depend on mass. With twice the charge and the same $V$, the helium nucleus gains twice the energy, so the ratio is $2:1$ (C).

questions.question: At the surface of a planet of radius $r$, the gravitational field strength is $g$ and the gravitational potential is $U$. Which of the following gives the gravitational field strength and gravitational potential at a height $2r$ above the surface?
questions.answer: A height $2r$ above the surface is a distance $3r$ from the centre. The field strength $g=\frac{GM}{r^2}\propto\frac{1}{r^2}$ becomes $\frac{g}{9}$, and the potential $U=-\frac{GM}{r}\propto\frac1r$ becomes $\frac{U}{3}$ (B).

questions.question: A beam of monochromatic light is shone on a diffraction grating that has $6.00\times10^{5}$ lines m$^{-1}$. The angle between the second-order maxima is $49^\circ$. What is the wavelength of the light?
questions.answer: The second-order maxima lie on either side of the central maximum, so each is at $\theta=\frac{49^\circ}{2}=24.5^\circ$. The slit spacing is $d=\frac{1}{6.00\times10^5}=1.667\times10^{-6}$ m. From $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$: $\lambda=\frac{1.667\times10^{-6}\sin24.5^\circ}{2}=3.46\times10^{-7}$ m (B).

questions.question: An experiment is set up according to the diagram to investigate the photoelectric effect. Which of the following is essential to the measurement of the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons?
questions.answer: The variable source is connected so that it opposes the flow of photoelectrons. The voltage at which the photocurrent just falls to its minimum (zero) is the stopping voltage $V_0$, and $K_{max}=eV_0$. So the voltmeter reading when the current is at a minimum is the essential measurement (C). The intensity affects only the size of the current.
options: the wavelength of light that passes through the filter
the intensity of the light source
the reading on the voltmeter when the current is at a minimum value
the reading on the ammeter when the voltage is at a maximum value

questions.question: Two loops of wire are placed next to each other. An alternating current is supplied to loop 1 and an ammeter is connected to loop 2, as shown. The variation of the current with time in loop 1 is shown by the solid line in each graph. Which of the following best represents the variation of the current in loop 2 (dotted line)?
questions.answer: The emf induced in loop 2 is proportional to $-\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, i.e. to the negative of the rate of change of the current in loop 1. For a sinusoidal current $I_1\propto\sin\omega t$, the induced current in loop 2 is proportional to $-\cos\omega t$. It is therefore a sine-shaped wave of the same frequency shifted by a quarter of a period from loop 1, and it starts at its most negative value when loop 1 is zero and increasing. This is graph C. (A has the wrong phase, B has no induced current, and D is exactly out of phase.)

questions.question: Two polarising filters $A$ and $B$ are arranged as shown in the diagram. Filter $A$ is fixed and filter $B$ can be rotated. Unpolarised light of intensity $I_0$ is shone on filter $A$ and the intensity of the light is observed on the screen. With the arrangement shown, the intensity of the light on the screen is observed to be $\frac13I_0$. Filter $B$ is rotated clockwise through an angle of $\theta$ such that maximum intensity is observed on the screen. Which of the following is a possible value of $\theta$?
questions.answer: Filter $A$ reduces the unpolarised light to $\frac12I_0$. Then by Malus' law $\frac13I_0=\frac12I_0\cos^2\phi$, so $\cos^2\phi=\frac23$ and $\phi=35.3^\circ$ between the axes of $A$ and $B$. Maximum intensity occurs when the axes are parallel, i.e. when $B$ is rotated by $35^\circ$ in one direction or $180^\circ-35^\circ=145^\circ$ in the other. Of the options only $145^\circ$ works (D).

questions.question:
The table below gives the orbital data for four moons. Three of the moons orbit planet $P$.

| Moon | Radius of orbit (m) | Period of orbit (Earth days) |
|---|---|---|
| A | $1.31\times10^{8}$ | $1.41$ |
| B | $1.91\times10^{8}$ | $2.52$ |
| C | $2.65\times10^{8}$ | $4.14$ |
| D | $4.5\times10^{8}$ | $5.28$ |

Which of the following is not a moon of planet $P$?
questions.answer: Kepler's third law: for moons of the same planet, $\frac{r^3}{T^2}$ is constant. In units of $10^{24}$ m$^3$/day$^2$: A: $\frac{2.248}{1.988}=1.13$; B: $\frac{6.967}{6.350}=1.10$; C: $\frac{18.61}{17.14}=1.09$; D: $\frac{91.1}{27.9}=3.27$. Moon D does not fit the pattern, so it is not a moon of $P$ (D).

questions.question:
Matthew is conducting an experiment on Earth where he shines a beam of light onto a stationary mirror (relative to him). He observes that it took the beam of light $0.2$ seconds to reach the mirror. At the same time, Anna is travelling in a spacecraft moving at $0.78c$ relative to the Earth, in the direction from the light source towards the mirror, and she observes the same experiment on Earth. Which of the following does Anna observe about Matthew's experiment?

| | Time taken for the beam of light to reach the mirror | Speed of the beam of light |
|---|---|---|
| A | More than $0.2$ seconds | $c$ |
| B | Less than $0.2$ seconds | $c$ |
| C | More than $0.2$ seconds | $0.22c$ |
| D | Less than $0.2$ seconds | $0.22c$ |
questions.answer: The speed of light is $c$ in every inertial frame, which eliminates C and D. The emission and arrival of the light are not at the same place in Matthew's frame, so $0.2$ s is not a proper time and simple time dilation does not apply. Using the Lorentz transformation with $\Delta x=c(0.2)$ and Anna moving at $v=0.78c$ in the direction of the light: $\Delta t'=\gamma\left(\Delta t-\frac{v\Delta x}{c^2}\right)=1.598(0.2)(1-0.78)=0.07$ s. This is less than $0.2$ s (B). In Anna's frame the mirror moves towards the light, so the light has less distance to cover.

questions.question: Two polarising filters, $P_1$ and $P_2$, are placed in the path of an initially unpolarised light source travelling towards point $A$ such that it passes through $P_1$ followed by $P_2$. The polarising axes of $P_1$ and $P_2$ are perpendicular. Explain whether any light will be observed at point $A$.
questions.answer: No light will be observed at $A$. $P_1$ transmits only the component of the light polarised parallel to its axis. This light then meets $P_2$ at $90^\circ$ to its axis, and by Malus' law $I=I_0\cos^2\theta$ with $\theta=90^\circ$ gives $I=0$. $P_2$ has no component parallel to its axis to transmit.

questions.question: Unpolarised light passes through two polarising filters with perpendicular axes, and no light is transmitted. Identify which theory of light this supports.
questions.answer: The wave theory of light (Huygens' wave model). Polarisation requires light to be a transverse wave, which the particle (corpuscular) model cannot explain.

questions.question: A newly designed spaceship is travelling past Earth at $0.55c$ during its test flight. An engineer on Earth observes that the length of the spaceship does not match the measurement taken when the spaceship was stationary on Earth, however, the width does. Explain why there is a difference in the engineer's measurement for the length of the spaceship, but not for the width of the spaceship.
questions.answer: Due to relativistic length contraction, an object moving relative to an observer is measured by that observer to be shorter than its proper length. Length contraction occurs only along the direction of relative motion. The width is perpendicular to the direction of motion, so it is not contracted and the measurements agree.

questions.question: If a spaceship is travelling at $0.55c$ relative to an engineer on Earth and the engineer observes the length of the spaceship to be $154$ m, calculate the length of the spaceship when it was stationary on Earth.
questions.answer: The $154$ m observed by the engineer is the contracted length, $l=154$ m. Using $l=l_0\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}$: $154=l_0\sqrt{1-0.55^2}$, so $l_0=\frac{154}{0.8352}=184$ m ($1.8\times10^2$ m).

questions.question: An electrical power plant operating at $15$ kV delivers $450.0$ MW to external transmission lines. Voltage is stepped up to $350.0$ kV for transmission and stepped down to $240.0$ V for household use. The transmission lines have a total resistance of $25\ \Omega$. Assume that the transformers are all ideal. Explain why the voltage is stepped up for transmission.
questions.answer: Stepping up the voltage reduces the power lost in the transmission lines. For a given power $P=VI$, a higher voltage means a lower current. The power lost in the lines is $P_{loss}=I^2R$, so reducing the current greatly reduces the loss.

questions.question: An electrical power plant delivers $450.0$ MW to external transmission lines. The voltage is stepped up to $350.0$ kV for transmission, and the transmission lines have a total resistance of $25\ \Omega$. Assume that the transformers are ideal. Calculate the current in the transmission lines.
questions.answer: The transformer is ideal, so $P_{in}=P_{out}$: $450.0\times10^6=(350.0\times10^3)I$, giving $I=1286$ A.

questions.question: An electrical power plant operating at $15$ kV delivers $450.0$ MW to external transmission lines. Voltage is stepped up to $350.0$ kV for transmission and stepped down to $240.0$ V for household use. The transmission lines have a total resistance of $25\ \Omega$. Assume that the transformers are all ideal. Determine the power delivered to households.
questions.answer: The current in the lines is $I=\frac{450.0\times10^6}{350.0\times10^3}=1285.7$ A. Power lost in the lines: $P_{loss}=I^2R=(1285.7)^2(25)=4.13\times10^7$ W. Power delivered to households $=450.0\times10^6-4.13\times10^7=4.09\times10^8$ W $\approx409$ MW. The step-down transformer is ideal, so no further loss occurs.

questions.question: The rotor of a simple AC generator is rotated smoothly at $200$ revolutions per second and the loop generates a maximum emf of $12$ V. The direction of rotation is as shown in the diagram. Sketch the output emf from $G$ to $H$ against time $t$ on the grid. The rotor starts from the position shown in the diagram. Your sketch should include two complete revolutions.
questions.answer: The period is $T=\frac{1}{200}=0.005$ s, so two revolutions take $0.010$ s. The loop starts perpendicular to the field (as shown, flux is maximum) so the emf starts at $0$ and varies sinusoidally with amplitude $12$ V. From the direction of rotation and the magnet poles, positive charge accumulates at $H$ first, making $H$ the higher-potential terminal. The emf from $G$ to $H$ is therefore negative initially: $\varepsilon=-12\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{0.005}\right)$ V. The sketch is a sine wave starting at $0$, going down to $-12$ V at $0.00125$ s, back to $0$ at $0.0025$ s, up to $+12$ V at $0.00375$ s and back to $0$ at $0.005$ s, then repeating once more up to $0.010$ s.

questions.question: Describe the main function of the slip rings in the simple AC generator.
questions.answer: The slip rings allow alternating current to be supplied to the external circuit. Each ring stays connected to the same end of the rotating coil, so the output polarity reverses every half rotation, as the induced emf does.

questions.question: Describe how a simple AC generator can be changed to a DC generator.
questions.answer: Replace the slip rings with a split-ring commutator, which reverses the connection to the external circuit every half rotation so that the current in the external circuit always flows in the same direction.

questions.question: In a double-slit experiment, a laser is incident on a double slit with a fixed distance of separation between the slits. A viewing screen is placed on the other side of the slits and the distance from the slits can be adjusted. An interference pattern is observed on the viewing screen. Describe how this experimental setup can be used to determine the wavelength of the laser.
questions.answer: Set the screen at a measured distance $L$ from the double slits and measure the distance $y$ from the central maximum to the first-order bright fringe (or measure across several fringes and divide). The slit separation $d$ is known. Then use $d\frac{y}{L}=m\lambda$ with $m=1$ to calculate $\lambda=\frac{dy}{L}$. To improve accuracy, repeat for several values of $L$ and record $y$ each time. Plot $y$ against $L$ and the gradient equals $\frac{\lambda}{d}$, so $\lambda=d\times$ gradient.

questions.question: In a double-slit experiment, light from a laser passes through a double slit and forms a pattern of bright and dark fringes on a viewing screen. Explain why an interference pattern forms on the viewing screen.
questions.answer: Each slit acts as a source of coherent waves (the wavelets spread out by diffraction) and the waves from the two slits overlap on the screen and superpose, producing constructive and destructive interference. Where the path difference from the two slits is a whole number of wavelengths, $n\lambda$, the waves arrive in phase and interfere constructively, giving a bright fringe. Where the path difference is $\left(n+\frac12\right)\lambda$, the waves arrive out of phase (half a period apart) and interfere destructively, giving a dark fringe.

questions.question: Experimental results of the photoelectric effect have shown that: (1) a photocurrent only occurs when light above a certain frequency is incident on a metal; (2) the size of the current depends on the intensity of the light but not the frequency; (3) the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons depends on the frequency of the light but not the intensity. Explain how the predictions from the classical wave model contradicted the experimental results of the photoelectric effect.
questions.answer: (1) In the classical wave model the energy is spread over the wave and is absorbed continuously, so a photocurrent should occur at any frequency provided the intensity is high enough (or the light shone for long enough). There should be no threshold frequency. (2) The wave model predicts that the current should depend on both the intensity and the frequency. (3) The wave model predicts that the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons should depend on the intensity (greater wave energy gives electrons more energy), not on the frequency.

questions.question: Experimental results of the photoelectric effect have shown that: (1) a photocurrent only occurs when light above a certain frequency is incident on a metal; (2) the size of the current depends on the intensity of the light but not the frequency; (3) the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons depends on the frequency of the light but not the intensity. How did Einstein explain the photoelectric effect using the photon model of light?
questions.answer: Einstein proposed that light consists of photons, each with energy $E=hf$, and that an electron absorbs a single photon in a one-to-one interaction. (1) An electron is only emitted if the photon energy is at least the work function, $hf\ge\phi$, so there is a threshold frequency. (2) The intensity is proportional to the number of photons per second. More photons per second liberate more electrons per second, so the current depends on intensity (and not on frequency). (3) By conservation of energy, $K_{max}=hf-\phi$, so the maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency and not on intensity.

questions.question: Planes are designed to produce lift force ($F_L$) at the wings, perpendicular to the surface of the wing, when flying. When a plane changes direction, it banks in a circular path whilst maintaining altitude. The forces acting on the plane during the bank are shown in the diagram (angle $\theta$ to the vertical). On the diagram, accurately draw the centripetal force vector.
questions.answer: The centripetal force is the net force on the plane. The vertical components cancel (constant altitude), so the net force is the horizontal component of the lift force, $F_L\sin\theta$. The vector is drawn horizontally from the plane towards the centre of the circle, i.e. pointing in the same horizontal direction as the horizontal component of $F_L$ (to the right in the diagram).

questions.question: A plane banks in a horizontal circle while maintaining altitude. The forces on the plane are its weight $F_g$ and the lift force $F_L$, which is perpendicular to the wings and at an angle $\theta$ to the vertical. Calculate the centripetal force acting on a $757$ kg plane banking at an angle of $26^\circ$ to the vertical whilst maintaining altitude.
questions.answer: To maintain altitude the vertical forces balance: $F_g=F_L\cos\theta$, so $F_L=\frac{757\times9.8}{\cos26^\circ}=8254$ N. The centripetal force is the horizontal component: $F_c=F_L\sin\theta=8254\sin26^\circ=3.6\times10^3$ N. (Equivalently $F_c=mg\tan\theta$.)

questions.question: A $757$ kg plane banks in a horizontal circle while maintaining altitude. The forces on the plane are its weight and the lift force, which is perpendicular to the wings and at an angle $\theta$ to the vertical. The pilot adjusts the lift force to allow the plane to bank at an angle of $37^\circ$ (instead of $26^\circ$) whilst maintaining altitude. Explain how the motion of the plane will be affected if the radius of the bank remains the same. Include relevant calculations.
questions.answer: The weight is unchanged, so to maintain altitude $F_L\cos\theta=mg$: $F_L=\frac{757\times9.8}{\cos37^\circ}=9289$ N. Then $F_c=F_L\sin37^\circ=5.6\times10^3$ N, which is greater than the $3.6\times10^3$ N at $26^\circ$. With the radius unchanged, $F_c=\frac{mv^2}{r}$ shows the plane must be travelling faster (and so its period for a revolution is shorter).

questions.question: A space station is designed in the shape of a hollow doughnut so that it can rotate at a constant speed to provide artificial gravity. If the radius of the space station is $1.20\times10^{3}$ m, what should be its period of rotation such that a person standing on the outer wall inside the station experiences the same weight force as if they were on Earth?
questions.answer:
The normal force from the wall provides the centripetal force, and it must equal the weight on Earth: $mg=\frac{mv^2}{r}$, so $v=\sqrt{gr}=\sqrt{9.8(1.20\times10^3)}=108.4$ m s$^{-1}$. Then $T=\frac{2\pi r}{v}=\frac{2\pi(1.20\times10^3)}{108.4}=69.5\approx70$ s.

Note: The school's solution gives 69 s (truncating 69.53 s); correctly rounded to 2 significant figures the period is 70 s.

questions.question: A space station is designed in the shape of a hollow doughnut so that it can rotate at a constant speed to provide artificial gravity (the apparent weight is provided by the centripetal force of the outer wall). The radius of the space station and the speed of rotation can both be adjusted. Explain one way that the space station can be adjusted to simulate the gravity on Jupiter, given that $g_{Jupiter}>g_{Earth}$.
questions.answer: The apparent gravity is the centripetal acceleration $a_c=\frac{v^2}{r}=\frac{4\pi^2r}{T^2}$, so to simulate a larger $g$ the centripetal force on a person must be greater. This can be done, for example, by increasing the speed of rotation (shorter period) while keeping the radius the same, or by decreasing the radius while keeping the speed the same.

questions.question: The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is a circular particle accelerator with a radius of $4.2\times10^{3}$ m capable of accelerating particles such as protons to travel close to the speed of light. With reference to special relativity and circular motion, discuss why the LHC has such a large radius.
questions.answer: As the protons approach the speed of light their relativistic momentum $p=\frac{m_0v}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$ (and relativistic mass) increases enormously, so the particles have a very large momentum. To keep a particle moving in a circle, a centripetal force $F=\frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{pv}{r}$ is required (provided by magnetic fields), and this force becomes very large because of the large relativistic mass at speeds close to $c$. For a given particle momentum and speed, the force required is inversely proportional to the radius, so a large radius reduces the centripetal force (and so the magnetic field strength) needed to keep the particles in orbit.

questions.question: Describe the key components of an AC induction motor and how they allow the motor to function.
questions.answer: The stator is a set of fixed electromagnets (coils) arranged around the motor at different orientations. The rotor is a squirrel-cage-like structure of conducting bars running along its length, free to rotate inside the stator. Alternating current supplied to the stator coils in different phases produces a rotating magnetic field. The rotor experiences a changing magnetic flux, so by Faraday's law a current is induced in its conducting bars (in the direction that opposes the change in flux, by Lenz's law). The induced currents in the rotor lie in the stator's magnetic field, so by the motor effect they experience forces. These forces produce a torque that turns the rotor, which follows the rotating field.

questions.question: A space shuttle of mass $m$ is launched from the surface of the Earth (radius $r_E$, mass $M$) at point $A$. The kinetic energy given to the shuttle at launch is $K_A=\frac{5}{7}\frac{GMm}{r_E}$. The shuttle then enters a circular orbit of radius $R$ at point $B$. Explain why the space shuttle cannot escape the gravitational field of the Earth.
questions.answer: From $K_A=\frac12mv_A^2=\frac57\frac{GMm}{r_E}$, $v_A=\sqrt{\frac{10}{7}\frac{GM}{r_E}}$. The escape velocity from the Earth's surface is $v_{esc}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r_E}}$. Since $\frac{10}{7}<2$, $v_A<v_{esc}$ (equivalently, the launch energy $\frac57\frac{GMm}{r_E}$ is less than the $\frac{GMm}{r_E}$ needed), so the shuttle cannot escape.

questions.question: A space shuttle of mass $m$ is in a circular orbit of radius $R$ about the Earth (mass $M$). Show that the total energy of the space shuttle in its orbit is given by $E_{total}=-\frac{GMm}{2R}$.
questions.answer: The gravitational potential energy is $U=-\frac{GMm}{R}$. The gravitational force provides the centripetal force: $\frac{GMm}{R^2}=\frac{mv^2}{R}$, so $v^2=\frac{GM}{R}$ and $K=\frac12mv^2=\frac12\frac{GMm}{R}$. Then $E_{total}=U+K=-\frac{GMm}{R}+\frac{GMm}{2R}=-\frac{GMm}{2R}$.

questions.question: A space shuttle of mass $m$ is launched from the surface of the Earth (radius $r_E$, mass $M$) at point $A$ with kinetic energy $K_A=\frac57\frac{GMm}{r_E}$, and then enters a circular orbit of radius $R$ at point $B$. The total energy of the shuttle in this orbit is $-\frac{GMm}{2R}$. By using the conservation of energy, find $R$ in terms of $r_E$.
questions.answer: The total energy is conserved, so $E_A=E_B$. At $A$: $E_A=U_A+K_A=-\frac{GMm}{r_E}+\frac57\frac{GMm}{r_E}=-\frac27\frac{GMm}{r_E}$. Then $-\frac{GMm}{2R}=-\frac{2}{7}\frac{GMm}{r_E}$, so $\frac{1}{2R}=\frac{2}{7r_E}$ and $R=\frac74r_E$.

questions.question: A golf ball $A$ is in a sandpit. The golfer hits the ball to give it a velocity $u$ m s$^{-1}$ at $25^\circ$ to the horizontal. The horizontal component of $u$ is $6.2$ m s$^{-1}$. The ball is travelling horizontally as it reaches the point $P$ (at the top of the sandpit edge, a vertical distance $d$ above the ball's starting point). Assume that air resistance is negligible. Calculate the time taken for the ball to reach $P$.
questions.answer: $u\cos25^\circ=6.2$, so $u=6.84$ m s$^{-1}$ and $u_y=u\sin25^\circ=2.89$ m s$^{-1}$. At $P$ the ball is moving horizontally, so $v_y=0$: $0=2.89-9.8t$, giving $t=0.30$ s.

questions.question: A golf ball is hit from the bottom of a sandpit with velocity $u$ at $25^\circ$ to the horizontal, where the horizontal component of $u$ is $6.2$ m s$^{-1}$. The ball is travelling horizontally as it reaches point $P$, which is a vertical distance $d$ (the depth of the sandpit) above the starting point, $0.295$ s after being hit. Assume that air resistance is negligible. Calculate the depth of the sandpit, $d$.
questions.answer: $d=u_yt-\frac12gt^2=(2.89)(0.295)-\frac12(9.8)(0.295)^2=0.43$ m. (Equivalently $d=\frac{u_y^2}{2g}$ since $P$ is at the peak of the flight.)

questions.question: A golf ball is hit from the bottom of a sandpit with velocity $u$ at $25^\circ$ to the horizontal and lands at $P$, at the top edge of the sandpit, travelling horizontally at $P$. The ball is returned to the same location in the sandpit. This time the golfer hits the ball with the same speed $u$ but at an angle of $78^\circ$, and the ball also lands at $P$. On the diagram, sketch the new trajectory of the golf ball.
questions.answer: The trajectory starts at the same point, rises more steeply to a maximum height well above $P$, and then descends to arrive at $P$ travelling downwards at a steep angle (it does not reach its peak at $P$).

questions.question: A golf ball is hit from the bottom of a sandpit with speed $u=6.84$ m s$^{-1}$ at $25^\circ$ to the horizontal and arrives at point $P$ (a height $d=0.43$ m above the start) travelling horizontally at $6.2$ m s$^{-1}$. The ball is returned to the same location and hit with the same speed $u$ but at an angle of $78^\circ$, and it also lands at $P$. Compare the velocities at point $P$ for the two different trajectories.
questions.answer: The horizontal velocity is constant in each flight. For the first trajectory it is $u\cos25^\circ=6.2$ m s$^{-1}$; for the second it is $u\cos78^\circ=1.42$ m s$^{-1}$, which is smaller. The total speed at $P$ is the same for both: the ball starts with the same kinetic energy and gains the same gravitational potential energy in going to $P$, so by conservation of energy the kinetic energy (and speed) at $P$ must be the same, $6.2$ m s$^{-1}$. Since the horizontal component is smaller for the second trajectory but the speed is the same, the vertical component at $P$ must be larger: the first ball has $v_y=0$ at $P$, whereas the second has a downward $v_y\approx6.0$ m s$^{-1}$ (so it arrives at about $77^\circ$ below the horizontal). Check for the second ball: $0.43=6.69t-4.9t^2$ gives $t=1.30$ s, $v_y=6.69-9.8(1.30)=-6.03$ m s$^{-1}$, and $v=\sqrt{1.42^2+6.03^2}=6.2$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.question: The 'Hair Raiser' ride at Luna Park uses a platform to carry riders. The platform is lifted into the air and then dropped. It falls freely for some distance and before it reaches the ground, strong permanent magnets underneath the platform pass close to copper fins on the tower to act as a braking system. The velocity-time graph of the platform is shown (velocity is negative for downward motion). Analyse the motion of the platform by applying the law of conservation of energy. Your analysis should refer to gravity, the copper fins and include both qualitative and quantitative information.
questions.answer:
**Free fall (0 to about 2.2 s).** The graph is a straight line, so the acceleration is constant. Reading the graph, the velocity changes from $0$ to about $-20$ m s$^{-1}$ in about $2.2$ s, so $a\approx\frac{-20}{2.2}\approx-9$ m s$^{-2}$, which is about $g$ (the small difference is due to reading the graph). The distance fallen is the area under the graph, $\frac12(2.2)(20)\approx22$ m (or $v^2=2as$ gives $s=\frac{20^2}{2(9.09)}=22$ m).

**Energy in free fall.** Gravitational potential energy is converted to kinetic energy: $mgh=\frac12mv^2$. With $h\approx22$ m, $v=\sqrt{2gh}\approx20$ m s$^{-1}$, which agrees with the graph, showing that energy is conserved when only gravity acts (no losses).

**Braking (about 2.2 s to 3.2 s).** When the magnets pass the copper fins, the changing magnetic flux through the fins induces emf (Faraday's law, $\varepsilon=-\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$) and so eddy currents. By Lenz's law these currents flow in the direction that opposes the change, so the fins exert an upward magnetic force on the magnets that is much greater than the weight. The acceleration becomes positive (upward) with an initial gradient of about $+25$ m s$^{-2}$, and the platform slows rapidly.

**Variation of the braking force.** The induced emf and eddy currents are proportional to the rate of change of flux, so are largest when the platform is moving fastest. The braking force and deceleration are therefore greatest at about $2.2$ s, and decrease smoothly as the platform slows, so the velocity approaches zero with a gradient tending to zero (at about $3$ s).

**Overall energy.** The platform's gravitational potential energy is converted to kinetic energy in free fall. During braking its kinetic energy (and some remaining gravitational potential energy) is converted to electrical energy in the eddy currents and then to thermal energy in the copper fins. The total energy is conserved overall.

questions.question: Cosmic rays collide with air molecules in the Earth's upper atmosphere, at around $10$ km above the Earth's surface, to produce muons. The muons then travel at a speed of $0.99c$ towards the surface where some of the muons are detected by scientists. Muons are known to have an average lifetime of $2.2\ \mu$s when measured by an observer at rest relative to the muons. Explain how some of the muons are detected at the surface of the Earth when relativistic effects are considered from both the muons' and the scientists' perspective. Include relevant calculations.
questions.answer:
**Scientists' (Earth) frame: time dilation.** The $2.2\ \mu$s lifetime is a proper time, measured in the muon's frame. The scientists measure a dilated lifetime $t=\frac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}=\frac{2.2}{\sqrt{1-0.99^2}}=15.6\ \mu$s. In this time the muons travel $d=vt=0.99(3.00\times10^8)(15.6\times10^{-6})=4.6\times10^3$ m $=4.6$ km. Without dilation the average distance would be only $0.99c(2.2\ \mu\text{s})\approx650$ m. Because the lifetime is an average and the muons live this much longer, a significant fraction ($10\ \text{km}\approx2.2$ dilated lifetimes) survive the $10$ km trip, so some reach the surface.

**Muons' frame: length contraction.** In the muon's frame the atmosphere is moving at $0.99c$, so the $10$ km distance (proper length) is contracted: $l=l_0\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}=10\,000\sqrt{1-0.99^2}=1.41\times10^3$ m. The time to reach the surface is $t=\frac{l}{v}=\frac{1410}{0.99(3.00\times10^8)}=4.75\ \mu$s, which is about two lifetimes ($2.2\ \mu$s), so a fraction of the muons ($e^{-4.75/2.2}\approx11\%$) survive.

Both frames agree that some muons reach the surface.

Note: The school's solution states the distance travelled in the Earth frame as $4.631\times10^3$ km; the correct value is $4.63\times10^3$ m (4.6 km).

questions.question: What is the temperature of a black body whose intensity peaks at $5.4 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$?
questions.answer: $\lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{c}{f} = \dfrac{3.00 \times 10^{8}}{5.4 \times 10^{14}} = 5.56 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}$. Wien's law: $T = \dfrac{b}{\lambda_{\max}} = \dfrac{2.898 \times 10^{-3}}{5.56 \times 10^{-7}} = 5216\ \text{K} \approx 5.2 \times 10^{3}\ \text{K}$ (Wien's law gives the temperature in kelvin).

questions.question:
A 400 nm laser is shone through a diffraction grating which has 10 lines/mm. A screen is placed 3.0 m away, on which several bright bands are seen.

The pattern on the screen is best explained by:
options: The interference of light as each slit acts as a source.
Each band corresponding to a slit in the diffraction grating through which light is passing.
The interference of the laser with background light.
questions.answer: Each slit acts as a source of secondary wavelets (Huygens); the bright bands are where waves from the slits interfere constructively ($d\sin\theta = m\lambda$). This is a wave (interference) effect.

questions.question:
A 400 nm laser is shone through a diffraction grating which has 10 lines/mm. A screen is placed 3.0 m away, on which several bright bands are seen.

Calculate the distance from the central bright band to an adjacent bright band.
questions.answer: $d = \dfrac{1}{10\ \text{mm}^{-1}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}$. For $m = 1$: $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{d} = \dfrac{400 \times 10^{-9}}{1.0 \times 10^{-4}} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}$. For small angles $x = L\tan\theta \approx L\sin\theta = 3.0 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-3} = 1.2 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}$.

questions.question: What is the momentum of an electron which has been accelerated to $0.98c$ in a particle accelerator, as measured by a detector?

The diagram represents an experimental apparatus: unpolarised light passes through a polariser and then an analyser. The intensity of the (unpolarised) light entering the polariser is 513 lux.

What is the intensity of light as it leaves the analyser if the angle between the polariser and analyser is $17.0^\circ$?
questions.answer: The polariser halves unpolarised light: $I_1 = \tfrac{513}{2} = 256.5$ lux. Malus' law at the analyser: $I = I_1\cos^2\theta = 256.5 \times \cos^2 17.0^\circ = 234.6 \approx 235$ lux.

questions.question:
Diagram 1 shows the absorption spectrum of light produced by an incandescent filament, after it has been shone through a quantity of hydrogen gas. Diagrams 2 and 3 show the spectra obtained from two stars: Croesus and Dromus. The dark lines in the diagrams are absorption bands.

Which of the following conclusions CANNOT be drawn from the diagrams?
options: Dromus is rotating faster than Croesus.
Croesus has a higher surface temperature than Dromus.
questions.answer: Both stars show the hydrogen line pattern (B). Dromus's lines are broadened (rotation, A) and shifted towards the violet end (blueshift, approaching, C). Surface temperature comes from the peak wavelength / colour of the continuous spectrum, which these line diagrams do not show, so D cannot be concluded.

questions.question:
Which row of the table correctly matches the scientists to the type of experiment they performed when attempting to measure the speed of light?

| | Römer | Bradley | Fizeau | Foucault |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | Rotating component | Rotating component | Astronomical methods | Astronomical methods |
| (B) | Astronomical methods | Astronomical methods | Rotating component | Rotating component |
| (C) | Rotating component | Astronomical methods | Astronomical methods | Rotating component |
| (D) | Astronomical methods | Rotating component | Rotating component | Astronomical methods |
questions.answer: Römer (eclipses of Io) and Bradley (stellar aberration) used astronomical observations; Fizeau (rotating toothed wheel) and Foucault (rotating mirror) used rotating components.

questions.question: Some early experiments into the nature of cathode rays included the Maltese cross experiment, the paddle wheel experiment, deflecting a beam with a magnet, and deflecting a beam with an electric field. Which of the following conclusions could NOT be drawn from these early experiments?
options: Cathode rays consist of negatively charged particles.
Cathode rays travel in straight lines.
The mass of the particles in cathode rays.
questions.answer: Deflection by fields shows negative charge (A), the Maltese cross shadow shows straight-line travel (B), and the paddle wheel shows they carry momentum/energy (C). None of these experiments measures the mass of the particles (Thomson only found $q/m$; the mass needed Millikan's $q$ as well).

questions.question:
An oil drop is suspended between horizontal charged plates separated by 3.2 mm, with a potential difference of 4.7 kV across them and the positive plate on the bottom, as shown.

The oil drop was estimated to have a volume of $2.1 \times 10^{-16}\ \text{m}^3$. Given that the density of oil is $8.0 \times 10^{2}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$, how many excess or missing electrons are on the drop of oil?
questions.answer:
$m = \rho V = 8.0 \times 10^{2} \times 2.1 \times 10^{-16} = 1.68 \times 10^{-13}\ \text{kg}$; $E = \dfrac{V}{d} = \dfrac{4700}{3.2 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.47 \times 10^{6}\ \text{V m}^{-1}$.

Suspended: $qE = mg \Rightarrow q = \dfrac{1.68 \times 10^{-13} \times 9.8}{1.47 \times 10^{6}} = 1.12 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{C}$, so $n = \dfrac{1.12 \times 10^{-18}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 7$.

The field points up (from the bottom positive plate to the top negative plate) and the electric force must be upward, so the drop is positive: 7 electrons are **missing**.

questions.question: Two projectiles are launched horizontally from the same height. Projectile B has twice the initial velocity of projectile A. Which of the following statements is true? ($u$ = initial velocity, $t$ = time of flight, $R$ = range)
options: $u_{Ax} = \tfrac12 u_{Bx};\ u_{Ay} = u_{By};\ t_A = t_B;\ R_A = \tfrac12 R_B$
$u_{Ax} = \tfrac12 u_{Bx};\ u_{Ay} = u_{By};\ t_A = 2t_B;\ R_A = R_B$
$u_{Ax} = \tfrac12 u_{Bx};\ u_{Ay} = u_{By};\ t_A = t_B;\ R_A = R_B$
questions.answer: Both have $u_y = 0$ and fall the same height, so $t_A = t_B$. Range $R = u_x t$, so with half the horizontal velocity $R_A = \tfrac12 R_B$.

questions.question: A satellite revolves around a planet X1B2 with a period of $2.45 \times 10^{7}\ \text{s}$ at an orbital radius of $3.80 \times 10^{10}\ \text{m}$. What is the mass of X1B2?
questions.answer: $\dfrac{r^3}{T^2} = \dfrac{GM}{4\pi^2} \Rightarrow M = \dfrac{4\pi^2 r^3}{GT^2} = \dfrac{4\pi^2 (3.80 \times 10^{10})^3}{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times (2.45 \times 10^{7})^2} = 5.41 \times 10^{28}\ \text{kg}$.

questions.question:
The diagram shows a DC motor. The arrows show the direction of force acting on the sides of the coil.

What happens to the magnitude of the forces as the coil rotates?
options: The forces remain the same at all orientations of the coil to the vertical.
The forces vary as a sine component of the angle to the vertical.
The forces vary as a cos component of the angle to the vertical.
The forces initially increase and then stay constant.
questions.answer: The sides carrying the force stay perpendicular to the field as the coil rotates, so $F = nIlB$ is constant in magnitude (and direction). It is the **torque** $\tau = nIAB\sin\theta$ that varies with orientation, not the force.

questions.question:
Two satellites of equal mass, E and F, are orbiting the Earth at orbital radii of $2R$ and $5R$ respectively (measured from the centre of the Earth), $R$ being the radius of the Earth. Which row of the table is true? ($U$ = gravitational potential energy, $v$ = orbital velocity.)

| | Gravitational potential energy | Escape velocity from the surface of the Earth | Orbital velocity |
|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | $U_F = U_E$ | $5v_F = 2v_E$ | $v_F = \sqrt{2}\,v_E$ |
| (B) | $U_F = 2.5\,U_E$ | Equal | $v_F = v_E$ |
| (C) | $2U_F = 5U_E$ | $2v_F = 5v_E$ | $\sqrt{2}\,v_F = \sqrt{5}\,v_E$ |
| (D) | $5U_F = 2U_E$ | Equal | $\sqrt{5}\,v_F = \sqrt{2}\,v_E$ |
questions.answer:
$U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$: $U_E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2R}$, $U_F = -\dfrac{GMm}{5R}$, so $5U_F = 2U_E = -\dfrac{GMm}{R}$.

Escape velocity from the Earth's surface $v_{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/R}$ depends only on the Earth, so it is equal.

Orbital velocity $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$: $\sqrt5\,v_F = \sqrt5\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{5R}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R}} = \sqrt2\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{2R}} = \sqrt2\,v_E$.

*Note:* the original paper says “altitudes of $2R$ and $5R$”, but its answer (D) treats these as orbital radii; with altitudes (radii $3R$ and $6R$) none of the rows would be correct, so the question has been reworded.

questions.question:
The primary coil of a transformer has 450 turns and the secondary has 1800 turns. Which choice listed in the table is most appropriate for this ideal transformer?

| | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| (A) | 5.00 A, 23.0 V | 2.00 A, 92.0 V |
| (B) | 5.00 A, 23.0 V | 1.25 A, 92.0 V |
| (C) | 10.0 A, 46.0 V | 5.00 A, 184 V |
| (D) | 10.0 A, 46.0 V | 2.50 A, 69.0 V |
questions.answer: $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{1800}{450} = 4$, so the voltage is stepped up 4 times and (since $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$) the current is divided by 4: $23.0 \to 92.0$ V and $5.00 \to 1.25$ A. Check: $5.00 \times 23.0 = 1.25 \times 92.0 = 115$ W.

questions.question:
The diagram shows the top view of a magnet rotating above a copper disc in an anticlockwise direction.

Which statement correctly represents the motion of the copper disc?
options: The disc follows the magnet's rotation but at a higher speed than the magnet.
The disc follows the magnet's rotation but at a lower speed than the magnet.
The disc spins in the opposite direction to the magnet's rotation but at a higher speed than the magnet.
The disc spins in the opposite direction to the magnet's rotation but at a lower speed than the magnet.
questions.answer: The moving field induces eddy currents in the disc which, by Lenz's law, oppose the relative motion, so the disc is dragged round in the same direction as the magnet (as in an induction motor). It must always rotate slower, because if it caught up there would be no relative motion and no induced current.

questions.question:
The diagram shows three parallel current-carrying conductors, each of length 0.500 m and carrying 2.5 A in the directions shown: conductor 1 (top, current to the right) is 0.55 m above conductor 2 (current to the right), and conductor 3 (current to the left) is 0.15 m below conductor 2.

What is the force acting on conductor 2?
questions.answer:
$F = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\dfrac{I_1I_2 l}{r}$. From 1 (same direction, attracts, up): $F = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 2.5^2 \times 0.500}{0.55} = 1.14 \times 10^{-6}$ N up.

From 3 (opposite direction, repels, so pushes 2 up): $F = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 2.5^2 \times 0.500}{0.15} = 4.17 \times 10^{-6}$ N up.

Total: $5.3 \times 10^{-6}$ N up.

questions.question: A proton is moving through a circular path (in a particle accelerator, as shown) of radius 102 m with a velocity of $2.25 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Assuming the magnetic field is constant at all points in the path and is perpendicular to the motion, what is the magnitude of the magnetic field needed to maintain the circular motion of the proton?
questions.answer: $qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} \Rightarrow B = \dfrac{mv}{qr} = \dfrac{1.673 \times 10^{-27} \times 2.25 \times 10^{5}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19} \times 102} = 2.30 \times 10^{-5}$ T.

questions.question: A 10.0 cm conductor rod levitates in an external magnetic field of 4.20 T that is acting at right angles to the rod. A current of 2.50 A flows through the rod. What is the mass of this rod?
questions.answer: Levitating: $BIl = mg \Rightarrow m = \dfrac{4.20 \times 2.50 \times 0.100}{9.8} = 0.107 \approx 0.11$ kg.

questions.question: The diagram shows a metallic plate swinging (from position 1 towards position 2) through a region of uniform magnetic field directed into the page. At position 1 the plate is entering the field region; at position 2 it is leaving it. Which of the following statements about the motion is correct?
options: At position 1, the plate experiences a resistive force due to eddy currents flowing anticlockwise and at position 2, the plate experiences a resistive force due to clockwise eddy currents.
At position 1, the plate experiences an attractive force due to eddy currents flowing anticlockwise and at position 2, the plate experiences a resistive force due to clockwise eddy currents.
At position 1, the plate experiences a resistive force due to eddy currents flowing clockwise and at position 2, the plate also experiences a resistive force due to anticlockwise eddy currents.
At position 1, the plate experiences a resistive force due to eddy currents flowing anticlockwise and at position 2, the plate experiences a resistive force due to anticlockwise eddy currents.
questions.answer: Entering (1): flux into the page increases, so by Lenz's law the eddy currents make a field out of the page — anticlockwise. Leaving (2): flux into the page decreases, so the eddy currents make a field into the page — clockwise. In both cases the force opposes the motion (resistive, magnetic braking).

questions.question: Which of the following graphs shows the relationship between a photon's energy $E$ and its wavelength $\lambda$?
questions.answer: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, so $E$ is inversely proportional to $\lambda$: a hyperbola decreasing towards the $\lambda$-axis.

questions.question:
A ball of mass 0.130 kg is swung around on a string of length 95.5 cm at 5.00 revolutions per second in a vertical circle (assume uniform circular motion).

Determine the difference in tension on the ball at the top and the bottom points of the vertical circle.
questions.answer:
Centripetal force (the same at top and bottom since the speed is constant): $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T} = 2\pi \times 0.955 \times 5.00 = 30.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $F_c = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{0.130 \times 30.0^2}{0.955} = 122.5$ N.

Bottom (centre is up): $T_b - mg = F_c \Rightarrow T_b = F_c + mg = 122.5 + 1.27 = 123.8$ N.

Top (centre is down): $T_t + mg = F_c \Rightarrow T_t = F_c - mg = 122.5 - 1.27 = 121.2$ N.

Difference: $T_b - T_t = 2mg = 2 \times 0.130 \times 9.8 = 2.55$ N (greater at the bottom).

questions.question: Compare the structure and function of an AC generator with that of a DC motor.
questions.answer:
**Similarities.** *Structure:* both have a coil of wire (usually wound on an iron armature) that rotates on an axle in an external magnetic field produced by magnets or electromagnets, connected to the external circuit through brushes. *Function:* both involve a coil rotating in a magnetic field, and an emf is induced in the rotating coil in both (in the motor this is the back emf).

**Differences.** *Structure:* the AC generator connects the coil to the external circuit through **slip rings**, so the output current reverses each half turn; the DC motor uses a **split-ring commutator**, which reverses the current in the coil every half turn so the torque stays in the same direction.

*Function:* the AC generator converts mechanical (kinetic) energy into electrical energy — an external torque turns the coil and, by Faraday's law, an alternating emf is induced. The DC motor converts electrical energy from a DC supply into kinetic energy — the current in the coil experiences a force in the field (the motor effect, $F = nIlB$) producing a torque $\tau = nIAB\sin\theta$.

questions.question: The discovery of the interaction between magnetic and electric fields brought about many laws and applications. Analyse at least 3 laws or principles and at least 2 applications that arose from this discovery.
questions.answer:
**Motor effect.** A current-carrying conductor in an external magnetic field experiences a force $F = lIB\sin\theta$, because the field of the current interacts with the external field. This is the principle of the **DC motor**: forces on the sides of a current-carrying coil produce a torque $\tau = nIAB\sin\theta$, converting electrical energy into rotational kinetic energy (fans, pumps, electric vehicles); it is also used in galvanometers and loudspeakers.

**Force between parallel conductors (Ampère).** Each current produces a magnetic field that acts on the other: $\dfrac{F}{l} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\dfrac{I_1I_2}{r}$, attractive for currents in the same direction. This was used to define the ampere and must be allowed for in, e.g., spacing of transmission lines and busbars.

**Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction.** A changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an emf $\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$. This is the principle of the **generator** (a coil rotating in a field has an alternating emf induced, delivered via slip rings for AC or a commutator for DC) and of the **transformer** (an alternating current in the primary produces a changing flux in the iron core that induces an emf in the secondary, $V_p/V_s = N_p/N_s$), which allows high-voltage, low-current transmission of electricity with low resistive losses.

**Lenz's law.** The induced current flows in the direction that creates a magnetic field opposing the change that produced it — a consequence of conservation of energy. Applications: **electromagnetic (eddy current) braking**, where eddy currents induced in a moving metal disc or plate oppose its motion, converting kinetic energy to heat without contact (trains, roller coasters); and **back emf** in DC motors, which limits the current as the motor speeds up.

Together (and unified by Maxwell's equations), these principles underpin the generation, transmission and use of electrical energy.

questions.question:
Lauren throws a basketball with a horizontal component of velocity of $8.00\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The ball reaches the original height from which it was thrown after 3.00 s, and takes a further 0.11 s to reach the ground (ignore air resistance).

Calculate the horizontal range.
questions.answer: Total time of flight $t = 3.00 + 0.11 = 3.11$ s. Range $= u_x t = 8.00 \times 3.11 = 24.9$ m.

questions.question:
Lauren throws a basketball with a horizontal component of velocity of $8.00\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The ball reaches the original height from which it was thrown after 3.00 s, and takes a further 0.11 s to reach the ground (ignore air resistance).

Calculate the vertical component of the initial velocity.
questions.answer:
By symmetry the ball reaches its maximum height at $t = 1.50$ s, where $v_y = 0$. Taking up as positive, $a = -9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$:

$v_y = u_y + at \Rightarrow 0 = u_y - 9.8 \times 1.50 \Rightarrow u_y = 14.7\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (upwards).

questions.question:
Lauren throws a basketball with a horizontal component of velocity of $8.00\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The ball reaches the original height from which it was thrown after 3.00 s, and takes a further 0.11 s to reach the ground (ignore air resistance).

Given that the vertical component of the initial velocity is $14.7\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, calculate the initial angle of projection.
questions.answer: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{u_y}{u_x} = \dfrac{14.7}{8.00} \Rightarrow \theta = 61.4^\circ$ above the horizontal.

questions.question:
Lauren throws a basketball with a horizontal component of velocity of $8.00\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The ball reaches the original height from which it was thrown after 3.00 s, and takes a further 0.11 s to reach the ground (ignore air resistance).

Given that the vertical component of the initial velocity is $14.7\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, calculate the height at which Lauren threw the ball.
questions.answer:
When the ball returns to the launch height it is moving downwards at $14.7\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (symmetry). Taking down as positive for the last 0.11 s:

$\Delta y = u_y t + \tfrac12 g t^2 = 14.7 \times 0.11 + \tfrac12 \times 9.8 \times 0.11^2 = 1.617 + 0.059 = 1.68$ m.

questions.question:
The diagram shows the apparatus for the Geiger–Marsden experiment: a beam of alpha particles from a radium source is directed at a thin gold foil surrounded by a fluorescent screen.

Explain how the results of this experiment led Rutherford to develop his atomic model.
questions.answer:
Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil with little or no deflection, so most of the atom must be empty space. A very small fraction were deflected through large angles, and some even bounced back. Such large deflections of the massive, fast, positively charged alpha particles could only be caused by strong electrostatic repulsion from a concentrated region of positive charge containing most of the atom's mass (the Thomson 'plum pudding' model, with charge spread out, could not produce them). Because so few were strongly deflected, this region had to be tiny compared with the atom.

Rutherford therefore proposed the nuclear (planetary) model: a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre of the atom containing almost all its mass, with electrons orbiting it at a relatively large distance.

questions.question: Explain how experimental evidence led Chadwick to his discovery of the neutron.
questions.answer:
When beryllium was bombarded with alpha particles it emitted a very penetrating radiation that was not deflected by electric or magnetic fields, so it was neutral; others had assumed it was gamma radiation. When this radiation struck paraffin wax (rich in hydrogen), protons were ejected with very high energies (about 5.7 MeV).

For massless gamma photons to knock out protons with this energy, they would need an implausibly large energy (around 50 MeV) — inconsistent with conservation of energy and momentum for the reaction. Chadwick measured the recoil of protons and of nitrogen nuclei struck by the radiation and, applying conservation of momentum and energy to these collisions, showed the radiation consisted of neutral particles with mass approximately equal to that of the proton. He called them neutrons, which also accounted for the 'missing' mass of nuclei (mass number greater than atomic number).

questions.question:
Researchers conducted an experiment to determine the maximum kinetic energy of electrons emitted from a plate of potassium when irradiated with light of various frequencies.

| Frequency (Hz) | Max recorded KE (J) |
|---|---|
| $0.00 \times 10^{14}$ | 0.00 |
| $2.00 \times 10^{14}$ | 0.00 |
| $4.00 \times 10^{14}$ | 0.00 |
| $6.00 \times 10^{14}$ | $0.31 \times 10^{-19}$ |
| $8.00 \times 10^{14}$ | $1.63 \times 10^{-19}$ |
| $10.00 \times 10^{14}$ | $2.96 \times 10^{-19}$ |
| $12.00 \times 10^{14}$ | $4.28 \times 10^{-19}$ |
| $14.00 \times 10^{14}$ | $5.61 \times 10^{-19}$ |
| $16.00 \times 10^{14}$ | $6.93 \times 10^{-19}$ |

Plot the data on a graph of maximum kinetic energy ($\times 10^{-19}$ J, from $-6$ to $10$) against frequency ($\times 10^{14}$ Hz, from 0 to 18) and add an appropriately extrapolated line of best fit.
questions.answer: Plot all nine points with labelled axes and units. The first three points (zero KE, below the threshold frequency) are **not** part of the linear trend.
