questions.answer: The graph shows that $t_1$ is at the minimum of the sine curve, three quarters of the way through a cycle. The magnet rotates anticlockwise from N pointing up, through N left (1/4), N down (1/2), to N pointing right (3/4), as in C.

questions.question: A group of students uses the apparatus shown to determine the wavelength of the monochromatic light emitted from a discharge tube behind a narrow slit. A diffraction grating is placed at the end of the ruler and the students observe the diffracted image of the first order fringe. They move the pin P to align with the first order fringe and measure the distance $x$. Which of the following would improve the accuracy of the results?
questions.answer: The second order fringe is further from the central position, so the measured distance is larger and the same ruler uncertainty is a smaller fraction of it; this improves accuracy (D). Raising the voltage does not change the wavelength; repeating the experiment improves reliability/precision (it does not remove a systematic error); shorter rulers would not reach the fringe.
options: Increase the voltage supplied to the discharge tube.
Replace the two 1 m rulers with 30 cm rulers of the same scale.
Measure the position of the second order bright fringe instead of the first order.

questions.question: An aeroplane with a wingspan of 37.8 m is flying at a speed of $230\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ parallel to the Earth's surface. It travels through an area with a magnetic field strength of $4.59\times10^{-5}$ T. The magnetic field makes an angle of $25^\circ$ to the vertical. Which of the following is the induced emf between the ends of the aeroplane's wings?
questions.answer: Only the vertical component of the field is cut by the horizontal wings: $\varepsilon=B\cos25^\circ\times l\times v=(4.59\times10^{-5})(\cos25^\circ)(37.8)(230)=0.36$ V (B).

questions.question: A laser is positioned inside a space capsule exactly half-way between two emergency hatches P and Q. The hatches open automatically when light from the laser reaches them. The capsule travels past a scientist on Earth at a constant speed of $0.7c$ (towards Q) and the laser is switched on at the exact time it passes the scientist. Which of the following best describes the observation made by the scientist?
questions.answer: In the scientist's frame light travels at $c$ in both directions (second postulate), but hatch P is moving towards the light and hatch Q is moving away from it. The light reaches P first, so P opens before Q (A). (For observers in the capsule they open simultaneously: simultaneity is relative.)

questions.question: A particle P is placed at a height $h$ above the ground on a loop-the-loop track. The radius of the loop is $r$. If P is released from rest, what is the minimum value of $h$ in order for P to complete the loop?
questions.answer: Conservation of energy from release to the top of the loop (height $2r$): $\tfrac12mv^2=mg(h-2r)$, so $v^2=2g(h-2r)$. At the top, the minimum condition is that the normal force is zero, so gravity alone provides the centripetal force: $mg=\dfrac{mv^2}r$, i.e. $v^2=gr$. Then $2g(h-2r)=gr$, so $h=2.5r$ (B).

questions.question: The gravitational force $F$ acting on a planet due to the Sun's gravitational field varies with the planet's distance $r$ from the centre of the Sun as shown in the graph. Which of the following quantities of the planet is given by the area under the graph between X and Y?
questions.answer: The area under a force against distance graph is $\int F\,dr$, the work done by the force (a force multiplied by a distance, not by a time, so not an impulse). Work done by the field equals the negative of the change in gravitational potential energy, so the area gives the magnitude of the change in gravitational potential energy (B).
options: The impulse of the gravitational force
The change in the gravitational potential energy

questions.question: A proton enters a region of uniform electric field formed by two parallel charged plates with a potential difference of 25 V separated by $2.3\times10^{-2}$ m. The proton enters the electric field $6.5\times10^{-3}$ m below the positive plate and exits the field $4.1\times10^{-3}$ m above the negative plate. What is the work done on the proton by the electric field?

Astronomers detected an asteroid orbiting Proxima Centauri with a radius of $2.55\times10^{13}$ m. The asteroid was detected because of the small change in velocity of Proxima Centauri as the asteroid orbits it. The graph shows how the component of Proxima Centauri's velocity towards the Earth varied over time. Which of the following is closest to the velocity required for the asteroid to escape Proxima Centauri's gravitational field from its orbit?
questions.answer: The star's velocity oscillates with the period of the asteroid's orbit, which from the graph is $T=19$ days. $v_{orbit}=\dfrac{2\pi r}T=\dfrac{2\pi(2.55\times10^{13})}{19\times86400}=9.76\times10^7\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Escape speed from the orbit is $\sqrt2\,v_{orbit}=1.38\times10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (B), since $v_{esc}=\sqrt{2GM/r}$ and $v_{orbit}=\sqrt{GM/r}$.

questions.question: Describe the main differences between the models of light proposed by Newton and Huygens.
questions.answer: Newton proposed that light consists of particles (which he called corpuscles), while Huygens proposed that light is a wave, propagating as wavelets (every point on a wavefront acting as a source of secondary wavelets).

questions.question: In 1801, Thomas Young conducted his famous double slit experiment. Explain which model of light was supported by his experimental results.
questions.answer: When light was shone on a double slit, an interference pattern of alternating bright and dark fringes formed on a distant screen. Light from the two slits (diffracted at each slit) travels different distances to a point on the screen. Where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths ($n\lambda$) the waves arrive in phase and interfere constructively, producing a bright fringe. Where the path difference is $\left(n+\tfrac12\right)\lambda$ the waves arrive out of phase and interfere destructively, producing a dark fringe. Interference and diffraction can only be explained by waves, so the experiment supported Huygens' wave model of light.

questions.question: Two identical masses of 26.5 kg are placed with their centres separated by a distance of $d$ m. Given that $d=11.0$ m, calculate the gravitational force between the two masses.

Describe the graph of the gravitational force between the two masses as they are separated, and state the magnitudes of the force when the separation of the centres is $2d$ and $4d$ (as a sketch of force against separation). Take $d=11.0$ m.
questions.answer: The graph is an inverse-square curve: it decreases steeply and levels off, approaching the separation axis without touching it ($F\propto 1/r^2$). At $d$: $3.87\times10^{-10}$ N. At $2d$ the force is $\tfrac14$ of this: $9.7\times10^{-11}$ N. At $4d$ the force is $\tfrac1{16}$: $2.4\times10^{-11}$ N.

questions.question: A circular coil of diameter 125 mm has 450.0 turns. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 85 mT such that its plane is perpendicular to the magnetic field. Calculate the magnetic flux passing through the coil when it is in the position shown.
questions.answer: Flux does not depend on the number of turns. $\phi=BA\cos\theta=(85\times10^{-3})\left[\pi\left(\dfrac{0.125}2\right)^2\right]\cos0^\circ=1.0\times10^{-3}$ Wb.

questions.question: The coil (diameter 125 mm, 450.0 turns, in a uniform field of 85 mT, initially perpendicular to the field) is rotated through $90^\circ$ about the axis XX$'$ in a time of 135 ms. Calculate the average emf induced in the coil during this time.
questions.answer: After a $90^\circ$ rotation the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, so the final flux is zero. $\Delta\phi=0-1.0\times10^{-3}=-1.0\times10^{-3}$ Wb. $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{\Delta\phi}{\Delta t}=-450.0\times\dfrac{-1.0\times10^{-3}}{135\times10^{-3}}$. The average emf has magnitude about 3.5 V (3.3 V if the rounded flux of $1.0\times10^{-3}$ Wb is used, 3.5 V using the unrounded value $1.04\times10^{-3}$ Wb).

questions.question: Explain how the Hafele-Keating experiment validated Einstein's theory of special relativity.
questions.answer: In the Hafele-Keating experiment, very precise atomic clocks were flown on aeroplanes around the world, one eastward (in the direction of Earth's rotation) and one westward, and compared with identical atomic clocks that stayed on the ground. Atomic clocks were needed because the predicted time differences are tiny. The clocks on the eastward plane recorded less elapsed time, and those on the westward plane more, than the ground clocks, in agreement with the time dilation predicted by Einstein's theory. This was the first experimental validation using macroscopic clocks, confirming that the elapsed time depends on relative motion.

questions.question: Matthew takes a 1.00 metre ruler and sets off in a spaceship. He travels past Anna at a speed of $0.75c$ with the ruler aligned in the direction of travel. Matthew and Anna both measure the length of the ruler at the instant they pass each other. How long does Anna measure the ruler to be?

Matthew measures a 1.00 m ruler travelling with him, and Anna (measuring as he passes at $0.75c$) finds it to be 0.66 m. When Matthew returns, they compare the results of their measurements. How are they able to explain their seemingly contradictory results?
questions.answer: The results are consistent with Einstein's special relativity (length contraction). Matthew is at rest relative to the ruler (in the same inertial frame), so he measures its proper length, 1.00 m. Anna is in a different inertial frame, moving relative to the ruler, so she measures a contracted length, 0.66 m. Neither is wrong: lengths measured in different inertial frames of reference differ, and both frames are equally valid.

questions.question: Mimas is a moon of Saturn and orbits Saturn with a mean radius of $1.86\times10^8$ m and orbital period of 0.942 Earth days. Calculate the mass of Saturn.

Dione is another moon of Saturn and orbits Saturn with a mean radius of $3.78\times10^8$ m. Given that Mimas orbits Saturn with a mean radius of $1.86\times10^8$ m and orbital period of 0.942 Earth days, calculate the orbital period of Dione in Earth days.
questions.answer: Kepler's third law: $\dfrac{r_M^3}{T_M^2}=\dfrac{r_D^3}{T_D^2}$, so $\dfrac{(1.86\times10^8)^3}{(0.942)^2}=\dfrac{(3.78\times10^8)^3}{T_D^2}$, giving $T_D=2.73$ Earth days.

questions.question: Dione orbits Saturn in an elliptical orbit. Explain why the orbital velocity of Dione changes as it orbits Saturn.
questions.answer: In an elliptical orbit Dione's distance from Saturn's centre changes, so its gravitational potential energy changes. By conservation of energy the total energy is constant, so a change in gravitational potential energy results in an equal and opposite change in kinetic energy, and hence in speed. When Dione is closest to Saturn its potential energy is lowest and its speed is greatest; when it is furthest away its speed is lowest (consistent with Kepler's second law: equal areas swept in equal times).

questions.question: Coin A is placed on a rotating disc at 1.35 m from the centre of the disc. It has a mass of 15.0 g. The disc begins to rotate and when the frequency of rotation reaches 2.5 Hz, the coin flies off the disc. Give a reason for why Coin A flies off the disc.
questions.answer: The friction between the coin and the disc provides the centripetal force. At this speed the friction needed exceeds the maximum (limiting) friction available, so it can no longer keep the coin moving in a circle, and the coin moves off along a tangent.

questions.question: Coin A (mass 15.0 g) is at 1.35 m from the centre of a rotating disc. Calculate the centripetal force experienced by Coin A just before it flies off, when the frequency of rotation is 2.5 Hz.

Coin A is placed back in its original position, 1.35 m from the centre of a rotating disc. Another identical coin, Coin B, is placed on the same disc closer to the centre. The disc begins to rotate. Explain which coin will fly off the disc first.
questions.answer: Both coins are on the same disc, so they have the same period and angular velocity. Coin A is further from the centre, so it has a greater speed ($v=2\pi r/T$) and needs a greater centripetal force ($F_c=m\omega^2r$). The coins are identical, so the maximum friction force available is the same for each. Coin A reaches the limiting friction first, so Coin A will fly off first.

questions.question: The diagrams show the key components of two devices, a dynamo torch and an AC induction motor. A dynamo torch operates by squeezing the handle continuously, which causes a permanent magnet to rotate near a fixed coil inside the torch. Compare the physics principles that allow the two devices to operate. In your answer, make reference to the conservation of energy and the components of the devices.
questions.answer: Dynamo torch: squeezing the handle rotates the permanent magnet, so the magnetic flux linking the fixed coil changes continuously. By Faraday's law an emf is induced in the coil, and the current produced lights the bulb. By Lenz's law the induced current produces a magnetic field that opposes the change in flux (the rotation of the magnet), so work must be done by the hand: mechanical (kinetic) energy is converted to electrical energy, consistent with conservation of energy. AC induction motor: the stationary electromagnets of the stator are supplied with AC currents that are out of phase with each other, which creates a rotating magnetic field. The rotor (conducting loops or bars, with no electrical connection to the supply) sees a changing flux, so by Faraday's law currents are induced in it. By Lenz's law these currents oppose the change in flux, so the rotor is made to follow the rotating field. The induced currents in the rotor are in the stator's magnetic field, so by the motor effect the rotor experiences a torque and rotates. Electrical energy is converted to kinetic energy (with some lost as heat). Comparison: both depend on electromagnetic induction (Faraday's and Lenz's laws) and on a rotating magnetic field relative to a conductor. The dynamo (a generator) converts kinetic to electrical energy, while the induction motor converts electrical to kinetic energy. The torch has a rotating permanent magnet and a fixed coil, while the induction motor has fixed electromagnets (stator) producing a rotating field and a rotating coil/rotor in which the current is induced, and the motor also relies on the motor effect.

questions.question: KPLO is a satellite of mass 678.0 kg in a circular orbit about the Moon. Define gravitational potential of an object at a point in a gravitational field.
questions.answer: The gravitational potential at a point is the gravitational potential energy per unit mass at that point, $V=\dfrac Um=-\dfrac{GM}r$: the work done per unit mass in bringing a small mass from infinity (where $V=0$) to that point. (The school's marking guide describes this as work done by the field; the potential is negative, since the field does positive work and the zero is at infinity.)

questions.question: KPLO is a satellite of mass 678.0 kg in a circular orbit about the Moon. Point A is a point in KPLO's orbit and point B is a point on the surface of the Moon. Given that the gravitational potential energy of KPLO at A is 95% of its gravitational potential energy at B and the gravitational field strength at B is 1.622 N/kg, calculate the gravitational field strength at A.
questions.answer: $U_A=0.95U_B$, so $-\dfrac{GMm}{r_A}=0.95\left(-\dfrac{GMm}{r_B}\right)$, giving $r_A=\dfrac{r_B}{0.95}$. $g=\dfrac{GM}{r^2}$, so $g_A=\dfrac{GM}{(r_B/0.95)^2}=0.95^2g_B=0.9025\times1.622=1.46$ N kg$^{-1}$.

questions.question: At the end of the 1800s scientists recognised that there was a relationship between light and electromagnetism. They began performing experiments which used the apparatus shown (a light source shining on an emitter in a vacuum chamber, a receiver, an ammeter and a variable DC power supply). Discuss how the experimental results could only be explained by the development of a new model of light.
questions.answer: These are the photoelectric effect experiments, whose results could not be explained by the classical wave model, which prompted Einstein's photon (particle) model. Result: a photocurrent is detected only when the frequency of the light is above a threshold value, regardless of the intensity of the light (and the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons depends on the frequency, not the intensity). Wave model: energy is proportional to intensity, so light of high enough intensity should eject electrons at any frequency, and the electrons' energy should increase with intensity. The data contradict this. Photon model: light comes in photons with energy $E=hf$, and each electron absorbs one photon. If the photon energy is below the work function no electron is ejected, however many photons there are (high intensity); if it is above, electrons are ejected with $K_{max}=hf-\phi$, and a greater intensity (more photons) increases the number of electrons, and so the current, not their energy.

questions.question: In a video game, the player fires arrows at a fixed speed of $53.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from the top of a 45.0 m high castle tower, with the angle of projection $\theta$ adjustable. Assume air resistance is negligible. Show that the angle of projection of the arrow is $72.3^\circ$ if the arrow reaches a maximum height of 175.0 m above the ground.
questions.answer: At maximum height $v_y=0$, and the vertical displacement from the launch point is $175.0-45.0=130.0$ m. $v_y^2=u_y^2+2a_ys$: $0=(53.0\sin\theta)^2+2(-9.8)(130.0)$, so $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{2548}}{53.0}=0.9525$ and $\theta=72.3^\circ$.

questions.question: In a video game, the player fires arrows at $53.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ to the East from the top of a 45.0 m high castle tower. The target moves around the castle in a circular path of radius 180.0 m in an anti-clockwise direction (viewed from above), and takes 16.0 s to complete one revolution. The target is initially placed South of the castle. Given that the arrow will have a range of 180.0 m when projected at $72.3^\circ$, how long should the player wait before firing the arrow such that it will hit the target?
questions.answer: Time of flight: $s_x=u_xt$, so $180.0=(53.0\cos72.3^\circ)t_f$ and $t_f=11.17$ s. Anticlockwise from South, the target reaches East after a quarter of a revolution: $\tfrac14\times16.0=4.00$ s. Since $t_f>4.00$ s, the arrow cannot hit the target the first time it is East. It must hit it the second time, at $16.0+4.00=20.0$ s. The player must wait $20.0-11.17=8.83$ s.

questions.question: The diagrams show the front view and top view of a moving coil galvanometer. The fixed soft iron cylinder and magnets produce a uniform (radial) magnetic field between the magnets. The coil is able to rotate within this field. A current I flows in the coil in the direction shown. Explain which direction the pointer will move.
questions.answer: The current flows from D to C in the coil. By the motor effect (the right-hand palm rule, with the field from N to S) side DC experiences a downward force. The force on the opposite side is in the opposite direction, so the coil experiences an anticlockwise torque (as seen in the front view), and the pointer moves to the negative part of the scale.

questions.question: The coil of a moving coil galvanometer can be damaged when the galvanometer is transported due to the free rotation of the coil. A student suggests that the terminals of the galvanometer could be connected together to reduce the movement of the coil, which would make it less likely to be damaged. Evaluate the student's suggestion.
questions.answer: The suggestion is valid. If the terminals are connected together, the coil is part of a closed circuit. When the galvanometer is moved and the coil rotates in the magnetic field, the flux through the coil changes, so by Faraday's law an emf and a current are induced. By Lenz's law, the induced current produces a force (motor effect) that opposes the change that caused it, which is the rotation of the coil. This electromagnetic damping reduces the movement of the coil, making damage less likely.

questions.question: A photon of wavelength $6.924\times10^{-12}$ m collides with a stationary electron. What is the original energy of the photon in eV?

A photon collides with a stationary electron. After the collision, the photon travels back in the direction it came from with a greater wavelength. No other particles or photons are produced. Explain why the wavelength of the photon is greater after the collision.
questions.answer: By conservation of energy, the electron gains kinetic energy at the expense of the photon, so the photon loses energy. Since $E=hf$, the photon's frequency decreases. The photon still travels at $c$ ($c=f\lambda$), so a lower frequency means a greater wavelength.

questions.question: A photon of wavelength $6.924\times10^{-12}$ m collides with a stationary electron. After the collision, the photon travels back in the direction it came from with a new wavelength of $9.351\times10^{-12}$ m. No other particles or photons are produced. Calculate the speed of the electron after the collision.
questions.answer: Final photon energy: $f_f=\dfrac{3.00\times10^8}{9.351\times10^{-12}}=3.21\times10^{19}$ Hz, so $E_f=hf_f=2.13\times10^{-14}$ J. By conservation of energy the electron gains $E_e=2.87\times10^{-14}-2.13\times10^{-14}=7.45\times10^{-15}$ J. $\tfrac12m_ev^2=7.45\times10^{-15}$: $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2(7.45\times10^{-15})}{9.109\times10^{-31}}}=1.28\times10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. (This uses the classical kinetic energy, as in the school's solution; the speed is about $0.43c$, where relativistic effects start to matter.)

questions.question: Two proposals for a new power station to supply electricity to a rural town. Proposal 1: a DC power station (100.0 MW at 25.0 kV) connected by 15 km of transmission lines directly to the factory. Proposal 2: an AC power station (100.0 MW at 25.0 kV) with Transformer 1 stepping up to 500.0 kV for 15 km of transmission lines, then Transformer 2 stepping down to 240 V at the factory. The resistance of the transmission lines in both proposals is $3.21\times10^{-4}\ \Omega\,\text{m}^{-1}$. Assess the efficiency of the two power station proposals for the town and suggest a way to improve the efficiency of each proposal. Your analysis should include power delivered, conservation of energy and the efficiency of the transformer. Include both qualitative and quantitative information.
questions.answer: Line resistance: $R=(3.21\times10^{-4})(15\times10^3)=4.815\ \Omega$. Proposal 1 (DC at 25 kV): $I=\dfrac PV=\dfrac{100.0\times10^6}{25.0\times10^3}=4000$ A. $P_{loss}=I^2R=(4000)^2(4.815)=77.0$ MW. Power delivered $=100.0-77.0=23.0$ MW, an efficiency of about 23%. Proposal 2 (AC, 500 kV): for an ideal transformer $P_{in}=P_{out}$, so $I=\dfrac{100.0\times10^6}{500.0\times10^3}=200$ A. $P_{loss}=(200)^2(4.815)=192.6$ kW. Power delivered $\approx100.0-0.19=99.8$ MW, an efficiency of about 99.8% (for ideal transformers). Comparison: by conservation of energy, the power lost in the lines (as heat) is power not delivered. Stepping up the voltage by a factor of 20 reduces the current by a factor of 20 and the $I^2R$ loss by a factor of 400, so Proposal 2 is far more efficient. Real transformers are not 100% efficient: energy is lost as heat in the windings (resistance), eddy currents and hysteresis in the core, and incomplete flux linkage, so the actual power delivered in Proposal 2 would be a little lower than 99.8 MW. Improvements: Proposal 1 – a transformer cannot be used with DC (there is no changing flux), so reduce the loss by generating at a much higher voltage, or use thicker (lower resistance) cables, or shorten the line, or use AC with transformers. Proposal 2 – use a laminated, high-permeability soft iron core to reduce eddy current and hysteresis losses, thicker windings to reduce heating, or tighter winding to improve flux linkage (or lower resistance transmission lines).

questions.question: A ball is thrown horizontally from the top of a building with speed $v$, and it hits the ground with a range $R$ from the bottom of the building. A second ball is thrown horizontally from the top of the same building with speed $2v$. What is the range of the second ball?
questions.answer: Both balls have zero initial vertical velocity, so the time to fall the building's height, $t=\sqrt{2h/g}$, is the same for both. The horizontal motion is uniform, so $R=vt\propto v$. Doubling the launch speed doubles the range: $2R$ (C).

questions.question: Two satellites orbit Earth, as shown. Satellite A has a circular orbit and Satellite B an elliptical orbit. The velocities at different points are shown by arrows. Which of the following correctly describes the work done by the gravitational field of Earth on Satellite A as it moves from R to S, and on Satellite B as it moves from P to Q?
questions.answer: Work done is $W=F_\parallel s$. In a circular orbit the gravitational force is always perpendicular to the motion, the speed is constant and the potential energy does not change, so the work done on A is zero. In an elliptical orbit the force generally has a component along the path; from P (closest point) to Q (farthest point) satellite B slows down and its gravitational potential energy increases, so net (negative) work is done on it. Work on A is zero and on B is non-zero (B).

questions.question: Quantised energy levels within atoms can best be explained by
questions.answer: Treating the electron as a matter wave (de Broglie), only those orbits that can hold a whole number of wavelengths, i.e. standing waves, are stable. This restricts the allowed energies to discrete levels (D). A pure particle model (A) would predict radiation from the accelerating electron (Maxwell), and diffraction patterns (C) are unrelated to energy levels.
options: electrons behaving as individual particles with varying energies.
atoms having specific energy requirements that can only be satisfied by electrons.
electrons behaving as waves, with each energy level representing a diffraction pattern.
electrons behaving as waves, with only standing waves at particular wavelengths allowed.

questions.question: Actinium-227 can undergo either alpha- or beta-decay. What would be the product nuclei for either of the two modes of radioactive decay?
questions.answer: Alpha decay: $^{227}_{89}\text{Ac}\rightarrow{}^{223}_{87}\text{Fr}+{}^{4}_{2}\alpha$. Beta-minus decay: $^{227}_{89}\text{Ac}\rightarrow{}^{227}_{90}\text{Th}+{}^{0}_{-1}\beta+\bar\nu$ (mass number unchanged, atomic number up by one). Answer A.

questions.question: The cathode ray tube shown contains a rotating paddle wheel that is free to move. The tube's electrodes are connected to a high-voltage source. Which of the following statements about cathode rays does this apparatus provide evidence for?
questions.answer: The paddle wheel turns when struck by the cathode rays, so the rays transfer momentum (and energy) to it, which indicates they are particles with mass and momentum (C). The path of the rays is not visible so straight-line travel is not shown; the apparatus says nothing about production only in vacuum; and electromagnetic waves would not deliver enough momentum to turn the wheel.
options: Cathode rays travel in straight lines.
Cathode rays can only be produced in vacuum tubes.
Cathode rays are particles that have momentum.
Cathode rays are waves of high frequency and short wavelength.

questions.question: Which graph is consistent with predictions resulting from Planck's hypothesis regarding radiation from hot objects?
questions.answer: Planck's black-body curves (intensity against wavelength) have a single peak whose height increases and whose wavelength decreases as temperature increases (Wien's law). So the hottest curve (1650 K) is the highest, with its peak at the shortest wavelength. Graph B shows this. Graphs A and C order the temperatures the wrong way round and plotting against frequency (C, D) gives curves of a different shape (B).

questions.question: At two separate times, two charged particles approach a current-carrying wire (current to the left) and follow the trajectories shown. What are the signs of the charges for particles X and Y?
questions.answer: The right-hand grip rule gives the field of the wire: into the page above the wire and out of the page below it. Above the wire particle X moves to the right and is deflected upwards (away from the wire). Using the right-hand palm rule with $\mathbf v$ to the right and $\mathbf B$ into the page, the force on a positive charge is up, so X is positive. Below the wire $\mathbf B$ is out of the page; particle Y moves to the left and is deflected away from the wire (downwards). For a positive charge moving left in an out-of-the-page field the force would be up (towards the wire), so Y must be negative (A).

questions.question: Unpolarised light of intensity $I_0$ is incident upon a vertically polarised filter. The filtered light then passes through a pair of glasses whose lenses are polarising filters, with one lens polarised vertically (giving $I_y$) and the other horizontally (giving $I_z$). The filter undergoes a $180^\circ$ rotation about point $P$, as shown. Which of the following correctly compares $I_y$ and $I_z$ during the rotation (where $\theta$ is the angle through which the filter has rotated)?
questions.answer: By Malus's law, $I=I_{\max}\cos^2\theta$ where $\theta$ is the angle between the polarising directions. Initially the filter and the vertical lens (for $I_y$) are parallel, so $I_y$ starts at a maximum, falls to zero when they are perpendicular ($90^\circ$) and returns to maximum at $180^\circ$. For $I_z$ the filter and the horizontal lens start perpendicular, so $I_z$ starts at zero, rises to a maximum at $90^\circ$ and returns to zero at $180^\circ$. Graph B shows this.

questions.question: J. J. Thomson determined the charge/mass ratio of the electron by constructing a device which contained
questions.answer: Thomson used perpendicular electric and magnetic fields as a velocity selector ($qE=qvB$, so $v=E/B$). With the electric field removed, the magnetic field alone bent the beam into a circular arc of radius $r$, giving $\frac qm=\frac vBr=\frac{E}{B^2r}$ (D).

questions.question: Why is an iron core used in a transformer?
questions.answer: The soft iron core guides the changing magnetic flux from the primary coil through the secondary coil, increasing the flux linkage between them (C). Heating from eddy currents is reduced by laminating the core, not by using iron itself.
options: To increase the linkage of the flux

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a contribution by Maxwell?
questions.answer: Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism, predicted electromagnetic waves and calculated their speed ($c=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$). Radio waves were first produced and detected by Hertz, so D is not a contribution by Maxwell.
options: Predicting the velocity of electromagnetic radiation

questions.question: An electrical generator is shown in the diagram. The generator is turning clockwise. The voltage between P and Q and the magnetic flux through the loop are both graphed as functions of time, with voltage as a solid line and magnetic flux as a dashed line. Which one of the following graphs best shows the relationships for this electrical generator?
questions.answer: In the position shown the loop's area vector is parallel to the field, so the flux starts at a maximum, then falls to zero and reverses. By Faraday's law $\varepsilon=-N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, so the voltage is proportional to the negative gradient of the flux graph: it is zero where the flux is at a maximum or minimum and is at a maximum magnitude where the flux crosses zero, so the two curves are a quarter-cycle out of phase. Only graph D has the flux starting at a maximum with the voltage starting at zero and the two curves a quarter-cycle apart (D).

questions.question: A bar magnet and a solenoid are suspended next to each other from a fixed platform, as shown. The switch on the solenoid circuit is closed. Which choice correctly indicates the direction(s) the magnet and solenoid will move immediately after the switch is closed?
questions.answer: Closing the switch gives a current in the solenoid. By the right-hand grip rule for a solenoid, the current produces a north pole on the left end of the solenoid (the end facing the magnet). This attracts the south pole of the bar magnet, so the magnet moves right (towards the solenoid) and, by Newton's third law, the solenoid moves left (towards the magnet) (A).
options: Magnet moves right; solenoid moves left
Magnet moves left; solenoid moves right
Magnet moves right; solenoid moves right
Magnet moves left; solenoid moves left

questions.question: In a thought experiment, observer X is on a train travelling at a constant velocity of $0.95c$ relative to the ground. Observer Y is standing on the ground outside the train. As observer X passes observer Y, observer X sends a short light pulse towards the sensor. Which statement about the light pulse is correct as observed by X or Y in their respective frames of reference?
questions.answer: The speed of light is $c$ in both frames (so A is false). In X's frame the carriage is at rest and the pulse travels the proper length $L_0$ in time $L_0/c$. In Y's frame the sensor moves away from the pulse while it travels, so although the carriage is length-contracted the total distance the light covers is greater, $ct=\frac{L_0}{\gamma}+vt$, giving $t=\frac{L_0}{\gamma(c-v)}=\frac{L_0}{c}\sqrt{\frac{c+v}{c-v}}\approx6.2\frac{L_0}{c}$ for $v=0.95c$. So X sees a shorter distance and a shorter time than Y (B).
options: Its velocity observed by Y is $0.05c$.
X sees it travel a shorter distance to the sensor than Y.
X sees it take a longer time to reach the sensor than Y.
Both X and Y see it travel the same distance in the same amount of time.

questions.question: Two positive point charges, $q$ and $4q$, are placed 12 cm apart, as shown in the scale diagram. At which point along the straight line between the charges $q$ and $4q$ will a null point be found?
questions.answer: At the null point the electric fields of the two charges are equal and opposite: $\frac{kq}{r_1^2}=\frac{k(4q)}{r_2^2}$, so $\frac{r_2}{r_1}=\sqrt4=2$. The null point is therefore twice as far from $4q$ as from $q$: $r_1=4$ cm and $r_2=8$ cm from the charges. On the scale diagram this is point R (C).

questions.question: A carriage rolls down a rollercoaster track under the influence of gravity from point P, as shown. It proceeds along the track and around a vertical loop of radius $r$, before reaching the end of the track. Ignoring friction, which expression shows the decrease in speed from $u$ at point A (bottom of the loop) to $v$ at point B (top of the loop)?
questions.answer: Conservation of energy between A (bottom) and B (top, a height $2r$ higher): $\frac12mu^2=\frac12mv^2+mg(2r)$, so $u^2-v^2=4gr$. Then $(u-v)(u+v)=4gr$ and $u-v=\dfrac{4gr}{u+v}$ (C).

questions.question: Explain refraction using both Huygens' and Newton's theories of light.
questions.answer: **Huygens (wave model):** every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets, and the new wavefront is the envelope of these wavelets. When light enters a denser medium (e.g. water) it travels more slowly, so the wavelets are smaller in radius in the same time. The wavefront therefore pivots and the refracted rays bend towards the normal, with the wave speed decreasing in the denser medium.\n\n**Newton (corpuscular model):** light consists of particles (corpuscles). As a corpuscle approaches a denser medium, the matter in that medium attracts it towards the interface, so the component of its velocity perpendicular to the surface increases while the component parallel to the surface is unchanged. The net velocity vector therefore bends towards the normal. (This predicts that light travels faster in a denser medium, the opposite of the wave model.)

questions.question: A distant exoplanet, Methanos, has a single moon, Propedes. Compare the force of gravity exerted on Propedes by Methanos with the force of gravity exerted on Methanos by Propedes.
questions.answer: By Newton's law of universal gravitation, $F=\frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$, and by Newton's third law the two forces form an action–reaction pair. They have the **same magnitude** and **opposite directions** (each is directed towards the other body).

questions.question: The acceleration due to gravity on the moon Propedes is $2.2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ and on the planet Methanos it is $12.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Quantitatively compare the mass and weight of a 95 kg astronaut on Propedes and on Methanos.
questions.answer: Mass is a property of the astronaut and does not change: it is 95 kg on both. Weight $=mg$: on Propedes $95\times2.2=209$ N; on Methanos $95\times12.8=1216$ N. The astronaut's weight on Methanos is about 5.8 times the weight on Propedes.

questions.question: A square coil of conducting wire, 44.0 cm long, is placed in a 2.75 T magnetic field directed into the page, as shown in Figure 1. The shape of the coil is uniformly changed to a circular shape in 1.25 ms, as shown in Figure 2. Calculate the magnitude of the average induced EMF.
questions.answer: Square: side $=\frac{0.440}{4}=0.110$ m, area $=0.110^2=0.01210\ \text{m}^2$. Circle: $2\pi r=0.440$, so $r=0.07003$ m and $A=\pi r^2=0.01541\ \text{m}^2$. Change in area $=0.003306\ \text{m}^2$, so $\Delta\Phi=B\Delta A=2.75\times0.003306=9.09\times10^{-3}$ Wb. Then $|\varepsilon|=\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=\frac{9.09\times10^{-3}}{1.25\times10^{-3}}=7.27$ V. (The school's solution gives 7.26 V — a rounding difference.)

questions.question: A square coil of conducting wire is placed in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page and is uniformly reshaped into a circle of larger area (Figures 1 and 2). Identify the direction of the current that passes through the conducting wire as a result of the induced EMF.
questions.answer: The flux into the page through the loop is increasing. By Lenz's law the induced current opposes this change by producing a field out of the page inside the loop. By the right-hand grip rule this requires an **anticlockwise** current.

questions.question: In the 1840s, the French physicist Hippolyte Fizeau performed an experiment to measure the speed of light. He shone an intense light source at a mirror 8.50 km away and broke up the light beam with a rotating cogwheel. He increased the speed of rotation of the wheel until the reflected light beam could no longer be seen returning through the gaps in the cogwheel. The diagram shows a similar experiment. The cogwheel has 50 teeth and 50 gaps of the same width. Explain why specific speeds of rotation of the cogwheel will completely block the returning light. Support your answer with calculations.
questions.answer: At low speeds a pulse of light passes through a gap, reflects from the mirror and returns through the same gap, so the observer sees the light. The round-trip time for the light is fixed: $t=\frac{2d}{c}=\frac{2\times8.50\times10^3}{3.00\times10^8}=5.67\times10^{-5}$ s. As the wheel speeds up, the wheel turns further during this time. When, in this time, the wheel has turned through exactly the angular width of one gap-to-tooth step, a tooth has moved into the path of the returning light and blocks it. With 50 teeth and 50 gaps there are 100 equal sections, so each step is $\theta=\frac{2\pi}{100}=0.0628$ rad. The first speed that blocks the light is $\omega=\frac{\theta}{t}=\frac{0.0628}{5.67\times10^{-5}}=1.11\times10^{3}\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$ (about 176 revolutions per second). The light will also be blocked whenever the wheel advances by an odd number of steps in the round-trip time, so for odd multiples of this speed ($3\times1110$, $5\times1110$ rad s$^{-1}$, …); at even multiples the next gap lines up and the light is seen again.

questions.question: A polonium-218 atom, at rest, undergoes radioactive decay, with a decay constant of $0.2236\ \text{min}^{-1}$. The masses of the nuclei involved are: polonium → lead + helium-4: $218.00897\ \text{u}\rightarrow213.99981\ \text{u}+4.00260\ \text{u}$. Calculate the energy, in joules, released by this decay.
questions.answer: Mass defect: $\Delta m=218.00897-(213.99981+4.00260)=0.00656\ \text{u}$. Energy: $E=\Delta m\times931.5\ \text{MeV}=0.00656\times931.5=6.11\ \text{MeV}=6.11\times10^{6}\times1.602\times10^{-19}=9.8\times10^{-13}$ J. (Equivalently $\Delta m=0.00656\times1.661\times10^{-27}=1.09\times10^{-29}$ kg and $E=mc^2=9.8\times10^{-13}$ J. The school's worked solution has a sign typo in the mass line and gets $9.82\times10^{-13}$ J. The paper labels the nuclides polonium-118 and lead-114, but the masses given are those of polonium-218 and lead-214.)

questions.question: A polonium nucleus undergoes spontaneous alpha decay to produce lead-214. Identify whether the lead nucleus has a higher or lower binding energy per nucleon than the polonium nucleus.
questions.answer: Higher. The decay is spontaneous and releases energy, so the products are more stable (more tightly bound) than the parent nucleus: the lead nucleus has a higher binding energy per nucleon.

questions.question: A radioisotope has a decay constant of $0.2236\ \text{min}^{-1}$ when at rest in the laboratory. If an ion of this isotope is accelerated in a particle accelerator to $0.99945c$, what will be its decay constant as measured in the laboratory?
questions.answer: Because of time dilation the half-life in the laboratory is longer: $t_{1/2}'=\gamma t_{1/2,0}$, with $\gamma=\frac1{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$. Since $\lambda=\frac{\ln2}{t_{1/2}}$, the decay constant in the lab is $\lambda'=\frac{\lambda_0}{\gamma}=\lambda_0\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}=0.2236\times\sqrt{1-0.99945^2}=0.2236\times0.03316=7.4\times10^{-3}\ \text{min}^{-1}$ (about $1.24\times10^{-4}\ \text{s}^{-1}$).

questions.question: The first four wavelengths of the Balmer series of hydrogen are: $H_\alpha$ 656.3 nm, $H_\beta$ 486.2 nm, $H_\gamma$ 434.1 nm, $H_\delta$ 410.2 nm (transitions $n=3,4,5,6\to2$). Calculate the next wavelength, $H_\varepsilon$, in the Balmer series.
questions.answer: The next line is the $n=7\to n=2$ transition. $\frac1\lambda=R\left(\frac1{2^2}-\frac1{7^2}\right)=1.097\times10^{7}\left(\frac14-\frac1{49}\right)=2.519\times10^{6}\ \text{m}^{-1}$, so $\lambda=3.970\times10^{-7}$ m $=397.0$ nm.

questions.question: An astronomer measures the spectrum of a distant star. The $H_\alpha$ absorption line (rest wavelength 656.3 nm) is measured to have a wavelength of 673.2 nm. Ignoring the velocity of the Earth, determine the velocity of the star with respect to Earth.
questions.answer: The line is shifted to a longer wavelength (red-shifted), so the star is moving away. For $v\ll c$, $\frac{\lambda'-\lambda}{\lambda}=\frac vc$, so $v=c\frac{\lambda'-\lambda}{\lambda}=3.00\times10^8\times\frac{673.2-656.3}{656.3}=7.7\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ away from Earth. (The school's solution quotes $7.71\times10^6$; unrounded the value is $7.72\times10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.)

questions.question: The spectrum of a distant star shows intensity against wavelength with a peak at about 400 nm (the horizontal axis is labelled in µm in the paper but the wavelengths are in nm). The star is receding at $7.71\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, so the observed spectrum is Doppler shifted. Calculate the surface temperature of the star.
questions.answer: The observed peak is at 400 nm and has been red-shifted. The wavelength in the star's frame is $\lambda_{\text{peak}}=\lambda'\frac{c}{c+v}=400\times\frac{3.00\times10^8}{3.00\times10^8+7.71\times10^6}=390.0$ nm. By Wien's law, $T=\frac{b}{\lambda_{\max}}=\frac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{390.0\times10^{-9}}=7.43\times10^{3}\ \text{K}$.

questions.question: Geiger and Marsden performed their gold-foil experiment, measuring the number of alpha particles scattered at different angles. The results are shown (most particles pass straight through; very few are scattered through large angles, and a few are scattered back). Based on these results, Rutherford proposed his model of the atom. How do features of his model account for all the experimental evidence above?
questions.answer: Rutherford's model has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus containing almost all of the atom's mass, with electrons orbiting at distances much greater than the nuclear size, so the atom is mostly empty space. Because the atom is mostly empty space, almost all the alpha particles pass straight through the foil undeflected. (The electrons are far too light to deflect the heavy alpha particles significantly.) A very small fraction are deflected through large angles, some almost straight back, because they approach close to a gold nucleus and are strongly repelled by the electrostatic force between the positive nucleus and the positive alpha particle. The nucleus is massive compared with the alpha particle, so it can reverse its motion.

questions.question: Using examples from special relativity, explain how theories in science are validated in different ways.
questions.answer: Scientific theories are validated using the scientific method: the theory is used to make a prediction, an experiment is performed to test the prediction, and the results are compared with the prediction. If the results agree, the theory is supported; if not, it must be modified or rejected. Special relativity has been validated by several different experiments. **Muon decay (Frisch–Smith):** special relativity predicts that moving muons' lifetimes are dilated, so more muons reach sea level than would be expected from their rest half-life. Measurements of muons at altitude and at sea level showed the larger number predicted by relativity, supporting time dilation. **Particle accelerator experiments:** lithium ions accelerated to about one-third the speed of light had electron transitions that took longer, as measured in the laboratory frame, than those of stationary ions, again in agreement with time dilation. In both cases a prediction made by the theory (time dilation) was tested experimentally and found to agree, so the theory was validated in different ways (natural cosmic-ray muons and controlled laboratory accelerators). Thought experiments were used to develop the theory but are not validation, and the Michelson–Morley experiment preceded special relativity.

questions.question: Two experiments are performed with identical light sources having a wavelength of 295 nm. In experiment A, the light is incident on a pair of narrow slits 12 µm apart, producing a pattern of bright and dark bands on a screen located 2.0 m behind the slits. In experiment B, the light is incident on different metal samples inside an evacuated tube. The kinetic energy of any emitted photoelectrons can be measured. Results from experiment B: magnesium (work function 3.7 eV) gives a galvanometer reading of 3.26 µA; gold (work function 5.1 eV) gives 0.00 µA. How do the results from Experiment A and Experiment B support TWO different models of light? In your answer, include a quantitative analysis of each experiment.
questions.answer: **Experiment A – wave model.** Light passing through the two slits diffracts and the two waves interfere, producing alternating bright (constructive) and dark (destructive) bands. The band spacing is $\Delta y=\frac{\lambda L}{d}=\frac{295\times10^{-9}\times2.0}{12\times10^{-6}}=0.049$ m $\approx4.9$ cm. Only waves show diffraction and interference, so this supports the wave model.\n\n**Experiment B – particle (photon) model.** Photon energy: $E=\frac{hc}{\lambda}=\frac{6.626\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^8}{295\times10^{-9}}=6.74\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}=4.2\ \text{eV}$. For gold, $E=4.2\ \text{eV}<\phi=5.1\ \text{eV}$, so a single photon does not have enough energy to eject an electron, and no photocurrent is observed (0.00 µA) no matter how intense the light. For magnesium, $E=4.2\ \text{eV}>3.7\ \text{eV}$, so electrons are emitted with $K_{\max}=hf-\phi=4.2-3.7=0.5\ \text{eV}$ and the galvanometer registers a current. The current of 3.26 µA corresponds to $\frac{I}{e}=\frac{3.26\times10^{-6}}{1.602\times10^{-19}}=2.0\times10^{13}$ electrons per second. Emission depending on the energy (frequency) of individual photons rather than on intensity cannot be explained by the wave model and supports the particle (quantum) model.

questions.question: Three charged particles of identical mass, X, Y and Z, travelling along straight, parallel trajectories, enter a region in which there is a uniform electric field (directed downwards) which causes them to follow the paths shown: X and Y curve upwards (Y with the shallower curve) and Z curves downwards. Assume that the particles do not exert any significant force on each other. Explain the different paths that the particles follow through the electric field.
questions.answer: A charge in a uniform electric field experiences a constant force $F=qE$ parallel to the field (a force $-qE$ against it for a negative charge), so it has a constant acceleration $a=\frac{qE}{m}$ along the field and none perpendicular to it. The motion is therefore like a projectile: constant velocity perpendicular to the field and constant acceleration parallel to it, so the paths are parabolic. The field points down. X and Y are deflected up, opposite to the field, so they are negatively charged; Z is deflected down, in the direction of the field, so it is positively charged. Since the masses and field are the same, the sideways deflection depends on $\frac qm$ and the initial speed: $y=\frac12\frac{qE}{m}t^2$ with $t=\frac xv$. Particle Y has a shallower path than X, so it has either a smaller charge magnitude or a greater initial speed (it travels further along the field region before being deflected to the plate). Z has the same curved shape as X but deflected in the opposite direction, so it has a similar charge magnitude but opposite sign. There are no magnetic effects (no circular motion) and no significant forces between the particles.

questions.question: A simple motor consists of a flat rectangular coil with 175 turns in a uniform magnetic field of 0.25 T, as shown. The coil carries a current of 0.75 A. The motor drives a pulley of diameter 50 cm, and weights can be hung from either side of the pulley at point X or point Y. In order to prevent rotation, should a weight be hung at point X or at point Y? Justify your answer.
questions.answer: Using the right-hand palm rule, the force on the top side of the coil is to the left, so the coil rotates anticlockwise (as viewed in the diagram) and turns the pulley anticlockwise. A weight must be hung at point **Y** so that its torque on the pulley acts in the opposite (clockwise) sense and balances the motor torque.

questions.question: A simple motor consists of a flat rectangular coil with 175 turns in a uniform magnetic field of 0.25 T. The coil carries a current of 0.75 A (coil plane parallel to the field). The motor drives a pulley of diameter 50 cm. If the motor is just stopped by a mass of 0.2 kg hung from the pulley, what area does the coil have?
questions.answer: The torques balance: $\tau_{\text{motor}}=\tau_{\text{weight}}$. $\tau_{\text{motor}}=nIAB\sin\theta$, with $\theta=90^\circ$ (coil parallel to field), and $\tau_{\text{weight}}=mgr$ with $r=0.25$ m. So $A=\frac{mgr}{nIB}=\frac{0.2\times9.8\times0.25}{175\times0.75\times0.25}=0.0149\ \text{m}^2\approx0.015\ \text{m}^2$.

questions.question: A shot putter releases a 4.0 kg shot put at an angle of $45^\circ$ above the horizontal with a launch speed of $11.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from a height of 1.8 m above the ground. Determine the range of her throw.
questions.answer: $v_x=11.8\cos45^\circ=8.344\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and $v_y=11.8\sin45^\circ=8.344\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (upwards). Taking up as positive, $y=1.8+8.344t-\frac12(9.8)t^2=0$, i.e. $4.9t^2-8.344t-1.8=0$, so $t=\frac{8.344+\sqrt{8.344^2+4(4.9)(1.8)}}{2(4.9)}=\frac{8.344+10.24}{9.8}=1.896$ s. Range $=v_xt=8.344\times1.896=15.8$ m. (Equivalently: rise to peak 3.55 m above release in 0.851 s, then fall 5.35 m in 1.045 s.)

questions.question:
A beam of particles was fired at a metal crystal, resulting in a diffraction pattern on the detector screen. The speed of the particles was varied, and the diffraction pattern was used to determine the associated wavelengths. Results (1 pm $=10^{-12}$ m):

| Speed ($\times10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$) | 1.4 | 2.9 | 4.1 | 6.8 | 7.3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wavelength (pm) | 56.3 | 27.2 | 17.2 | 11.6 | 8.5 |
| Inverse of the wavelength (pm$^{-1}$) | 0.017 | 0.039 | 0.051 | 0.089 | 0.117 |

Plot a graph of the particle speed (horizontal axis) against the inverse of the wavelength (vertical axis), with labelled axes including units, and draw a suitable line of best fit.
questions.answer: Plot particle speed (in $10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$) on the horizontal axis and $1/\lambda$ (in $\text{pm}^{-1}$) on the vertical axis, with a linear scale and labelled axes with units, mark each data point (e.g. with a cross) and draw a straight line of best fit through the points, ignoring the point at 7.3 which lies clearly off the trend (the outlier). See the graph.

questions.question: Particles were fired at a metal crystal and their de Broglie wavelengths determined from the diffraction pattern. A graph of inverse wavelength $1/\lambda$ (vertical axis, in $\text{pm}^{-1}$) against particle speed (horizontal axis, in $10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$) gives a straight line of best fit passing through approximately $(2.0,\ 0.026)$ and $(6.6,\ 0.086)$. Use the graph to determine the mass of the particles.
questions.answer: From the de Broglie relation $\lambda=\frac{h}{mv}$, $\frac1\lambda=\frac mhv$, so the gradient of the graph is $\frac mh$. Gradient $=\frac{(0.086-0.026)\times10^{12}\ \text{m}^{-1}}{(6.6-2.0)\times10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}}=1.30\times10^{4}\ \text{s m}^{-2}$. Then $m=h\times\text{gradient}=6.626\times10^{-34}\times1.30\times10^{4}=8.6\times10^{-30}$ kg. (The school's solution has $13\,043\ \text{s m}^{-2}$ and $8.64\times10^{-30}$ kg; a least-squares line through the non-outlier points gives about $8.7\times10^{-30}$ kg.)

questions.question: The diagram shows the isotope half-lives against the number of protons ($Z$) and neutrons ($N$) for known nuclides, with the stable nuclides forming a narrow band. Outline features of the nuclear force that explain the stability of isotopes illustrated in the diagram.
questions.answer: Gravity is negligible between nucleons because of their tiny masses. The nuclear (strong) force is a strongly attractive force acting between neighbouring nucleons over a very short range (about 0.8–2.5 fm), and in this range it is much larger than the repulsive Coulomb force between protons, so it holds the nucleus together. It is charge independent: it acts between proton–proton, proton–neutron and neutron–neutron pairs, so neutrons add attraction without adding repulsion (which is why heavier stable nuclei have more neutrons than protons). At very small separations (below about 0.8 fm) the nuclear force becomes repulsive, which prevents the nucleus from collapsing.

questions.question: Which of the following scientists is credited with the mathematical unification of electricity and magnetism?
questions.answer: Maxwell's equations described electric and magnetic fields in one mathematical framework, unifying electricity and magnetism (and predicting electromagnetic waves).

questions.question: Which of the following is a standard assumption when analysing the motion of projectiles?
options: The path of the projectile is an ellipse
questions.answer: The standard projectile model assumes zero air resistance and a constant (uniform) vertical acceleration $g$ downwards, giving a parabolic path.

questions.question: The force of gravity between two objects is $F$. What happens to the force of gravity between both objects if the distance between the objects is doubled?
questions.answer: $F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$, an inverse-square law. Doubling $r$ gives $\dfrac{F}{2^2} = \dfrac{F}{4}$.

questions.question: Which of the following variables need to be aligned for a satellite to be in geostationary orbit around a planet?
options: The orbital velocity of both the satellite and the planet are equal.
The period of one revolution of the satellite is equal to the time taken for one spin of the planet on its axis.
The period of the planet and the satellite is equal.
The mass of the planet and the satellite must be equal.
questions.answer: A geostationary satellite stays above the same point on the surface, so its orbital period must equal the planet's rotational period (24 h for Earth), orbiting in the same direction above the equator.

questions.question: A person with a viral infection has their body temperature rise from 37 °C (310 K) to 40 °C. What is the change in the peak wavelength of electromagnetic radiation emitted?
questions.answer: Wien's law $\lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{b}{T}$: $\dfrac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{310} = 9.348\times10^{-6}$ m and $\dfrac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{313} = 9.259\times10^{-6}$ m. The peak wavelength decreases by $8.96\times10^{-8}$ m (higher temperature → shorter peak wavelength).

questions.question:
An 0.800 kg mass is swinging in a horizontal circle on the end of a conical pendulum as shown. The radius of the circle $r$ is 0.25 m and the period $T$ is 2.0 s.

What is the kinetic energy of the mass?
questions.answer: $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi(0.25)}{2.0} = 0.785\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, so $K = \tfrac12 mv^2 = \tfrac12(0.800)(0.785)^2 = 0.25$ J. (Note: options B and D in the original paper are identical, and both were accepted; 0.79 is the speed, not the energy.)

questions.question:
Several planets with identical size but different masses had their surface gravitational acceleration, $g$, plotted against their masses, $M$.

Which alternative best represents this graph?
questions.answer: $g = \dfrac{GM}{r^2}$. With $r$ the same for every planet, $g \propto M$: a straight line through the origin.

questions.question: How does back EMF affect the operation of an electric motor?
options: It prevents the motor from starting.
It increases the power output of the motor.
It increases the current drawn from the power source.
It reduces the current drawn from the power source when the motor speeds up.
questions.answer: As the coil rotates faster, the induced back emf (which opposes the supply emf, by Lenz's law) increases, so the net emf and hence the current drawn from the supply decrease.

questions.question:
The following graph plots data for a number of galaxies.

Which of the following is true about the trend shown in this graph?
options: It is linear because all galaxies are receding at the same rate.
It provides evidence for the 'Big Bang'.
It shows that the expansion of the universe is slowing.
It proves that every galaxy is redshifted.
questions.answer: The graph shows Hubble's law: recession velocity is proportional to distance, so more distant galaxies recede faster. This expansion of the universe is evidence for the Big Bang. (Galaxies recede at different rates; one data set cannot show slowing or *prove* every galaxy is redshifted.)

questions.question: The role of a commutator in a DC motor is to:
options: change the direction of current relative to the coil.
keep the current flowing in the same direction relative to the coil.
questions.answer: The split-ring commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn, so the torque on the coil keeps acting in the same rotational direction.

questions.question: Calculate the wavelength of a tennis ball of mass 59.4 g travelling at 170 km h$^{-1}$.
In each diagram below, a rectangular coil connected to a split-ring commutator sits in a magnetic field (dotted arrows). Which of the following scenarios will produce the greatest torque on the coil?
questions.answer: $\tau = nIAB\sin\theta$. In B the plane of the coil is parallel to the field (maximum torque) and the coil has two turns, so $n$ is largest. In C the field is perpendicular to the plane of the coil, giving zero torque.

questions.question: Which of the following is an observation from the Hafele–Keating experiment that supports Einstein's theory of special relativity?
options: Clocks flown westward (in the opposite direction to Earth's rotation) were slowed the most.
Clocks flown eastward (in the same direction as Earth's rotation) were slowed the most.
Clocks flown eastward and westward were equally slowed.
Clocks flown eastward and westward were not slowed.
questions.answer: Relative to an inertial frame at Earth's centre, eastward-flying clocks move fastest (plane speed adds to Earth's rotation), so they experienced the most time dilation and lost time relative to ground clocks; westward clocks moved slowest and gained time.

questions.question: A Ferris wheel car covers an arc distance of 62.8 metres in 2 minutes. If the radius of the Ferris wheel is 10 metres, what is the angular velocity in degrees per second?
questions.answer: $\theta = \dfrac{s}{r} = \dfrac{62.8}{10} = 6.28$ rad $= 360^\circ$, in 120 s. $\omega = \dfrac{360^\circ}{120\ \text{s}} = 3.00^\circ\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

questions.question:
The apparatus shown below was set up to measure the force between two parallel current-carrying conductors 1.5 cm apart, each carrying a current of 12 A. Before the current was turned on, the scale was zeroed; with the current on, the scale reads 0.042 g.

Determine the length $L$ of the two current-carrying conductors shown in the image above.

A car of mass 1200 kg is driving in a horizontal circular track of radius 50 metres with a constant speed of 20 m s$^{-1}$. If the coefficient of friction between the car's tyres and the track is 0.1, what is the work done by friction over one complete revolution?
questions.answer: Friction provides the centripetal force, which always acts towards the centre, perpendicular to the velocity. A force perpendicular to the displacement does no work ($W = Fs\cos 90^\circ = 0$); consistent with this, the speed and kinetic energy are constant.

questions.question: If the value of Planck's constant, $h$, was higher than it is, the effect on a photoelectric effect experiment would be:
options: the photoelectric current would be greater.
the energy of incident photons would be less.
the threshold frequency would be greater for all metals.
the threshold frequency would be lower for all metals.
questions.answer: Threshold frequency $f_0 = \dfrac{\phi}{h}$. For the same work function, a larger $h$ gives a smaller $f_0$ for every metal. (Photon energy $hf$ would be larger, not smaller.)

questions.question: How long does it take to emit one million photons from a 10 mW laser with frequency $4.5 \times 10^{14}$ Hz?

A ring of area $A$ is hung by a fishing line so that it sits within a uniform magnetic field $B$ directed into the page, as shown below (the plane of the ring is perpendicular to the field).

Determine the change in flux when the ring spins from its position by $120^\circ$.
questions.answer: $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$. Initially $\theta = 0$: $\Phi_i = BA$. After $120^\circ$: $\Phi_f = BA\cos120^\circ = -\tfrac12 BA$. $\Delta\Phi = -\tfrac12 BA - BA = -\tfrac32 BA$.

questions.question:
The following experimental set-up can be used to produce a 'Poisson Spot': a bright spot that can be seen in the centre of a circular object's shadow.

Which of the following would increase the size of the Poisson Spot?
options: Moving the light source closer to the circular object
Moving the circular object closer to the screen
Increasing the wavelength of the light source
Increasing the diameter of the circular object
questions.answer: The Poisson spot is produced by diffraction of light around the edge of the object and constructive interference at the centre of the shadow. The amount of diffraction (and so the size of the spot) increases with wavelength.

questions.question: A current-carrying conductor of length 1.5 m is placed in a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.5 T. Determine the magnitude of the magnetic force experienced by the current-carrying conductor if the current through the conductor is 0.6 A and the current flows perpendicular to the magnetic field.
questions.answer: $F = lIB\sin\theta = 1.5 \times 0.6 \times 0.5 \times \sin 90^\circ = 0.45$ N

questions.question: Describe how spectra provide information about TWO features of stars.
questions.answer:
Stellar spectra are absorption spectra: a continuous spectrum crossed by dark lines where gases in the star's outer layers absorb particular wavelengths.

- **Chemical composition:** each element absorbs at its own characteristic set of wavelengths, so matching the dark lines in a star's spectrum with laboratory spectra of elements identifies the elements present in the star's atmosphere.
- **Translational (radial) velocity:** if the absorption lines are shifted towards longer wavelengths (lower frequency, red shift) compared with laboratory values, the star is moving away from the observer; a blue shift means it is approaching. The size of the shift gives the speed.

Other acceptable features: surface temperature (peak wavelength of the continuous spectrum, Wien's law, and which lines are present); density (broad, wide lines indicate dense stars with high-pressure atmospheres, narrow lines less dense giants); rotational velocity (light from one edge is red-shifted and the other blue-shifted, broadening the lines).

questions.question:
Following a lesson on Special Relativity, a student made the following statement:

> “The surface of the Earth is not an inertial frame of reference”

Assess the validity of this statement.
questions.answer:
An inertial frame of reference is one that is not accelerating (moving at constant velocity), in which Newton's first law holds. A point on the surface of the Earth moves in a circle as the Earth rotates on its axis, and the Earth also orbits the Sun, so the surface is continually changing direction — it has a centripetal acceleration. Therefore the surface of the Earth is strictly a non-inertial frame, and the statement is valid.

(For many everyday experiments these accelerations are very small, so the Earth's surface is often *approximated* as an inertial frame — but strictly the statement is correct.)

questions.question:
On 4 May 1989, the objective of the Magellan mission to Venus was to place a satellite in orbit to image the entire surface of the planet.

Mass of Venus $= 4.867 \times 10^{24}$ kg; mass of satellite $= 3445$ kg; orbital radius $= 6.346 \times 10^{6}$ m.

Determine the orbital period of the satellite around Venus. Assume a circular orbit.
questions.answer:
$$\frac{r^3}{T^2} = \frac{GM}{4\pi^2} \Rightarrow T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2 r^3}{GM} = \frac{4\pi^2(6.346\times10^{6})^3}{6.67\times10^{-11}\times4.867\times10^{24}} = 3.108\times10^{7}$$

$T = 5.57\times10^{3}$ s (about 92.9 minutes).

questions.question:
On 4 May 1989, the objective of the Magellan mission to Venus was to place a satellite in orbit to image the entire surface of the planet.

Mass of Venus $= 4.867 \times 10^{24}$ kg; mass of satellite $= 3445$ kg; orbital radius $= 6.346 \times 10^{6}$ m.

How much additional work would need to be done for the satellite to escape the planet, Venus? Use relevant equations and calculations to support your answer.
questions.answer:
For a satellite to escape to infinity its total mechanical energy must be raised to (at least) zero.

In a circular orbit, $K = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ and $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$, so the total energy is

$$E = U + K = -\frac{GMm}{2r} = -\frac{6.67\times10^{-11}\times4.867\times10^{24}\times3445}{2\times6.346\times10^{6}} = -8.81\times10^{10}\ \text{J}$$

The additional work required (e.g. by rocket boosters) is $8.81\times10^{10}$ J, increasing the total energy from $-8.81\times10^{10}$ J to zero.

(Note: the paper's sample answer writes $8.81\times10^{13}$ J in its final sentence; its own working gives $8.81\times10^{10}$ J, which is correct.)

questions.question:
A space organisation is planning to send an astronaut to a distant planet, $P$. The spacecraft will travel at a speed of $0.8c$ and the journey is expected to take 15 years, as measured by observers on Earth. The spacecraft and astronaut have a combined mass of 1500 kg.

Calculate the distance to $P$, as measured by observers on Earth.
questions.answer:
$d = vt = 0.8c \times 15\ \text{years} = 12$ light-years.

$d = 0.8 \times 3\times10^{8} \times (15 \times 365 \times 24 \times 60 \times 60) = 1.14\times10^{17}$ m

questions.question:
A space organisation is planning to send an astronaut to a distant planet, $P$. The spacecraft will travel at a speed of $0.8c$ and the journey is expected to take 15 years, as measured by observers on Earth. The spacecraft and astronaut have a combined mass of 1500 kg.

Determine how many years will have passed on the spaceship's clock when observed by Earth.
questions.answer:
The spaceship's clock records the proper time $t_0$; Earth observers measure the dilated time $t = 15$ years.

$$t = \frac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}} \Rightarrow t_0 = t\sqrt{1-0.8^2} = 15\times0.6 = 9\ \text{years}$$

questions.question:
The diagram below shows a simplified power distribution network.

Explain why transformers are used in the distribution of energy.
questions.answer: Transformers change the voltage of the AC supply. The power lost as heat in the transmission lines is $P_{\text{loss}} = I^2R$. At the power station a step-up transformer increases the voltage to a very high value; since the power transmitted $P = VI$ is (ideally) unchanged, the current is reduced by the same factor, so the $I^2R$ energy loss in the long transmission lines is greatly reduced and power can be transmitted efficiently over long distances. At the consumer end a step-down transformer reduces the voltage to a safe, usable level (e.g. 240 V for homes).

questions.question:
Before an experiment to find the half-life of a radioactive isotope, a nuclear scientist switched on her radiation counter in the lab for five 60-second intervals and recorded the following background readings (counts/min): 1123, 1126, 1128, 1127, 1121.

The scientist then placed a sample of radioactive isotope $X$ near the counter and measured the counts per minute every second Monday for 14 weeks. Counting the first week as week 0, her results are shown in the table below.

| Time (weeks) | Total radiation recorded (counts/min) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 11125 |
| 2 | 7725 |
| 4 | 5525 |
| 6 | 4125 |
| 8 | 3125 |
| 10 | 2425 |
| 12 | 2075 |
| 14 | 1625 |

Draw a graph to show the relationship between time and the radiation of $X$.
questions.answer:
First subtract the background count. Mean background $= \dfrac{1123+1126+1128+1127+1121}{5} = 1125$ counts/min.

| Time (weeks) | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 14 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Corrected count rate (counts/min) | 10000 | 6600 | 4400 | 3000 | 2000 | 1300 | 950 | 500 |

Plot corrected count rate (vertical axis) against time in weeks (horizontal axis), with labelled axes and units and uniform scales, and draw a smooth exponential-decay curve of best fit through the points (not a dot-to-dot line).

questions.question:
Before an experiment to find the half-life of a radioactive isotope, a nuclear scientist switched on her radiation counter in the lab for five 60-second intervals and recorded the following background readings (counts/min): 1123, 1126, 1128, 1127, 1121.

The scientist then placed a sample of radioactive isotope $X$ near the counter and measured the counts per minute every second Monday for 14 weeks. Counting the first week as week 0, her results are shown in the table below.

| Time (weeks) | Total radiation recorded (counts/min) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 11125 |
| 2 | 7725 |
| 4 | 5525 |
| 6 | 4125 |
| 8 | 3125 |
| 10 | 2425 |
| 12 | 2075 |
| 14 | 1625 |

After subtracting the background radiation, the count rates are plotted against time and a curve of best fit drawn. Use the graph to show that the half-life of $X$ is approximately 3.4 weeks.
questions.answer: The corrected initial count rate is $11125 - 1125 = 10000$ counts/min. Half of this is 5000 counts/min. Reading across from 5000 counts/min to the curve of best fit and down to the time axis gives $t \approx 3.4$ weeks (between the week 2 value of 6600 and the week 4 value of 4400). So $t_{1/2} \approx 3.4$ weeks.

questions.question:
Before an experiment to find the half-life of a radioactive isotope, a nuclear scientist switched on her radiation counter in the lab for five 60-second intervals and recorded the following background readings (counts/min): 1123, 1126, 1128, 1127, 1121.

The scientist then placed a sample of radioactive isotope $X$ near the counter and measured the counts per minute every second Monday for 14 weeks. Counting the first week as week 0, her results are shown in the table below.

| Time (weeks) | Total radiation recorded (counts/min) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 11125 |
| 2 | 7725 |
| 4 | 5525 |
| 6 | 4125 |
| 8 | 3125 |
| 10 | 2425 |
| 12 | 2075 |
| 14 | 1625 |

Given that the half-life of $X$ is approximately 3.4 weeks, calculate the decay constant.
questions.answer:
$$\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}} = \frac{0.693}{3.4} = 0.20\ \text{week}^{-1}$$

(Note: the paper's marking guidelines give $\ln 2/3 = 0.23\ \text{week}^{-1}$, which uses a half-life of 3 weeks; with the 3.4-week half-life the decay constant is $0.20\ \text{week}^{-1}$. Answers consistent with the student's own half-life were accepted.)

questions.question:
A uniform magnetic field of strength 0.5 T is directed into the page. An electron and a proton are both fired simultaneously into the magnetic field at $1 \times 10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$: the proton enters from the left moving to the right, and the electron enters from the right moving to the left, as shown. Assume the particles do not interact with each other.

Describe the paths that the particles will follow through the magnetic field. Support your answer with relevant calculations.
questions.answer:
Each particle experiences a magnetic force $F = qvB$ perpendicular to its velocity, so each moves in a circular arc (uniform circular motion) with $qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, i.e. $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.

Electron: $r = \dfrac{9.109\times10^{-31}\times1\times10^{4}}{1.602\times10^{-19}\times0.5} = 1.1\times10^{-7}$ m

Proton: $r = \dfrac{1.673\times10^{-27}\times1\times10^{4}}{1.602\times10^{-19}\times0.5} = 2.1\times10^{-4}$ m

Direction (right-hand rule): the proton (moving right) is pushed towards the top of the page and curves anticlockwise; the electron (moving left, negative charge) is also pushed towards the top of the page and curves clockwise. Both therefore curve upwards initially, in opposite rotational senses. Because the proton's mass is about 1840 times greater, its circular path has a radius about 1840 times larger than the electron's very tight circle.

questions.question:
Below is a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram with two labelled stars, X and Y. The reaction that produces energy in Star X can be summarised as

$$4\,{}^{1}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} + 2\,{}^{0}_{+1}\text{e}$$

| Nucleus | Mass (amu) |
|---|---|
| ${}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ | 4.002603 |
| ${}^{1}_{1}\text{H}$ | 1.007825 |
| ${}^{0}_{+1}\text{e}$ | 0.000549 |

Calculate the energy released from this reaction.
questions.answer:
Mass defect: $\Delta m = 4(1.007825) - 4.002603 - 2(0.000549) = 0.027599$ u

$\Delta m = 0.027599 \times 1.661\times10^{-27} = 4.584\times10^{-29}$ kg

$E = \Delta m c^2 = 4.584\times10^{-29}\times(3\times10^{8})^2 = 4.13\times10^{-12}$ J (about 25.7 MeV, since $0.027599 \times 931.5 = 25.7$ MeV).

(Note: the original paper wrote the emitted particles as ${}^{0}_{-1}\text{e}$; charge conservation requires positrons, ${}^{0}_{+1}\text{e}$, as above. The calculation is unchanged.)

questions.question:
Below is a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram with two labelled stars, X and Y. The reaction that produces energy in Star X can be summarised as

$$4\,{}^{1}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} + 2\,{}^{0}_{+1}\text{e}$$

| Nucleus | Mass (amu) |
|---|---|
| ${}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ | 4.002603 |
| ${}^{1}_{1}\text{H}$ | 1.007825 |
| ${}^{0}_{+1}\text{e}$ | 0.000549 |

Compare the energy production in Star Y to Star X.
questions.answer:
Similarity: both X and Y lie on the main sequence, so both produce energy by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores.

Differences: Star Y is a hot, high-mass main sequence star (about 20 000 K, luminosity about $10^{2}$–$10^{3}$ times the Sun), whereas X is a cool, low-mass red dwarf (about 3000 K, luminosity about $10^{-4}$ of the Sun). Y's higher core temperature and pressure mean it fuses hydrogen at a far greater rate (much higher energy output/luminosity), and it produces most of its energy by the CNO cycle, while X produces energy mainly by the proton–proton chain. As a result Y will use up its core hydrogen and leave the main sequence much sooner than X.

questions.question:
A student performed an experiment to investigate the light emitted from discharge tubes containing various gases. The student's observations are shown: hydrogen glows pink, neon glows red and argon glows violet.

Explain why the gases emit different colours inside the discharge tubes.
questions.answer:
A high potential difference between the metal electrodes causes a current to pass through the low-pressure gas. Collisions transfer energy to electrons in the gas atoms, exciting them from the ground state to higher energy levels. When an excited electron returns to a lower energy level, the energy difference is emitted as a photon with $E = hf = E_{\text{upper}} - E_{\text{lower}}$.

Each element has its own unique set of electron energy levels, so the allowed transitions — and therefore the frequencies (wavelengths) of the emitted light — are different for each gas. The combination of emitted wavelengths gives each gas its characteristic colour.

questions.question:
A student performed an experiment to investigate the light emitted from discharge tubes containing various gases. The student's observations are shown: hydrogen glows pink, neon glows red and argon glows violet.

The spectra of light from the discharge tubes are examined through a spectroscope. How will these spectra differ from those produced by an incandescent filament?
questions.answer: The discharge tubes produce emission (line) spectra: a discontinuous spectrum of a few bright coloured lines at specific wavelengths, characteristic of each gas, on a dark background. An incandescent filament is a hot solid that emits a continuous (black body) spectrum containing all visible wavelengths, with no gaps.

questions.question:
A physics student, who is also a model train enthusiast, is combining their two interests to undertake a study in electromagnetic induction. They rig up one of their trains with a strong bar magnet on its load carriage and have its track pass through a solenoid. The solenoid is attached to a galvanometer to measure the induced current.
